articles.title: SOCIAL CHAR NCTERISTICS OF LONDON LIFE.
articles.text:
SOCIAL CHAR NCTERISTICS OF
LONDON LIFE.

BY ‘, SCOURGE."

No. I.—TILE "MUSIC-HALLS."

The London Music Halls,after having rapidly
become one of the "social characteristics" of the
metropolis, are as rapidly degenerating into
one of its "social evils," arising not only from
their increasing numbers, but from the manner
in which they are generally conducted. This
may be thought at first reading a harsh and
undeserved condemnation, but its truth will
become apparent upon examination.
When Mr. Morton, the present proprietor of
the Oxford, and the originator of these music
halls, first opened the Canterbury Hall in the
Upper Marsh, Lambeth, some dozen years
since, the public were gratified and surprised
at the vast improvements he had effected over
the old "free and easies," and "cock and hen
clubs," until then patronised by the working
lasses; and the press spoke unanimously and
deservedly in favourable terms of his under-
taking. Mr. Morton, though he opened the
Canterbury as a commercial speculation, at the
same time combined with it a sincere desire to
improve the musical taste of the masses. With
this, view he surrounded himself with A: staff of
male and female vocalists, who, if not pre-
eminent in their profession, were all possessed
of respectable talent; were good musicians,
with good voices; and were capable of rendering
the glees and catches of Bishop, or the songs
and ballads of Dibdin, Russell, Balfe, &c.,
which formed the staple of the entertainment,
in a pleasing and effective manner. The lighter
or comic business was confided to a gentleman
of experience and education (Mr. Sam. Cowell),
possessed of a large fund of genuine comic
humour, who had earned considerable popularity
as a low comedian on the :legitimate stage, and
who fully sustained his reputation at the
*"
Canterbury." In this satisfactpry manner
Mr. Morton for two or three years carried on
his establishment, ever on the alert to place
before his patrons musical novelties of a
character suited to it. -Under this good manage-
ment the "Canterbury" soon gained a name;
its fame spread far and wide, and it became
the nightly resort of those why, at the end of
their day's labour, wishektepass a pleasant
hour of recreation in listening to some healthy
songs tolerably well sung. The success of this
establishment called up a host of competitors
amongst the proprietors of public houses of
large dimensions but small respectability, and
among scheming speculators, but unfortunately
competition did not improve the quality of the
article. Money was the main object with the
new competitors, and the elevation of the taste
of the people was either entirely overlooked,
or thought of only as a secondary consideration.
The love of musical art was unknown to or
unthought of by them. .The result was not
surprising. Instead of producing an enter-
tainment by which the tastes of their visitors
-could be improved, they lowered the standard
of the entertainment to suit the previous habits
of their patrons, and as the "halls" increased
in number, the proprietors, to retain their
patrons, and "drawl' an audience, vied with
one another in producing" sensation novelties,"
no matter how absurd or out of place in a
"music hall," so long as it brought "grist to
the mill" or "money to the till." Even the
"Canterbury" itself was compelled in some
degree to succumb to the rage thus created for
"sensation," and its proprietor was con-
strained either to close his establishment, or
follow in this" sensation movement," although
it has never descended so low as most of the
so-called "music halls," where the chief attrac-
tions are acrobats, gorillas," juggling, "tub
running," bad nigger singing," the 'Cure' sung
by a man standing on his head," and a class of
songs, and style of singing, that would hardly
have been tolerated in the old "free and easy"
of the public-house, but is hailed with delight
in the well-lighted, gaudily-decorated, and
spacious "music hall."

That these " halls " have become a great
"social evil" must be patent to all who have
taken a glance at their interiors; and there is
no exception from the " university " hall of the
West End to the "sailor's delight" in the East.
The class of entertainments provided in them,
and the nature of the scenes nightly enacted in
the drinking bars, stalls, and saloons, with
which these " halls " are now supplied, are
identical. As regards the entertainments,
there is generally, to keep up appearances, one
really good selection of music sung from some
popular opera, with more or less talent, but the
rest is made up of hacknied songs by second
and third-rate vocalists, " comic " singing by
men and women destitute of one spark of genu-
ine humour, for which deficiency they make
up by slang, obscenity, and buffoonery; nigger
"melodies" by minstrels who have sung them-
selves hoarse by their exertions in the streets
during the day, and by the " sensation " feats
of the acrobat and trapezist—the latter clever
enough in their way, but suited only to open-
air amusements, or gardens, such as Cremorne
or Highbury, and totally out of place in a
"music hall." One, however, of the most ob-
jectionable features in the entertainments, and
which has done much to bring music halls into
disrepute, has been the introduction of" female
comic singing." None of these halls now con-
sider their company complete without one or
more "Comic," or " serio-comic "—the new
name for fast and :slangy dialogue—ladies.
These "comic ladies" are mostly devoid of any
real talent or humour, and are generally third
or fourth-rate actresses,, who have failed on
the regular stage as "singing chambermaids,"
and whose only attraction lies in their fine dress,
a liberal display of their legs, suggestive atti-
tudes, the utterance Cif double entendres, slang
and sentiment unwomanly and unnatural, and
a boisterous vulgarity and brazen impudence,
which; though it niay excite the laughter and
admiration of the fast clerk, or the unthinking
apprentice, causes the reflecting and judicious
run to grieve to see women place i in so equi-
Vocal a position for a few shillings per night.
.knother objectionable feature is the sense-
less encore system now pursued in these halls,
and encouraged by the proprietors, as by com-
pelling the singers to appear tWo or three times
in succession, they save expense by keeping
the number of their company at the minimum.
Formerly, an
encore was only given as a mark
of satisfaction by the audience at the extra
'e xertion, or superior, talent of the person so
honoured, and was accepted by him as a just
tion of his se •
recogni rvices, but now, it is the
invariable custom to encore every song, save
only the good musical selections; no matter
how rubbishina the song, or wretched the style
of the singer, the encore follows as a matter of
course; and 'the gin-and-water voice of the
conductor may be heard exclaiming,
will oblige again," In the ease of comic singers,
this system is carried so far that three encores
is the rule. This 'absurd practice takes away
all emulation from the singer, and disgusts
the great majority of the audience, being indul-
ged in chiefly by boy and youths, "out for a
lark," and who, by their noise and clamour,

No. 54.

drown the remonstrant hiss of the more
rational listeners. _ .

So much for the entertainments; in them-
selves quite a sufficient condemnation of the
claim put forward by the proprietors of these
"halls" to be considered instrumental in "im-
proving the musical taste of the masses."
It is, however, in the scenes Enacted in the
drinking bars, saloons, and stalls, attached to
these "halls," that the greatest evils exist—
evils which exercise a fatal influence upon the
frequenters of these places, of both sexes, who,
in the first instance, "go to hear a song," but
become initiated in .vice and immorality, ren-
dered more easy and dangerous by the seduc-
tive influences with which they are surrounded.
The more "respectable" the "hail" the more
prominent is this feature. These bars, saloons,
and stalls, are filled by men about town" of
all ages and conditions, with and without cha-
racters; there may be seen the young and in-
experienced clerk, the beardless apprentice, the
heartless skittle sharp and blackleg, the patri-
cian roue, and the plebeian "fancy man ;" and
there also may be seen, and heard too, the real
"social evil," the members of the "frail
sisterhood," some decked out in gaudy trap-
pings and finery, others in plain garb, assu-
ming a virtue if they have it not," but all intent
on one thing—the taking in of any "young
man from the country" who may fall in their
way. This mixed crowd of folly and vice keep
up a continued chattering of obscene jests
and vulgar repartees, to the great annoyance
of the decent tradesman or working man, who,
accompanied by his wife or sweetheart, may
have visited the "hail" in the delusive hope
of hearing some good singing, but whose ears
are thus polluted with vulgarity and slang.
It is this sort of thing that is driving the re-
spectable portion of society from these "halls,"
and it is to provide attraction for the more
"spicy" patrons that "comic ladies' and other
"sensation performances" have been introduced.
In these saloons the scenes that used to be
enacted in the lobbies and saloons of the thea-
tres are reproduced even in a worse and more
offensive form.

What is the difference between the saloons
of these music halls and the saloons at "Kate
Hamilton's" in Leicester-square, or the" Pic-
cadilly Saloon," except in the hour of the night
at which they are open? The class of fre-
quenters and the proceedings are the same.
The music halls close at twelve, the Haymarket
saloons open about that hour. It would appear
that what is vicious, and obscene, and immoral,
in the Haymarket saloons between twelve and
lot% in the morning, is harmless and innocent
between nine and twelve at night in the saloon
of the "music hall."

There is no doubt but that such respectable
proprietors as Messrs. Morton, of the Oxford,
Stanley, of the Canterbury, and Weston, of the
Holborn, would gladly reform the present
system, but for the fierce competition existing.
Let the system with which the " Canterbury "
was inaugurated be acted upon, with all neces-
sary and desirable improvements, and nothing
' more could be required. Let the present
system continue, and "music halls" will, like
the "penny gaffs," become a public nuisance,
and be treated accordingly.

DEATH or SIR BENJAMIN BRODIE. - This eminent
surgeon died on Wednesday. He was in his 80th
year.
ADMISSION OF THE PUBLIC TO VIEW THE HOUSE OF
LORDS.—Yesterday morning, by command of Lord
Willoughby D'Eresby, the Lord Great Chamberlain,
notice was issued that, after Saturday, the Ist of No-
vember, the public would only be admitted to view the
House of Lords on the Saturday in each week between
the hours of ten and four.
AFFAIRS IN NEW ORLEANS.—Adviees from New
Orleans report the arrest of Mr. J. G. Lingham, a
British subject, by General Butler, and his incarceration
for three years in Fort Pickens, for being one of the
directors of the Merchants' Bank, which, it is alleged,
made some over issues. The abolishing of habeas corpus
leaves Mr. Lingham without a chance of being favour-
ably heard, and the particulars have been sent to his
relations in London for representation to the Govern-
ment, who have, with becoming promptitude, sent. out
instructions to the Embassy at Washington. Until
lately Mr. Lingham acted as Vice-Consul in New Or-
leans, and was partner in the 'firm of W. H. Haynes
and Co. there. His brother, the Rector of Lambeth,
arrived in this town on Friday, and has been most
assiduous in concerting measures for his brother's
release.—Liverpool
POISONING BY STRYCHNINE.—An inquest was held
at the Cross Keys, Balsall-street, on Saturday, before
De. Biet Davies, borough coroner, on the body of
Edwin Bates, a Britannia-metal smith, residing at
No. 2 Court, Cheapside. From the evidence of
deceased's widow it appears that he was found dead
in bed on Thursday morning last. His wife had got
up at six o'clock to attend to her household duties, and
she took him a cap of tea at eight. He told her to
put it on the table and he would drink it by and by.
She did so, and went downstairs. In the course of
about twenty minutes or half an hour, she heard
deceased vomiting, but as he was frequently in the
habit of doing so in a morning she took no notice of
the circumstance. Shortly afterwards, however, she
went upstairs and found deceased dead in bed. She
immediately called in the assistance of some neigh-
bours. They found two papers near him—one of
them labelled 'Hunter's Infallible Vermin Destroyer;'
and the other, which also bore the name of
'Hunter,' was marked Poison.' The tea was
gone; but in the saucer which was standing
on a table near the bed, there were traces of
a blue mixture, similar in colour to the remains of the
powder found in the papers. He also took some stuff
, of the same sort on the day previous to Good Friday,
1861.; but he afterwards told her that he had done so,
and she gave him an emetic, which caused him to
• eject it from his stomach. During the past five weeks,
she said he had been like a person derauged. He had
pledged his clothes, and everything he could lay hold
of, for drink. Mr. Porter, surgeon, stated that he had
• made a post-mortem examination of the body of the
deceased, and he was of opinion that he died from
• asphyxia, produced by strychnine. The coroner hav-
ing summed, up, the jury returned a verdict to the
6 effect that Deceased poisoned himself while in a state
, of temporary intapity, produced by hard, drinking,'

articles.title: LONDON, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1862.
articles.text:
LONDON, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1862.

THE WAR

Mn.• WESTERN WOOD, M.P., ON AMERICAN
AFFAIRS.—Mr. Western Wood, one of the members
for the City of London, presided on Tuesday at the
annual dinner of the West Kent Agricultural Society ,
at Bromley, and, in addressing the conipany, made the
following allusions to the fratricidal war in America:
—There was one subject so intimately connected with
the interests of those present that he could scarcely
avoid referring to it; that was the horrible war in
America, which was causing so much distress in one
part ot our own country, The suffering people were
entitled not only to our sympathy but to a helping
hand, and their conduct had shown us most clearly
one of the finest examples of the blessings of education.
The workmen in the North knew the causes of
their distress, otherwise we should not have seen them
so quietly and peaceably submitting to their lot.
They knew that it was inevitable. They • knew
that it was no fault of the Government or •of
their employers, and they submitted to the calamity in
a manner which did them the greatest honour.
With regard to the war itself, nothing more
horrible had ever taken place in this world. It was a
struggle between brothers, between men speaking the
same language; and the accounts which reached us
were most frightful. There appeared at present to be
no prospect of an end to the struggle, which seemed to
be as far from a settlement as it was at the commence-
ment. Our sympathies, to a great extent, went with
one side; but with the quarrel itself we bad nothing
to do. He hoped, for the sake of the honour and glory
of this country, that her Majesty's Government wou.d
persevere in that course which they had laid down and
so religiously followed, and which had received the
approbation of the country at large, and that they
would continue to observe a strict neutrality between
the contending parties. We had nothing to do with
their quarrels, and could only offer oar sincere and
earnest prayers that it would please God to point out
to the belligerents the enormity of
,the offence they
were committing, and induce them to consent to a
peace which would restore not only prosperity to
themselves but to a most important portion of our
country.
Mn. DIFNLOP ON THE WAR IN AMERICA.—Mr, Dun-
lop, M.P., addressed his constituents on Monday
night, in the New Town Hall, Greenock. The hon.
gentleman, in a speech of great length, reviewed the
past session, and concluded by some reference to Con-
tinental affairs and the war in America. Respecting
the latter topic, the hon. gentleman said---' As regards
the civil war in America, I retain the opinions I
expressed last year. I then said that I considered
the Southerners were utterly unjustifiable in their
secession, but that] the prudent course for the
Northerners would have been to have said, 'lf you
will break up the Union and leave us, we will not try
'to keep you by force; let us part on friendly terms,
and in a brotherly spirit.' The events which have
since occurred show how much wiser such a course
would have been than the internecine war, accom-
panied with such a fearful sacrifice of life and means,
which is still so ruthlessly carried on, and with so
little prospect of being brought to a close. One
thing, I think, is clear—namely, that the South is
much more sealously in earnest in seeking to estab-
lish its independence than the North to maintain
the Union, otherwise it is impossible hat that the
North, with its larger population and more extensive
resources, must I.y this time have achieved a much
more decided advantage over its opponents. This leads
me to expect an ultimately successful issue for the
South. But I cordially approve of the policy of
neutrality so steadily pursued by our Government
hitherto, and apparently so little appreciated by the
men of the North, whose perverse injustice to us in
judging of our feelings and conduct in reference to
them, has very greatly alienated our sympathy with
them, and even created a feeling in favour of a recog-
nition of the Southern States, which would doubtless
greatly promote the interests of this country. I have
still, however, the most intense repugnance to our
recognising a State, the corner-stone of which is the
perpetual maintenance of slavery. I trust that if we
do consent to recognise the Southern Confederacy it
will only be on this condition, that they utterly
abandon the slave trade, and adopt the principle of
gradual emancipation and the ultimate abolition of
slavery. If such a result as that could be purchased
by the recognition, I would, notwithstanding all my
Northern predilections, gladly hail it as a blessing to
mankind.'

articles.title: BRITISH. EMPIRE MUTUAL LIFE ASSVRA_ZVCE COMPANY.
articles.text:
THE BRITISH. EMPIRE MUTUAL
LIFE ASSVRA_ZVCE COMPANY.

The directors of this company met their London
agents on Tuesday, Oct. 14th, at Radley's Hotel, Black-
friars. Mr. John Gover, the chairman, who presided,
explained that the object of the meeting was the pro-
motion of the business of the Company during the re-
mainder of the year.
Mr. W. H. Watson wished to say a few words re-
lative to the progress of the company. In 1851 the
income was £21,000; in 1854, £36,000; in 1857,
£53,000; in 1861, £68,000. No argument could equal
such a demonstration as that of constant progress.
The chairman had adverted to the fact that every life
assurance company must have a certain accumulation.
Actuaries were by no means agreed what the amount ,
should be, and their estimates ranged from one-third
to one-half. All agreed that if you have 50 per cent.
of the premiums, then you are not only safe, but in a
condition of great prosperity in that respect. This
company had not simply one-third, or even one-half,
but nearly 60 per cent, of the money deposited in their
hands accumulated ready to meet any claims that might
arise. In 1851 the accumulated fund was £26,000; in
1854, £70,000; in 1857, £124,000; and in 1861, £228,000.
Let the fact never be lost sight of, that this £228,000
was not other people's money on which interest had to
be paid, but their own, and was being employed for
their own benefit. So that, in truth, all persons who
became insured in the Company were made partners
in a good business, carried on with an ample capital.
' Mr, Saul, the Secretary, called attention to the
character of the work in which the agents were
engaged. When you persuaded a man to assure, you
made him more thoughtful, and the blessings you
conferred on his family were incalculable. If a man
devoted £150,000 to the purposes of charity, it was
thought a great thing, and so it was, but when doled
out it came in the form of charity; a like amount,
however, distributed through the medium of an insti-
tution like this, came without any humiliating draw.
backs. When he sometimes tried to realise in his
mind all the advantages, direct and indirect, that
would flow from the £1,900,000 already assured in
this office, he was lost in a maze. No actuary could
compute the good that the Company had done and
was destined to do.
The proceedings terminated with a vote of thanks
to the Chairman.

articles.title: TRADES' GARIBALDIAN DEMONSTRATION COMMITTEE.
articles.text:
TRADES' GARIBALDIAN DEMON-
STRATION COMMITTEE.

An influentially attended meeting of the officers and
members of trade societies assembled at the BEEHIVE
office, 2, Bouverie-street, Fleet-street, on Wednesday
evening last, pursuant to an invitation which appeared
in the columns of this paper on Saturday last, for the
purpese of considering the desirability of the trades
taking part in an intended public demonstration of
welcome to General Garibaldi on his expected visit to
this country. The persons assembled were all mem-
bers of trades societies, but, with one or two excep-
tions, attended only on their own responsibility, and
their presence at the meeting did not pledge their trade
to any future action. A deputation from the London
Trades' Council attended, and officers and members
of the following trades were present :—Stonemasons,
City Ladies' Shoemakers, Wire Workers, Amalga-
mated Society of Carpenters, Friends Gf Freedom, do.;
Silver Cup, do.; Progressive do.; West End Boot
Closers' Amalgamated Society of Painters, Hand-in-
Hand, do.; Book-binders, Printers, West End Ladies'
Shoemakers, Bricklayers, Ropemakers, &c., &c.
Mr. Cremer (joiner), having been called to the
chair, said the meeting had been called to take counsel
together as trades unionists, as to the propriety •of
taking part in a public welcome to the great hero of
the day. They were not'met as directly representing
any society, but simply as society men to state what
they believed to be the feeling of their brethren, and
discuss the feasibility of the proposed suggestion by
the parties who had issued the, notice in the BEHRIVE
convening this meeting.
Mr. Hartwell said, on behalf of himself and one or
two friends, he had taken the responsibility of calling
this meeting. He had seen a private letter from
General Garibaldi in which he had expressed his
intention of visiting this country to thank his friends
personally for their sympathy in his behalf, and their
support of the cause in which he was engaged. it was
intended to give this illustrious man a public welcome,
and it was thought desirable to ascertain the feeling of
trade societies as to their taking part in this welcome.
He had waited upon the trades' council, who had
warmly entered into the subject, and agreed to send a
deputation to the meeting. He was happy to see that
deputation present. The plan was not sufficiently
matured to state what shape the demonstration would
take, but that would not affect the question to be
decided, which was, did the meeting think that the
trades generally would fall in with the suggestion. He
thought by doing honour to Garibaldi—one of the
noblest men, living—they would also do much honour
to themselves. (Hear.)
Mr. Charles Murray (boot closer), said he would
answer for his society, that they go heart in hand with
the suggestion. To bring the matter fairly before the
meeting he begged to propose the following resolu-
tion :—"Phat this meeting, composed of officers and
members of various Metropolitan Trade Societies,
having been made acquainted with the intention of
General Garibaldi, as soon as the state of his health
will permit, of visiting England for the purpose of
thanking, in person, the English people for the sym-
pathy they have bestowed upon him, and the cause in
which he is engaged—the unity of Italy—and having
heard that it is intended to give the illustrious Italian
patriot a public welcome to London, hereby recom-
mend the Trades Societies and Friendly Societies of
the metrlpolis to take part in such public demon-
stration, in such manner as may hereafter be deter-
mined.' _ _

Mr. DaNis (painter) seconded the resolution, which
was supported by Mr. Odgers (shoemaker) ; Gray
(mason); Potter (joiner) ; Burgess (joiner) • Tremlett
(joiner); Thurnell (ropemaker), and others, all express-
ing their belief that their societies would readily fall
in with the proposal. The resolution was carried
unanimous] y.
Mr. Odgers (shoemaker), proposed the next resolu-
tion, as follows :—'That every Trade Society or Friendly
Society willing to co-operate in such a demonstration
of welcome to General Garibaldi, be requested to
appoint a delegate or delegates, to assist in carrying
out the object on behalf of their respective Societies;
and that in the meantime the persons present form
themselves into a Provisional Committee, with power
to add to their numbers, to act until the delegates are
appointed.'
Mr. Tremlett (joiner), seconded-the resolution, which
was supported by Mr. Smith, (ropemaker), Nelson,
(wire-worker), Castle, (shoemaker), and also agreed to.
Mr. Hartwell was elected to act as Honorary Secre-
tary to the Committee, with instructions to place him-
self in direct communication with General Garibaldi,
and Mr. George Potter was appointed to act as Trea-
surer, to receive any contributions that may be sent to
the Committee. _

A Sub-Committee, consisting of Messrs. Cremer,
Odgers, Gray, Tremlett, with the Treasurer and the
Hon. Secretary, were appointed to draw up an address to
the London Trade and Friendly Societies; and the
meeting then adjourned, until Tuesday, the 4th of
November.

The meeting was a most enthusiastic one, and it
was the general opinion that if the demonstration
took place, it would equal, if not exceed, that for the
Dorchester labourers in 1835, when 70,000 trades'
unionists marched in procession to the Home Office.
It is hoped that those societies who intend appoint-
ing delegates will lose no time in so doing, as the
provisional committee intend calling them together on
an early day. Any officer or member of a trade
society, willing to serve on the provisional committee
will be pleased to communicate with Mr. Hartwell,
Hon. Secretary, at the BEEHIVE Office, 2, Bouverie-
street, Fleet-street, in order that their names may be
appended to the Address to the Trades,' which will
appear in the BEEHIVE next week. All communica-
tions on the subject to be addressed as above.
The provisional committee will meet again at the
BEEHIVE Office on Tuesday evening, Nov. 4, at 8
o'clock, when none but members of trade societies will
be admitted.

An. ELECTRIC TELEGRAPH WITHOUT WIIIES.—A new
discovery has been made, says the Court Journal. A
telegraph without wires can pass through earth and sea,
and every one may establish his own. It is at present
a very great secret in scientific circles, adds our autho-
rity. It is evident that wonders will never cease. The
idea of an electric telegraph without wires, however,
though not yet fully realised, so far as we know, is not
so new as our authority appears to imagine. A Dundee
gentleman, lately deceased, actually laid (if we may so
speak) an electric telegraph across Portsmopth harbour,
without wires, and worked it too, by permission of the
Government. He also telegraphed across the Tay in the
same way. Although no wires crossed the river or the
harbour, however, a wire with earth plates at right
angles was requisite at either side. The. °bort Journal's
secret would seem to realise the old original idea of the
magical telegraph, which consisted simplY of two alpha-
bets set in circles with a pointer to each, but without
any connecting wires, and by mean% of which it was
said that two correspondents could in.idually communi-
cate their ideas, however far they might be separated
throughout the world, so long as each possessed his.

It was thought, naturally, that this traditional idea

. CeSSary appendage, which has only been preparing- the
way for the introductn of the old Orifiinal telegraph of
antiquity.—Zoilder..

articles.title: PRICE Two PENCE.
articles.text:
PRICE Two PENCE.

THE EAST LANC.ASHIRE CENTRAL
RELIEF CalinfITTEE.

The weekly meeting of the executive for the relief of
the distress in East Lancashire, was held on Monday
evening, at the Central Committee Rooms, Padiham.
The President, the Rev. E. A. Verity, 8.D., rector
of Habergham, occupied the chair, and there were
also present—Messrs. L. Shackleton, J. Pinder, G.
Robinson, James Denbigh, J. Howarth, J. Heap,
Wm. Wilkinson, G. Hargreaves, W. Hodgkinson,
&c. The minutes of the former meeting having been
confirmed, the Chairman announced the receipt of
£lO from the BEEHIVE in two remittances of £5 each,
and expressed a hope that the next number would
show an increased interest manifested towards the
distress in Lancashire, by many more subscriptions.
The Secretary, in his report, gave a favourable
account of the good feeling evinced by the operatives
of Liverpool, Leeds, Birmingham, and Huddersfield.
Also mentioned the kind proposal of the Miners'
Journal and Cassel's Family Paper,' to insert the
advertisements gratis and transmit collections.
Mr. Shackleton explained the extent of the distress
in Burnley, where, on Thursday, a lecture was to
be delivered on the subject, and subscriptions col-
lected the following week. He described the thank-
fulness of the distressed families in that town for
the gifts of fieur distributed by the committee.
Mr. James Denbigh thought it was not fair on the
part of the gentry and aristocracy to receive salaries
for officiating on relief committees, and was displeased
to see the eagerness which many of the upper classes
were displaying in collecting monies from working men
and poaching on working men's preserves. He hoped
the working classes would have more sense than to
send their subscriptions to any other than the Ope-
ratives Central.

The following resolutions were then passed.—
' That the Secretary put himself in communication
with the secretaries of all benefit and trade societies
throughout the United Kingdom, and invite such
societies to form relief committees, and to send their
weekly subscriptions either to the BEEHIVE or direct
to Rtdiham.'

Mr. Peacock thought that the Amalgamated Engi-
neers and other influential societies might make liberal
grants to the fund. He had written to them, but it
was too soon to expect a reply.
The accounts were then audited, and a balance
sheet ordered to be sent to the BEEHIVE for inser-
tion.

Mr. George Hargreave thought some gifts of clothing,
coal, &c., would be acceptable.
Mr. Wilkinson stated it as his opinion, judging from
the number of distressed applications from Padiham
alone, that it would require £5OO per week alone for
that town; the unemployed and destitute, he thought,
would reach 5,000 souls.
Mr. Shackleton felt convinced no adequate provision
was secured for Burnley, which required £2,000 weekly
to properly relieve them.
Other resolutions were passed, and the Executive
then proceeded to apportion the weekly grants for
Burnley, Habergham, and Padiham. Several other
towns wish to enter into the Central, but the funds are
too limited at present to admit them. The distress is
increasing in severity and extent every week.

articles.title: BOOKBINDARS' PROVIDENT ASYLUM SOCIETY.
articles.text:
BOOKBINDARS' PROVIDENT
ASYLUM SOCIETY.

The twenty-fourth anrual general meeting of the
members of this society was held Monday evening in
the theatre of the London Mechanics' Institution,
Chancery-lane, Mr. Franklin in the chair, for the trans-
action of the usual business. There was a good attend-
ance, and a number of the female subscribers were
present, and took much interest in the proceedings.
Mr. Jeffrey, the secretary, read the report, which
regretted tbs. apathy existing in the trade respecting
an institution which had conferred so many benefits
upon it. The asylum could not be finished owing to
want of funds, the subscriptions having materially
fallen off during the last few years, consequent upon
the death of so many of the older subscribers. The
report strongly recommended the formation of an en-
dowment fund, and urged upon the trade generally
the great necessity that existed for their coming
forward with more spirit and unanimity on behalf of
the Asylum Society. The revival and extension of the
auxiliaries was also recommended. The attention of
the trade was also called to an intended raffle by the
committee of a gold watch and for some Asylum
prints etill on hand. The financial statement showed
the total receipts for the year to be £251 Os. 2d., and
the expenditure £l5l 19s. 101, leaving a balance of
£99 Os. 4d.

The report having been received and adopted, after
some discussion, it was then agreed that the Pension
Supplement should take place as usual, in April, and
the watch raffle in September next, to avoid any clash-
ing between the two.
The consideration of the alterations was then ad-
journed to a meeting to be convened for that purpose
on the 10th of November.

_
In the previous part of the day an election of two
candidates took place into the asylum. The following
were the numbers polled :—Mr. Andrew Shaw, age 66,
1917; Mr. S unuel Hogg, age 60, 1349; Mr. John
Colville, ago 70, 873; and Mrs. Sarah Hodgson, age
56, 441. The two first were declared duly elected.

articles.title: 1-OTE BY BALLOT.
articles.text:
THE 1-OTE BY BALLOT.

The committee of the Society for Promoting the
Adoption of the Vote by Ballot has just issued the fol-
lowing address to the municipal electors of England
and Wales :

'Our annual municipal elections are about to take
place. The committee of the Ballot Society therefore
takes the opportunity of respectfully urging the muni-
cipal constituencies to select as candidates and return
as councillors gentlemen favourable to the adoption of
the vote by ballot, both at parliamentary and municipal
elections. The bribery and intimidation which dis-
grace our parliamentary elections extend also to our
municipal contests, and tend to foster habits of corrup-
tion amongst all classes of the community, and to
injure our representative institutions, by undermining
the foundation on which they are based—viz., the duty
and the right of freely and indifferently elect•
ing the men who will, in the voter's judg-
ment, be the best representative. If any can
be still unconvinced that the ballot would
be an effectual remedy for those evils, the committee
recommends attentive consideration of the evidence of
its working in those of our colonies in which with the
assent of the Queen and Government, secret voting has
been introduced amongst the institutions of the empire.
A bill to establish the ballot at municipal elections was
in the last session brought into the House of Commons
and read a first time. The motion for the second read-
ing was lost, owing partly to the bill not properly
securing the secrecy of the vote, and therefore not
commending itself to any energetic support on the part
of the friends of the ballot in or out of Parliament.
The committee feel, however, that this first step should
be followed up, and therefore earnestly and respect-
fully solicit the friends of the ballot to require, as one
of the qualifications of their town councellors, that
they will give all possible support to the pviposal for
establishing the vote by ballot at municipal elections;
which, if carried, would speedily be followed by its
adoption at parliamentary elections. The election of
friends of the ballot to the town councils would
materially aid in promoting the adoption of that only
effectual protection to the voter. Parliament can
scarcely refuse to yield the ballot to municipal con-
stituencies if the town councils demand it for their own
elections; and if the councils, which are the local par-
liaments of the constituencies, petition for its adoption
at parliamentary elections, a great moral force would.
be added to the movemeni in its favour. For these
reasons the committee of the Ballot Society urge their
fellow-countrymen to return to their town councils, at
the coining elections, friends of the vote by ballot.—
By order of the Committee,
F. HENRY F. BERKELEY, Chairman.
EDWARD C. WHITERURST, Vice Chairman.
J. F. BONTEMS, Hon. Secretary.
5, Guildhall-chambers, London, Oct. 22.

articles.title: HYDE PARK ON SUNDAY LAST.
articles.text:
HYDE PARK ON SUNDAY LAST.

The precautions taken on the 12th instant for the
preservation of the public peace in Hyde-park were
again adopted on Sunday last in their entirety. As on
the previous Sunday, military pickets were stationed
at all the entrances to the park to prevent the ingress
of any soldiers not on duty, military and police patrols
traversed the park in various directions, while in the
barracks attached to the powder magazine were placed
strong detachments of the Coldstream, Grenadier, and
Fusilier Guards, a company of the 3rd Buffs from tha
Tower, and a large body of mounted and foot police,
under the immediate command of Captain Harris, the
police commissioner. These precautions, formidable
as they appear, were not altogether unnecessary, inas-
much as during the week information had been con-
veyed to the authorities that it was intention of a large
body of working men, supported by parties in a higher
station, ID hold a meeting in the Park, on the sub-
ject of Sir R. Mayne's proclamation, with the view of
testing its legality, and that the leaders of Cardinal
Wiseman's dear Irish children,' emboldened by the
proceedings of their brethren at Birkanhead, had also
threatened to attend, and prevent such meeting being
held. The morning being tolerably fine, soon after
two o'clock some 5,000 people had assembled under and
around the clump of trees near to Grosvenor.-gate, two-
thirds of whom consisted of respectably-dressed arti-
sans and a fair sprinkling of persons in a higher
station of society, the other third comprising all the
, elements of mischief and disorder in the shape of that
class known as roughs.' Mingling with the crowd it
became evident from the conversation taking place in
the little knots in which they were assembled that
something was expected to take place. About three
o'clock a couple of thousand had been added to the
assemblage, and numbers of people were coming along
the various paths in the park leading to where the crowds
were standing. Fortunately, at this time, as on the pre-
vious Sunday, the rain, that powerful police auxiliary and
peace preserver, came down very heavily, not only
damping the ardour of those assembled but preventing
any large addition to their numbers. After waiting
about an hour, and the leaders of the expected meet-
ings, if any such had been intended, having failed to
put in an appearance, deterred either by the weather
or yielding to prudent advice, in the face of the for-
midable preparations made for their reception, the
more respectable portion of the crowd began to dis-
perse homewards. The rain still falling steadily,
without any prospect of its clearing off, by five o'clock
the people had nearly all left, and the park resumed
its usual quiet aspect. The military detachments and.
police, however, did not leave until after dusk.

articles.title: CATHERINE WILSON.
articles.text:
CATHERINE WILSON.

The following is a verbatim copy of a letter written
by this extraordinary woman since her condemna-
tion:—

"Gaol at Newgate, Oct. 6, 1662.
'Dear Uncle and Aunt,—With great pain I received
your letter, and with greater pain I sit down to answer
it; for it recalls to my mind past scenes too painful to
dwell upon.
'My dear Friends—All of you—l must decline your
very kind offer of visiting me. I could not bear an
interview; it would be too painful for us all. You
must think of me as you last saw me; that is best for
you to do. Twelve months ago, who coula have thought
of me being here. Six months to-day I have been in.
prison. How much better it was for me when I feared,
God, and thought of pleasing Him inure than man.
Although innocent of the dreadful crime with which I
am charged, I am a great sinner, and I have lived in
wickedness and sin. Though I could deceive the
world, I could not deceive the Almighty.. May He be-
more merciful to me than man has been, is my earnest
prayer. During my imprisonment I have received
many letters and seen many friends; one lady from
Boston has visited me, and written to me since my
condemnation, but I got a lady to answer it for me.
I felt that I would answer this to you myself, and I
dare say it is the last letter I shall write; at least, I think
I so. lam in ill health, and cannot bear much. Ido
not receive visits from any one now. I have this
morning seen my solicitor; he is a very kind gentle-
man; I have received great kindness from him and his
wife. I felt the interview very painfully this morning.
I have received a letter from a gentleman at Lincoln
wishing for an interview, which I declined. I cannot
see anyone excepting the religious ladies who visit the
prison.
'My time upon earth is very abort. I shall be exe-
cuted on the morning of the 2,oth inst., at eight
o'clock in the, morning, I suppose. May God in his
mercy receive my soul! Jesus is a present help in
time of Double; on Hun I cast my burden. It
matters little how the body dies; may I be found
right before the judgment-seat of God t I care not
what man thinks of me; it avails nothing now to me.
My dear relations—all of you—l take it as a great
kindness you sending me this letter. You once thought
much of me. This letter has cost me many tears. I
have often thought of you all. And now, dear friends,
I give you my dying love. Farewell.
From your unfortunate relative,
CA.TRERINE WrLSTS:

articles.title: BALLOON ASCENT F1?O21" WINCHESTER BARRACKS.
articles.text:
THE BALLOON ASCENT F1?O21"
WINCHESTER BARRACKS.

The following letter appears in the Time.:—.
'Sir —Mr. Coxwell having stated to me that our
flight in his balloon from Winchester to Harrow, on
Tuesday last, was one of the most successful and in-
teresting which have been made, I am disposed to
offer a few additional observations to those of your
previous correspondent. He made a slight mistake as
regards the time in which the journey was performed,
the distance being got over in one hour and six
minutes—four minutes less than he computed. It
being necessary. to move upwards with great velocity,
an additional interest attached to the ascent. The
moment the rope was loosed by our guide, we felt firet
a gentle movement, then a bound into space, almost a
realisation of the translation' of good men of
old. It is hardly possible to describe how thia
movement outstripped thought. A fleeting vi-
sion passed the minds of friends near becoming
instantly distant, amid the waving of handkerchiefs,
the strains of music, and the cheers of the crowd; we
were high in air, however, before we could return
these salutations. At this period our velocity could
not have been leas than at the rate of three miles a
minute, our course describing a parabolic curve, the
balloon being moved by two forces....-upwards by the
dense masses of the lower air, and northwards by the
wind. This pace gradually lessened till we reached our
extreme altitude upwards of two miles, when we took
the more moderate rate of seventy miles an hour, and
travelled at the same elevation until almost over
Chertsey, when we descended, in a parabola of less
inflection, upon Staines. This descent was of great
velocity, although the only effect felt by the aeronauts
was the rotation of the balloon slowly. This was
rapidly checked by the delivery of a sandbag, when
for some time we preserved an altitude of about 900
feet; subsequently it became necessary to ascend
to 1,000 feet to clear Harrow-hill with the grapnel.
which hung 100 feet below us, and was a scale—by
which we could estimate height, and our altitude was
now gradually lessened until the descent was accom-
pliihed. It was interesting to note the difference of
the aerial currents. Until we passed over Staines,
rippled -waters were observable, and we anticipated a
rough descent; near there, however, some smoke was
seen to blow towards the west, althoegh our direction
was northerly, indicating a lower and. different current
of wind. After our descent upon Staines we noticed
our pace was diminished, and that we were probably
moving at the rate of about 35 miles an hour, which
pace appeared uniform until half a minute before
touching ground, under the shelter of Harrow-hill.
London was to be seen, a great bank of fog, with
buildings in its outskirts, which we left on our right.
I ought not to forget to mention a very brilliant effect
produced by the sun striking on a cloud over the Isle
of Wight. The cloud shone with an intensity equal to
electric light. Nor should I forget our passage over
the familiar scene of much military pomp in which we
had figured—the great dust plain and hideous huts of
Aldershott. There a solitary bugle call was detected
by the sharp ears of our helmsman, who pointed out
the value of balloons in military reconnoissance.
Although at the height of two miles, any manoeuvres
upon the dust plain could have been easily seen. Even
troops secreted behind the reserveir, or in the hollowa
of Ca3sar's Camp, would have been unable to hide from
the searching eye of the aerostatic observer.
A. IL

articles.title: SERMON ON THE AMERICAN WAR.
articles.text:
SERMON ON THE AMERICAN WAR.

On the evening of Sunday, the 28th ult., the Rev.
Henry Ward Beecher delivered a sermon on the
President's proclamation, in the course of which he
examined the question of slavery in his own peculiar
manner, and proclaimed himself an unswerving, un-
faltering Abolitionist. He drew one of his celebrated
pictures of the evils of slavery, asserting that family
virtue throughout the South was sapped; that most of
the people in Dixie were profoundly ignorant; and
that now God was punishing them for upholding the
institution of slavery. The South was corrupt at the
core. They were neither democratic nor republican;
but were aristocratic, and verging close upon monarchy.
They had turned back upon the barbaric periods, and
they were 400 years back of where his hearers stood.
The South was behind the days of the Reforma-
tion ; they were on their way to the Red Sea, and
God would chuck them in. (Laughter.) Mr. Beecher
alluded to the circumstance attending the organisation
of the Federal Government, and in a humorous strain
spoke of South Carolina as being the rotten stave of
the barrel. For the last fifty years we had a race of
statesmen who were bribed and corrupted, who had
said, 'Let us not disturb the prosperity of this great
nation.' Would they see the fruits of the seeds of
peace that had been sowing for fifty years? Go to
Sharpsburg and the valley of the Chicka.hominy. Vir-
ginia had the most terrible punishment, for what was
beautiful as Paradise a few months ago, wee now a
desolation. Was that an accidental fact? He noticed
the part which the women of the South had taken in
favour of slavery, for she was being punished now in
being deprived of her natural protector. The North,
too, was suffering to an extent to which she had winked
at slavery for the sake of commerce. When the
North had paid two thousand millions of taxes
(and only just begun) he thought that the Lord
would get back pretty much all the North
made out of slavery. God is the great tax-
gatherer. He is out now, and He will have a good
time. (Great laughter.) Every nation that had
anything to do with the curse of slavery (especially
England) was now suffering, for the commercial classes
of England had. thriven and made their wealth out of
slave labour- In conclusion, he said that the Lord God
Almighty was now walking forth in clouds and thunder,
and for a people to refuse to believe that God rewarded
liberty and punished slavery against their educated
historic ideas—against all the canons of their political
structure, and all the sympathies of the human heart,
was monstrous infidelity. We were about to more
with gigantic force in one way or the other, and it was
necessary that we should fall back upon some great
principle and take our direction, not from the mutable
counsels of cunning men, not from those wetiving poli-
ticians that had enmeshed us in times past, until we
struck some great and immutable principle of God.
What, then, he asked, is to be our policy for
the future? What are we to do? What is the remedy
for such times as these? It is to repent and break
away from the past. It is to call God to witness that
in time to comb we will consecrate, individually and
nationally, every energy to repair the mischief of
slavery—to do away utterly, and to establish the reign
of universal liberty. That is the path of 'safety, and
blessed be -God He has sent the porter. He has opened
the door by the hand of the president. He has lifted
the silver trumpet of liberty, and the blast is blown
that rolls through the forest, and goes along the
mountain side, and spreads wide over the prairies. It
is known on the hither and on the thither ocean;
the waves of the Pacific and the waves of the At-
lantic lift themselves up and sound together notes of
gladness because that policy is enunciated which can-
not be taken back:. As long as it was a question
whether the president meant to declare, as Commander-
-in-Chief of the army and navy of the United States, as
a military necessity, universal emancipation, as long
as it was a matter of doubt, the North was in danger
of being divided into two „parties, the one attempting tp
make him proclaim liberty, and the other attempting.
to make him stand up for slavery. He has taken his
• choice. There can be only two parties, one for
liberty and the President, and the other for the South
and slavery. (Manifestations of applause.) The Presi-
dent has taken ground; and since the Administration
is fixed an the aide of liberty, the old original spirit
of our constitution and the doctrine of our father; we
are going to have the Union as it never was, but as
it was meant to be. The Union as it was meant to
be, and not the Union as it was, is to be our doctrine;
because the Union as it was was a monstrous outrage
on your rights and on mine. The Union as it was
guaranteed men the right of speech, and I should
have paid for that right by my life in Virginia, flit,
,Carolinas, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas,
and Missouri. i should not have gone there. and
spoken words that I have spoken here to-night
without praising God to-morrow morning in another
world. (Laughter.)

It has been very unjustly said of a certain great states-
man of modern times, that he was a reed painted like
iron ; with much more truth it might be said of Cavour,
that he was a bar of iron painted like a reed.—.De la
Rive s Cavour.

THE RECOGNITION OF TILE sarmr.

The following correspondence has ,been handed to um
for publication _ _ _

'Manchester, Oct, 13, 1862.
Sir,—A great deal of misapprehension exists in this
district regarding what you are reported in the rims
newspaper, of Thursday hst, to have said in the Town.
hail, Newcastle' on Tuesday evening, when speaking
on American affairs.

People here have interpreted your words to mean
that our government intend to recognise the Southern
States of America, and, as a consequence, the whole
trade in cotton and cotton goods is thrown into a state
of doubt and uncertainty that has had the effect of
completely paialysing it.
Tnis is not all; your speech has induced the coun-
terrnanding of orders already sent abroad for cotton,
and the suspending of others on the ewe of being aent,
thus stopping supplies of that which our population
stands so much in need of.

'lt would be most desirable to know if what you
said had not the meaning put upon it, and that it was
not your intention to say or infer her Majesty's Go-
vernment contemplated recognizing ihe Southern
States of America ; and I trust you will not consider
me intrusive in asking an explanation, as the bubject is
one of national importance, which should not be left in
doubt and uncertainty as at present.
I beg therefore you will grant me a reply, as your
silence may bear the interpretation already put on your
words.—l nave the honour to remain, &e.,
(Signed) THOMAS MOSLEY.
Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, M.P.'
11, Downing-street, Whitehall, 16th Oct., 13G2.

pointed terms, of an opinion which Mr. Gladstcuie.has
long ago stated in public, that the efforts of .the.
Northern States to subjugate the Southern ones is hope-
less, by reason of the resistance of the latter.—l am,
Sir, your obedient servant,
(Signed) CHARLES L. RTA24.

A melancholy accident happened on Friday after-
noon last, at the New Priestfield Colliery, \Villen-
hall, about three miles from Wolverhampton, which
resulted in the instantaneous and frightful death of
four men. The colliery is the property of Mr. Henry
Ward, ironmaster, by whom it is being worked. At
about half-past four on the day named live men were
ascending the shaft of a stone pit. They were all
riding in a 'tackle' which was attached to the wind-
ing chain, and covertd with a temporary roof or
bonnet ' formed of plate iron, to protect the men
from anything falling from the bank. This shaft
was about eighty yards deep, and the men had
reached to about the centre, when there came
upon them with fearful force a massive skip,'
used to convey the minerals to the surface.
The 'skip' did not alight upon the roof of the tackle,'
but the ' nevertheless, came upon theirs with such
terrible violence that four of the five instantly became
mutilated corpses, and the sides of the shaft were dis-
figured with sickening evidences of the terrible reality.
The fifth, who was on the opposite side of the cage,
happily escaped with only a slight bruise on the temple,
but he had to cling to a portion of the machinery of
the tackle' to save himself. Men descended as
speedily as possible, and performed the distressing
duty of collecting the scattered and quivering remains
of their deceased comrades, and sending them to the
surface. By this accident three women have been
made widows and ten children orphans. The banks-
man says that by the wind; which was blowing a still
breeze at the time, the skip was impelled over the
mouth of the shaft. On Saturday an inquest was
formally opened.

The bark Emma, Captain Wells, belonging to Messrs.
T. Ward and Co., has arrived at Mull from Cumberland
Inlet. The crew of the Emma have not seen a whale
during the whole of their stay on the fishing grounds.
Captain Wells brings very unfavourable news. He states
that from the time he left Hull, on the loth of March
last, up to his arrival at the Orkneys on his return voyage,
there has been a succession of violent storms. Nearly
all the sailing vessels have returned clean, and many
have been lost, the ice having closed in upon them almost
without warning. Their crews have Leen compelled in
many instances to travel over many hundred miles of ice
to get to other vessels, or to some settlement. Captain
Wells states that during the whole of his experience he
has never met with sucn dreadful weather. At one time
the crews of 12 vessels, numbering .in all 600 men, were
standing on.th.e ice daring a severe storm, every moment
expecting to see their vessels crushed to pieces. The
Abram, of Kirckcaldy, was crushed with such sud-
denness that, although provisions, boats, clothes, Sr.c.,
were on deck in readiness for an emergency, everything
went down With the vessel, and the crew was with diffi-
culty saved. On Thursday morning Messrs. Brown,
Atkinson and Co,, managers of the Hull Whale and
Seal Fishing Company, were advised of the arrival of the
Truelove,ooaptain It. Wells' at Lerwick, with about 30
tuns of oil. The Truelove is the oily sailing ship belong-
ing to this port that has had any success whatever this
year. Captain Wells reports the Lady Seale steamer
with 11 fish (70 tuns), and the Diana steamer. Neither
of these steamers has arrived. • All the above vessels be-
long to the Hull Whale and Seal Fishing Company.
Messrs. J-. Belton and Co., High-street, have heard from
Captain Couldrey, announcing his arrival at Copenhagen
With the remainder of the Lord Gambier's crew,. also
with 28 of the Chieftain's and some belonging to the
Abram, Resolution, and Alexander. , Thus in one season,
tne'Chieftain having been lost, although her crew were
Saved, the Kirkealdy.fleet of three vessels has been to-
tally destroyed.

ZOSTERA..MARINA.—The annexed suggests a method
for obtaining specimens of the Zostera martna Oxford
Villa, Ilayerstock-hill, London, Oct. is, 1862, Sir,—
The Peninsular and Oriental and Royal Mail Steam-
packet Companies have most handsomely offered to pro-
cure and send to. me, free of expense, specimens of
Zostera marina, or sea grass collected from sundry

By7this means the plant as it exists in various latitudes
may , be .compared, and reliable information obtained.
May `i ask the editors of newspapers in seaports to
notice this communication ?—I am, Sir, your obedient
servant, HENRY HARDEN.'

LORD PAIMERSTON.—Whatevor may be the merits or
demerits of Lord Palmerston, every one knows that hia
name is feared and respected throughout the world.
Foreigners, indeed, in general fall into the mistake of
greatly overrating his powers. I have seen the rough
soldiery on the military frontier of Austria and Turkey
crowd round a traveller to see the fac-simile of his sig-
nature upon a passport, and the Tyrolese, who love the
House a Hapsburg, have a doggerel distich—
'lf the devil has a son,
i 'Sure it s Lord Palmerston.'

Everywhere his name is taken as the synonym of the
British Lion and the state a the world is such at pre-
sent that all good patriots feel that the British Lion
must be ready to roar at theahortest notice.—Mr. Grant
Dui at 31acduf.

Lord Stan, M.P., presided at a late meeting of the
committee of the Tipperary Farming Society. The
meeting went througha large amount of routine business
connected with the awards of the late show, Bce., in the
whole of which Lord Stanley took a lively interest; and
at the close of the proeemli gs, in reply to a warm vote
of thanks, which was carried by apelamatioa.. he stated
his determination to be present at the annual gathering

As all the successful competitors at the late show werk3

articles.title: PROPOSED COOKING KlTeffE.N* FOR ails WORKING CLA6SES.
articles.text:
PROPOSED COOKING KlTeffE.N*
FOR ails WORKING CLA6SES.

We are happy to be able to announce that an in-
fluential tfirm in this city has taken the necessary steps
to open, shortly, a commodious kitchen in a central
locality, where the unemployed operatives will be sup-
plied with the best food at cost price, and where the
factory women and girls out of work will be taught to
cook. Permission has been granted by the improve-
ment committee for the occupation of the vacant
ground in Bancroft-street, opposite the entrance to the
police yard, for a temporary building for the kitchen.
It is not certain, however, that this site will be
occupied, for if suitable unoccupied premises can be
found, the operations of the kitchen will begin earlier
than if a building has to be erected for the purpose. 11l
any case, it is hoped that the kitchen may be in opera-
tion about the middle of next month, and, therefore,
before the winter is fully upon us. This undertaking
is solely with the view of contributing to the relief of
the distress. There will be no profit made; while, at
the same time, it is hoped that the kitchen will be self-
supporting. The
.original outlay wilt be defrayed by-
subscription, as also will any loss in the working, if
there snould be any. The benefits from this institu-
tion will be twofold. First, it will be the means of
teaching the art of plain cookery to a large number of
operatives whole present ignorance in that respect
causes both a wasteful expenditure of food and uncom-
fortable, because not properly. cooked, meals. In this
respect the kitchen will, for its importance and useful-
ness, take precedence of those admirable institutions,
the sewing classes. One part of the project, which is
not yet complete in all its details, will be to have an
arrangement with the Provident-Society and 'other relief
committees for the attendance at the k ttchen of a number
of girls, in-rotation. These girls will be:taught to cook,
and will be employed in all the necessary cleaning. Thus,
the production of tem eooked meals will be without cost,
except for the material t The second benefit will be in
thesupply of excellent food at the cheapest possible rate.
. Each ration will be charged one penny. The man-
agement of the kitchens at Glasgow, which have been
in successful operation for some time, will afford much
information to guide in the establishment of the
central kitchen iin -Manchester. Upwards of 300)000
penny rations are supplied by the Glasgow kitchens
every month, and they include the following :-55,000
. basins of broth and soup, 62,000 plates of beef, 82,000
rolls and slices of bread, with and without butter ;
54,000 cups of tea and coffee, 14,600 bowls of porridge,
33,000 plates of potatoes, 7,000 eggs, and 14,000
tumblers of milk. There -will be accommodation in
the Manchester kitchen for the meals to be • eaten in
the building, or the food. may be purchased and taken
to the buyer's home. A reading-room will also be
provided, in which any operative may take his penny,
cup of tea or coffee, and read the daily papers. The
scheme is one of the best that has been , called into
existence by the pressure of the times, and we heartily
wish that it may have a full measure of success.—
Manchester Guardian.

articles.title: ORLEAIVS PRINCES.
articles.text:
THE ORLEAIVS PRINCES.

The Count de Paris has addressed the following
letter to General Sickles :

'Claremont; Sept. 11, 1862.
'My dear General—l have just read the letter you
wrote to the New York Times in answer to the mis-
representations circulated 'lout our departure from
America, and I hasten to thank you for having taken
up the pen under these circumstances.
. . _

Altkiough we are accustomed to calumny and despise
it, nevertheless it is very gratifying to see the facts
put in their true light, and our situation so well
understood and so clearly explained, especially by a
member of the army with whose destinies we were
associated during nearly a year. •We shall always
remember that campaign with the artny of the Potomac
as one of the best and most interesting epochs of our
youth. It is with regret that we left our companions
in arms, and nothing can be more valuable to us than
such testimonies of remembrance and esteem. I need
not add that our hearty wishes still accompany them,
that the distance has only strengthened the interest
we take in the success of the great cause for which we
found together.

'Deped upon it, however ignorant and prejudicial
may be the public at large, there are still on this side
Of the Atlantic some hearts who follow with emotion
the struggle of a great and free nation for her institu-
tions, and who cannot believe in the ultimate success
of the efforts of a deluded minority to establish a new
community whose corner-stone shall be so odious, so
dangerpue, and so precarious an institution as that of
Slaver. _ _ _

'B4/ore ending this letter—for the bad English of
which I must apologise—let me still tell you, my dear
general, how glad I should be to shake hands again
with you, and to talk once more with you, of your
winter quarters in that wild corner of Maryland, or of
the summer days when your tent was pitched on the
field of battle of Fair Oaks.

'I beg you, my dear general, to believe me always,
very truly yours,
'Louis Pirmirrn D'OurarANs,
'Count de Paris.'

articles.title: .RF,CENT WILLS AND BEQUESTS.
articles.text:
.RF,CENT WILLS AND BEQUESTS.

The will of the Most Noble Mary, Duchess Dowager
of Buckingham and Chandos, relict of the late duke, and
daughter of the first Marquis of Breadalbane, K.T., was
administered to in the London Court of Probate by her
son, the present Duke of Buckingham, the sole executor
nominated in the will, which bears date November, 1855,
by which the testatrix disposes of the property she in-
herited from the estates of her father, and over which she
had a right of disposition according to • the orthr of the
Court of Session in Scotland, to her only son, subject to
a small bequest to her only daughter, who, under the
clause for younger children, is otherwise provided for.
The will of John Lewis, of Tilney-street, Park-lane,
was proved in the London Court under £300,000 per-
sonalty by the trustees and executors—Sir Charles
Locock, Bart (the testator's son-in-law), Alexander
Trotter, Esq.; James Bury Capel, Esq.; and Charles
Brodie Locoek, Esq., the testator's grandson. The will
was executed in 1859, and a codicil in 1861. The testa-
tor has made ample provision for his two daughters, and
has directed that the residue of his property, real and.
personal, shall be divided into five parts of equal value,
leaving to each of his five grandsons an equal portion.
There is a legacy of £lOO left to the fund for decayed
members of the Stock Exchange, to be paid free of duty.
The will of Alexander Giovanni Cassavetti, Esq., of
Porchester-terrace, and of New Broad-street, merchant,
was proved in London by three of the executors, namely,
Michael Spartali, Esq., of Gresham House; Constantine
Geralopulo, Esq., of Pembridge-gardens ; and Euterp
Cassavetti, the relict; power being reserved to Sophocles
Constantinides, Esq., of New Broad-street, and of
Alexandria, in Egypt,(imerchant, to prove hereafter. The
personalty in this country was sworn under £lBO,OOO.
The will bears date January, 1862, and there are two
codicils, executed in February and March following. To
his relict the testater has left an absolute sum of 1.0,000,
together with an annuity of £5OO and a share of the residue
of his entire property for her life, giving her a power,
with directions, to leave some portion thereof to her own
relations. The residue of his property he leaves to be
equally divided between his son and two daughters. The
testator has also given directioas to his trustees that,
upon the decease of his widow, a certain portion of the
share of the residue enjoyed by her shall be .applied for
philanthropic purposes in Greece and Thessaly, the latter
being his native country.

INDIAN TELEGRAPH.—The authorities at the India-
office have resolved to take immediate steps for complet •
ing the land line of telegraph now in existence as far as
Bagdad on the head of the Persian Gulf, and to lay a sub-
marine sable thence to Gwadel on the coast of Beloo-
chistan, from which point a land line is being con-
structed to join the Indian system of telegraphs at
Kurrachee.

BRINGING COTTON TO MARRET.—The plan for bring-
ing forward to market the cotton of the South, alluded
to a few days ago, is still under consideration. It is
understood that it has met the entire approbation of the
Secretary of the Treasury, and is regarded by all prac-
tical business men and financiers to whom it has been
confided as the great desideratum of the country. If
carried into effect it will enable the Government to fitr-
nish an average supply of cotton to foreign manufac-
turers, and to realise easily the means of paying the in-
terest upon the public debt in coin or its equivalent. It
will also 'enlist the interest of influential parties in the
South in the maintenance of the Federal Union. It is
the only measure that has yet been proposed calculated
to touch the pocket nerve of the South, and to make
Southern produce the means of sustaining public credit.
—Washington Journal.
A COMING DELUGE.-11., Mathieu (de la Drome)
writes to the Siecle to communieate a note -which he has
addressed to the Academy of Sciences, and according to
which all the watercourses in the south-east of France,
and in the whole south of Europe, will experience a very
great augmentation from the 28th inst. to the Bth of
November. e predicts great inundations in Italy, and
still greater ones in countries to the east of Italy. In
France only a few departments will be visited by this
scourge. The 17th degree of longitude is the region
whore it will be most severely felt. The overflow of
rivers will take place, according to M. Mathieu, through-
out a zone of more than 600 leagues, parallel to a line
drawn from Cette or Marseilles to a point beyond the
Black Sea, grazing the south of the Crimea. The
neighbourhood of seas will, it is said, be chiefly affected,
and advice is given to the populations of the districts in-
dicated to take such precautions as may be in. theirpower
before the Btll inst,

articles.title: US TRA LIAN EXPLORATION.
articles.text:
A US TRA LIAN EXPLORATION.

(From the Times.)
1 Good news for the Geographical Society ;—two new
rivers have been d!scovered in Queensland, and, still more
important, Mr. Landsborough, the bold and dashing
Queensland explorer, arrived in Melbourne about a fort-
night back, having completed his expedition clean across
the continent (something to the east of Burke's route)
from the Gulf of Carpentaria. It was an interesting
coincidence that Mr. Landshorough himself was present
at the meeting of the Exploration Committee of our Royal
Society on the oecasion of the presentation by Sir Henry
Barkly to John King (the survivor of Burke and Wills's
expedition) of the gold watch forwarded to him by the
Duke of Newcastle on behalf of the Geographical Society.
There was a great gathering on the occasion, including
many ladies. Finally and satisfactorily is it now estab-
lished that the vast interior of this land is not a great
sandy desert. Mr. Landsborough informs us that on
starting he followed up a stream for 150 miles through a
fine country, south-westerly, intending, if possible, to
reach Stuart's route, but that owing to the time lost
through the wreck of the Firefly (attendant on the earlier
part of the expedition) he was unable to effect this object.
He states that he reached the source of this stream; that
it commenced with a fine spring, three feet deep, very
rapid, and sufficiently strong to turn a wheel. Returning
down this stream, he found that at about 80 miles from
the Gulf it threw off two streams, the one flowing into
the Nicholson river, the other into the Albert river. He
then proceeded for the Flinders, having failed to dis-
cover the tracks of Burke's praty, and followed up that
river for 400 miles through what he describes as 'mag-
nificent country.' At this point the party left the
Flinders (which Mr. Landsborough thinks is about 500'
miles long), and in about 20 miles reached the watershed
of the- T fivtapson, one of the •main 4eads;, of the Cooper
river. l'iodbeding thence -abet* a hundred-miles, he
came upon a tree marked by some other explorer, and,
although,then only about 150 milesfrom Burke's depot,
he was obliged, from shortness of supplies, to forego the
journey to that place, and therefore he at once struck
across about 40 miles for the main head of Cooper's
Creek. Reaching this point, the party followed Cooper's
Creek until they struck the Warrego, and then followed
the Warrego until they came on the Darling. Here,
being in settled country, Mr. Landsborough first . heard
of the fate of the party of poor Burke and Wills. In
answer to questions from members of the society, Mr.
Landsborough informed them that the most elevated land
on the Flinders did not exceed 1,000 feet; that the wet'
season in tropical Australia began about January; that
thunderstorms and rainy weather last until the end of
April or beginning of May; that on the heads of the
Gregory river the country is of a balsatic character, and
on the Flinders quartz and iron bark trees (and thprefore,
probably, gold) abound. The dividing range between
the Flinders and the Cooper's Creek country is estimated
as being from 1,000 to 1,500 feet high. Mr. Lauds-
borough said he had no doubt that the rivers on the east
side of the range separating the Flinders from the Thomp-
son were supplied by springs. He had never been to the
west of the Thompson, and he saw no indications of
southern streams. On returning to the Albert river from
his expedition to the south-west, he came on another
river, well supplied with water. In the water-holes,
which he followed down for 70 miles, he found plenty of
fish, and he thought these fish came up from rivers further
to the south-west; but, as it w as the dry season.he could see
no water where it had spread for miles in the wet season.
Further down, he had no doubt he should have got on to
a large river. The country he passed through was so
well grassed that the horses looked as if they had been
stable-fed.' So healthy are the shores of the Gulf of
Carpentalia that although living in the open air, and
not having the best of food' (as Mr. Landsborough says),
the country agreed admirably with him, and there was
no fever or ague among any of the party. I have since
had a few hours of Mr. Landsborough to myself, and he
informs me that he has no doubt that within twelve
months the whole of the country between this and the
Gulf of Carpentaria will be taken up by settlers. Here,
then, covering many degrees of latitude, salubrious, well-
grasped, and upon the whole much better watered than
we had ever before surmised as probable, is the last ex-
tensive addition to the habitable world. How many
millions of energetic men—and women too, including
perhaps a portion of Miss Rye's governesses—may in a
very years animate these new solitudes!

of the precious triad, _Nana ;Sahib, Bala Rao, and
Bao.Sahib, the adopted sons of the PEISHIVA. the pm-
sioner of the British_ Government. Mr. MACSABB'
Acting Deputy. Commissioner of the Punjaub, received
intelligence that RAO SAIIIB was in disguise in the
territory of Jummoo. The active Dcputy got the
Maharajah of Jummoo to pretend that it. was necessary
to send a secretary to a Tehsild.y, or revenue agent,
near Chineanee, where RAO SAHIB was concealed. The
secretary :took fifty armed men with him, and his sup-
posed wife was in a curtained litt9r. Mr. MAPNABB
himself took the place of the lady. Alter ninety hours

MACNABB suffering from severe illness, the party suc-

THE LAST ENTRY.—Tho following is the last entry
in the journal of Mr. Wills, who with Mr. Burke, his
leader, perished in the last Australian exploring expedi-
tion. We quote it from a narrative of the expedition,
published by Messtsnmith, Elder, and Co. ;—‘ Friday,
June 28.—Clear, cold night; slight breeze from the
east; day beautifully warm and pleasant. Mr. Burke
suffers greatly from the cold, and is getting extremely
weak. He and King start to-morrow up the creek, to
look for the blacks: it is the only chance we have of
being saved from starvation. I am weaker than ever,
although I have a good appetite, and relish the nardoo
much, but it seems to give us nb nutriment, and the
birds are are so shy as not to be got at. Even if we got
a good supply of fish, I doubt whether we could do much
work on them and the nardoo alone. Nothing now but
the grestest good luck can save any of us; and as for
myself I may live four or five days if the weather con-
tinues warm. My pulse is at forty-eight and very weak,
and my legs and arms are nearly skin and bone. I can
only look out like Mr. Micawber 'for something to turn
up. Starvation on nardoo is by no means very un-
pleasant hut for the weakness one feels and the utter
inability to move oneself; for as far as appetite is con-
cerned it gives me the greatest satisfaction. Certainly
fat and sugar would be more to one's taste; in fact,
those seem to me to be the great stand-by for one in this
extraordinary Continent; not that I mean to depreciate
the farinaceous food, but the want of sugar and fat in
all substances obtainable here is so great that they
become almost valueless to us as articles of food u ithout
the addition of something else.—(Signed,) W. J. WILLs.'

EXTRAORDINARY RISE OF THE TIDE AT LIVERPOOL.
—On Friday morning one of the most extraordinary tidal
phenomena occurred on the Mersey, the circumstances
presenting most remarkable features, and well worthy
the attention of the scientific world. According to the
tide table, high water was at 25 minutes pastS in the
morning, previous to which the vessels in the river (of
which there was a considerable number) had their heads
pointed down the river) towards the Fort and Rock Light-
house. When the :tide turned and was on the ebb, of
course, their positions were reversed, the vessels point-
ing with their heads up the river, towards Garston and
Runcorn. Half-an-hour after the ebb of the tide had
commenced it began to rise, and so continued until it
had attained 18 ioc.hes. above high water, the vessels in
the river again swinging round with their bows to the
entrance of the river, to the great astonishment of all on
board the different ships. The phenomenon was
witnessed by all, the pier-head masters and many
persons on the different pier-heads, as well as by the
boatmen on the river, and has since been the subject of
much conversaion among nautical men. This double
rise of the tide cannot be attributable to the strong
N.N.W. wind blowing at the time, and so forcing a large
body of water into the Mersey, as we have had frequent
gales from the same quarter, and such a singular eir-
cumstmicg W 44 Pffer Witnessed before. Liverpool
