The Times Melbourne correspondent ails-. writes upon
his subject :
Touching these poor governesses, I must, without
further delay, keep a promise I made to you a mail or
two back. For my present purpose all women may be
'classified as either useful or ornamental, or both useful
and ornamental, or neither. Now, your average colonist
generally wants a useful wife, a comfort and a support,
not a burden and a hindrance in life. Accordingly, an
active servant girl, handsome or ugly, has no difficulty
in getting a husband. She generally seems to come to
the colony with—among other necessaries of life—a male
cousin, who is delighted to sit in your kitchen and serve
her for nothing, while she professes to serve you for
some 3(:)_ or 140 a year. In due time the cousin be-
_ _ . _

comes her husband; die then, as his help-mate, cooking,
working, &c., stat te for herself. This i the rule with
the class of women just referred to. There can be no
t;uch rule for educated women. Why? Because their
education not only unfits them for common service, but
makes it revolting to them. The educated woman does
not care to resort to the company of people below her in
condition and culture—people who, bytheir own con-
versation and habits, can scarcely be meet company
for her; while they, a gain, would be scarcely easy in
her society, could she even feel easy in theirs. Unless,
therefore, she have friends in- the colony, or light on the
-are good foitune of a situation in some family by whom
she will be treated with sespect due to her, she must
hold a very isolated position indeed, repelled at one by
(it may be) vulgar wealth above her and by uncon-
genial coarseness blow her. But next, what are her
chances of obtaining the desirable situation I have
imagined for her F. There are not one -per cent. of all
the families in these_ colonies who have at once the

means and the inclination to engage a competent private
governess for their children. A few hundred squatters,
an equal number of merchants and professional men,
comprise the whole available patronage .for governesses.
et us, however, suppose—against these chances—the
eituation obtained, whence is to coins the husband?

Why, have we not hundreds of eligible and unmarried
.-oung men? And is there not some maxim somewhere
to the effect that almost any woman may, if she choose,
marry almost any man? Well, we have the young men,
and I have either met with or dreamt the maxim, and do
not believe in it. Ilad the maxim-monger said that
almost any woman may marry almost any man, in her
own rank of life, the assertion might approach a little
nearer ta experience, and would not shock common
sense; for there is no doubt that a woman may, when
sill lays her mind to it, especially under favouring cir-
cumstances, do much in thisway. But then a governess
cannot marry a mechanic, even if a mechanic could afford
to marry her; and young men of the upper section of
the middle class have usually family and social connex-
ions of their own either in the colony or in the mother
country. Instances have I known among my own ac
qnaintances--barristers, merchants, and pastoral follows
of colleges—who have come out, first made things snug,
and then sent home.for the girls they had left behind
them. In the greater number of cases, however, these
eligibles, when they do marry, connect themselves with
the families of settled colonists; yet very frequently they
do not marry at all; and too common, even here, are
attractive and respectable young single women who, if
not born to blush unseen,' are yet compelled to waste
their sweetness,' and sometimes their sourness, on the
desert air.'

Nor is this entirely the fault of unappreciating men.
No doubt, the old story about clubs cafes, and the in-
numerable modem comforts of bachelorhood, accounts
somewhat for this too great prevalence of single life;
but female education has also something to do with it.
Girls of every rank in life but the humblest always seem
to think any kind of work shameful. Moreover, they
generally look for a husband as well placed in life as
their parents. If this meant only that the husband must
be in every way, short of wealth, socially fit company
for the parents, there is nothing to be said against it, and
much for it. But, unfortunately, it seems to be too fre-
quently assumed that at once, with marriage, the new
pair are to start pretty nearly where the old people leave
off, with, if not a carriage and servants, at any rate some
usual indications of station, and of the necessary style.'
True, the altogether inevitable tradesmen's bills must
sooner or later disturb the harmony of this dream; but
still the dream itself too frequently ends in discontent,
envy of superior wealth, pretence, keeping_ up appear-
ances,' and all the meannesses and small vices necessary
to that great end, an end, after all, which is never
achieved. Such considerations as these scare away
from matrimony many a man who is by no means averse
from domesticity in itself. At the same time I think'
this state of things becomes somewhat modified in
colonies. So many men go upon land, so many in young
communities must take to new forms of industry and
submit to new conditions of life, that even imported
female gentility frequently becomes accustomed to the
atmosphere of the kitchen and the poultry-yard, without
prejudice to remaining as delightful as over in the draw-
ing-room. May it not be, then, that in the curious
action and reaction between mother country and depen-
dencies colonial experience may tell upon the stereotyped
forms of English life, and that the spinsters of Miss Rye,
wholesale, retail, and for expiztation; may be helped
off as the result? If not, growing spinsterhood, in Bel-
gravia or anywhere else, would appear to be a hopeless
complaint, for only the units among marrying men can
support women merely for ornament, and even they soon
tire of their toys.

articles.title: .1 CORE- TOWN .COUNCILLOB AND LORD DUNDREARE
articles.text:
.1 CORE- TOWN
.COUNCILLOB AND
LORD DUNDREARE

Mr. Bernard Sheehan is an original and a unique
specimen of a town councillor and poor-law guardian.
He is a rata avis in terris, for we believe there is not in
the kingdom, or indeed in the world, anybody4tvhose
character and cast of mind bear the slightest resemblance
to his. Were it not for his unintentional jokes and his
laughable blunders, many of our local meetings would
be of the dullest and most uninterersting kind. But,
although he has figured week after week for a great
number of years past in the columns of all the newspapers
in this city, and has been laughed at even in the
remotest parts of the country, he never caused more
amusement than he did on Wednesday at the meeting
of the board of guardians, by his simplicity and his
credulity. Amongst the gentlemen present was one
from England, who attended the meeting, we presume,
with the intention of seeing how business was done in
Cork, and, we have been told, of hearing the celebrated
Barney Sheehan. The curiosity of the latter gentleman
was aroused by the appearance of the stranger, and he
inquired his name. Pew people who know Mr. Sheehan
kink of answering him except with a jest, and so he
was told that the gentleman who had attracted his atten-
tion was Lord Dundreary. Mr. Sheehan has not much
knowledge of the peerage list, nor an extensive acquaint-
ance with the nobility; and not being much of a reading
man, it is not surprising that he had never heard the
name of Lord Dundreary before. After a short time he
rose with great solemnity, and having expressed his
sense of the honour conferred upon the board by the
visit of a nobleman of such an exalted station as that of
Lord Dundreary, he thought he might as well
turn his lordship's visit to some practical account.
Perhaps, my lord, you would be so obliging as to
tell us what the people's dresses cost in your union
if you plaze ' The scene that followed may be
imagined. All business was suspended for some minutes
and every one abandoned himself to a paroxysm of
laughter, in which the strange gentleman, who was
supposed to be Lord Dundreary, heartily joined. There
was not a grave countenance in the room except Mr.
Sheehan's ; and he, seeing, from the manner in which
his compliment to the supposed nobleman was received,
that he was mistaken, seized the gentleman who had
misinformed him by the ear, and cried, 'This purty boy
tould me he was Lord Dundreary. Well, now you see
what a lot o' lies there is in the world; I declare you
can't depend on half what you are told. 0, ye are a fine
lot o' lads.' This speech, part of which was uttered in the
style of a man sorrowfully moralising upon the de-
pravity of human nature, and another part in a manner
which showed that Mr. Sheehan himself enjoyed the
joke, was succeeded by another burst of laughter, and
the guardians did not cease to smile till the board ad-
journed.—Cork Reporter.

Mons Corrox FROM BOMBAY.—The arrivals of cotton
at Liverpool from East India still continue, and on
Saturday last three more ships entered the Mersey from
Bombay, viz. :—Arkwright, with 4,196 bales; Africa,
with 5,181 bales; and Sir Charles Napier, with 4,135
bales; making a total of 13,512 bales.
MR. COBDEN AND FRENCH CLARETS.—At the Edin-
burgh Chamber of Commerce, on Wednesday, the chair-
man, Mr. James Richardson, in the course of his re-
marks, said Last week I had the pleasure of spend-
ing an evening with Mr. Cobden in the house of our
deputy-chairman, Mr. Duncan Al`Laren. The conver-
sation naturally turned to the French treaty, and he
then stated to me the difficulty of getting good cheap
claret in any hotels you go to in Scotland, and thought
it was much to be deplored that hotelkeepers did not
see it to be their interest to forward the sale of these
lighter wines. In a letter which I received from Mr.
Cobden, his views were expressed in the following terms:
The only way in which the consumption of French
wines can be greatly promoted in this country is by
their being generally introduced at moderate prices in
the hotels. In the long run more money is made by
selling low-priced than high-priced articles. This has
been proved by the sale of penny- newspapers, although
the trade is only in its infancy. The same rule has held
good in Rowland Hill's postage reform. I wish some
measure could be taken to tempt or shame the innkeepers
into the sale of genuine French wines at moderate
prices. The success of the French treaty greatly depends
upon this being done

Russux STOVES.—If we could bring about, in the
warming of our houses, the cleanliness of Russian firing,
the little labour called for, and the long steady heating
given out, advantages would evidently follow to both
master and servant, mistress and maid, over the whole
of Great Britain. Now the Muscovite firing is performed
in stoves, generally brick stoves, but this is not their
national peculiarity. We have stoves in our own halls,
and Germany has them in every apartment, sometimes
of Metal and sometimes of earthenware, sometimes small
and sometimes large, and serving two or more rooms or
passages; but in all these cases the fires in them are red
just like our open fires, i. e., by co: Is, or billets of wood;
kept in the room, or wherever the door of the stove is,
and thrown on the embers from time to time, whenever
the fire would otherwise be in danger of dying out for
want of fuel. Now, that is not the essential principle
of a Russian stove at all, either of the largest or smallest
size, and whether they be cased externally with metal,
china, brick, or stone. With it, on the contrary, the
burning of the fuel is merely a short preliminary opera-
tion, and the proper or chronic action of the stove is that
of a large fixed chafing dish, without combustion but
with heated matter cooling inside it, and giving off its
heat in a graduated manner to the rooms requiring it.--
Three Cities of Russia.

AN IITNHA.pry MARRIAGE. —When I was at the large
town of in Armenia, the Pasha governing part
of the country was ch inged. us successor was
i Georgian, sold n his childhood to a wealthy Turk. The
boy grew and prospered, and after passing through sub-
ordintte offices, he was, some years previous to the time
,I speak of, intrusted with the command ota district. On.
his depoxture from Constantinople the Sultan waspleased
to give him to wife, as is not unusual, a lady from the
Royal harem. With her he lived most happily for three
years, when by some means, whether a mutual recol-
lection of some incident which had happened, or some
spot which had been seen in childhood, I know not what,
these two, man and wife, discovered that they w ere brother
and sister. The wife; like the husband, had been sold
away from her country, and met her brother in this
strange, wretched manner. They fortunately had had.
no children, and the marriage was immediately dissolved,
but they say that the Pasha has never smiled since the
discovery. Vacation Tourists.

AUTUMN ON THE CLYDE.—There is a subdued silvery
light on the,sea to-day, and the hills across the water
look like blue clouds. The air is SO still, that you may
hear the beating of the paddles of a steamer miles dista .t,
unseen in the veil of mist. There as been drizzling rain
at intervals through the morning; and the road by the
' sea-side, yesterday ankle deep in dust, is Pleasantly firia
and cool; and the trees, just beginning to be touched by
the Atlantic breezes of the early days of September,look
green again as in May, in the glints of silvery light from.
the clouded sun. You may see many fair scenes within
the compass of Britain; but yesterday morning, when the
sky was sapphire blue, and the sunshine was the bright-
est ;—when that expanse of sea shut in by noble hills
was glassy smooth, and the yellow corn-fields round,
bounded by green hedges, looked so still and rich in the
quiet air, not without a touch of bracing crispness; you
would have said that there could be hardly anything
fairer in the world than a bit of the homely Clyde.—
Fraser's Magazine.
DR. GOODALL. OF ETON.—This gentleman was prover-
bially fond of punning. About the same time that he
was made Provost of Eton, he received also a stall at
Windsor. A young lady of his acquaintance, while con-
gratulating him on his elevation and requ.sting him to
give the young ladies of Eton and Windsor a ball during
the vacation, hippened to touch his wig with her fan,
and caused the powder to fly about. Upon which" the
doctor exclaimed—' My dear, you see you can get the
powder out of the cannon, but not the ball.'—Capt.
Gronow's Reminiscences.
WOMAN'S NATURE A COMPLEX MACHINE.—` What a
complex machine a woman's nature is! says a great
modern sage. I think there is a time in the lives of
most men when they are rather disposed to resent the
aphorism. It seems such a simple matter; after all,
the mystery is no mystery at all, or, at least, is so easily
penetrated. The best and the werst of the sex are
united by a Monotonous uniformity. The lorette, as
well as the titled gentlewoman or the untainted maiden,
can do generous things with a free hand and a warm
heart. It is not Traviata alone who takes a childish
pleasure in the masquerade or the milliner. The opera-
cloak that goes to the casino does not conceal very dif-
ferent feelings—in so far as positive value is concerned
—from those hidden by the cloak that goes to the ball
at the palace. Frail Sophie, day after day, sits beside
the frailer Marie who is coughing away her lungs in
the infirmary, and never fancies that her patient kind-
ness will be recorded to her credit above. The Angel of
Death hovers overhead; but she does not fear him;
when the fear of love has departed out of life, death
ceases to terrify. She puzzles her little head in con-
sidering how much the coffin will cost; how much Mr.
Mould will charge for a decent burial; for she has
promised the dying girl that the emaciated body will
not be sent to the surgeons, and the forsaken sinner has
nlo relatives who will even consent to bury her out of
sight. The steady undemonstrative sense of duty which
actuates her, has nothing about it that is touched by
any romance; she entertained no violent attachment to
the other during life; her death causes her no violent
regret; the little interests of her dress and toilet have
remained quite as attractive as ever; and perhaps the
strongest emotion that she felt was when she found that
it would be necessary to send her new silk to the pawn-
broker for a day or two, to enable her to discharge Mr.
Mould's peremptory account. Looked at from one side
her conduct, has been noble and sacrificial; looked at
from the other, all the motives appear poor, meagre,
unsentimental—Fiaser's Magazine.
EXTRAORDINARY FEAT.—One day at Niblo's cele-
brated Garden in New York, where the Ravel Family and
Blondin were engaged in fulfilling a successful engage-
ment, the ordinary morning rehearsal was agreeably en-
livened by a novel incident : —A performance, illtstrative
of some of the Bedouin Arabs, was being gone through,
ready for that evening's programme, and at a particular
stage of the business one person represented a prisoner
surrounded by a crowd of soldiers armed with muskets
and fixedbayonets, from the midst of which he had to clear
himself by a vigorous leap. Antoine Ravel, whO was to
make the :jump, was busy re-arranging the grouping of
the soldiery, it not being exactly to his mind, and Mon-
• sieur Blondin, attired in ordinary citizen's costume, stood
close by, watching With a curious eye the slow progress
of affairs. Suddenly, by one of those erratic impulses
which at times come over him and impel him to attempt
the most hazardous enterprises, and without the slightest
intimation of his intention, he took three or four hurried
steps, and then with a tremendous bound threw a donble
summersault over the entire group—Antoine' soldiers,
muskets, and all—and instantly subsided eat his former
attitude of repose, as though he had done nothing at all
out of the way and the moving mass of bayonets were
only so many bulrushes.—Banks * Lift of Blondin.
SUPERSTITION IN THE EAST. The superstitions of
antediluvian ages, when genii guarded the Pyramids,
magicians built Memphis, enchanters quarried the rocks,
priests smelted the iron, and demons and talismans in-
terfered in every act of life, are not yet entirely departed
from modern Cairo. They are, on the contrary, far
more rife, and occupy a far more important place in the
thoughts of certain classes than they are ready to admit
—especially to a Frank. We remember once travelling
in Syria with a defeated pasha. The chief inhabitants
of a town came to wait :upon his excellency and condole
with him. After the usual formalities the conversa-
tion changed from fate and luck to enchantments. The
pasha spoke as a believer in the latter, and I, as a Frank,
was appealed to for cenfirmation. Not being willing
to:sacrifice truth to politeness, I hesitated; when, in a
moment, it was curious to observe every physiognomy,
even of bearded old sages, turned towards me with an
imploring look, as if they themselves knew the thing to
'
be an error, but they deemed it to be cruel to deprive
the defeated pasha' of the comfort to be derived from his
faith by any rade disclaimer of its soundness.—Colburn'
Hew Monthly.
MARRIAGE BY PURCHASE.—A system of marriage by
purchase is not without its inconvenience, particularly
when managed by men remarkable for sharpness in bar-
gaining, and with very undeveloped ideas as to the obli-
gations of honesty. The sale of a daughter afforded an,
admirable field, both to match-making mammas and cash-
loving papas, for a display of auctioneering talent. It
was their interest to puff the young lady's charms, and
they did this with so much success that the law came to
the assistance of over-persuaded bachelors. It was de-
clared, that if a man bought a maiden, with cattle, and
the father had deceitfully misrepresented his daughter's
attractions, the husband should be at liberty to return
her, and receive back his money.--The Anglo-Saxon
Home. By John ThrupP•
OLD SERMONS.—But how little trace remains of many,
things! All the work of preparing that sermon, and coin-
raitting it to memory; all the anxiety of the Sunday
all
morning ; u the mtones in which it was given; all
the warmth of heart it wakened in the people who listened
to it; all the volume of simple but telling Praise that pre-
ceded and followed it; have left no more trace than
that inscription of June 24th, 1817. I see the people
e
walking away home, by the various Paths which lead
from the church-door. ; I imaglil how the poor little
children in many homes were
count of the sermon, and coolrequired to give some ac-
count not do it; I think of the
good old clergyman going home from church, and having
a quiet turn in his garden; and of the sun going down
over each dwelling in the pastoral district which I can
see: and here is what stands for all that: in faded ink,
:he date I have already told you. And when a clergy-
man who is still living and preaching turns over his
stock of sermons, and looks at the inscription at the end
of each, which states the churches and the dates at which
each was given, he cannot but feel how little vestige re-
mains of the circumstances in which it was preached,
and of the impression made byit.—Frager's Magazine.

AN *ANECDOTE 017 ,JEMAIT WOOL
THE GLOOVBSTER .BAIVKER:'

This ,wealthy and. extraordinary' individual died on
the 20th April, 1836, having attained the age of eigh'y
years. Jemmy Wood—for by that name he was usually
recognised—wanthe sole -proprietor•of the old Glouces-
ter Bank, which had been established by his grandfather
in the year 1716, being one of those primitive banking
concerns which took their rise in a shop' business', 'of
which, perhaps, hardly one example now survives.
Weed's bank was conducted to the last by the proprie.
tor and two or three clerks, at the end of a cdmmon
chandlery shop, which they also attended
,to. Wood
wag latterly considered as the richest commoner in the
kingdom. His habits were those of a thrifty old
bachelor. In the bank or shop his whole time was
passed; he went to no one's house, and never invited
any person to his. It was his habit on Sundays to go to
church regularly, eat his dinner on his return, and then
take a walk into the country. lie left several wills of a
conflicting character, and, as a matter of course, these
'documents caused litigation, and gave employment to
lawyers and attorneys for years. Many anecdotes
illustrating his penuriousness are told, among others the
following :—One Sunday before leaving his house to
proceed to church, he gave to a little boy, who acted as
his servant, a chicken, which he intended to be roasted
for dinner. The cooking process was commenced; and
as the bird was turned and basted, the savoury steam
which it gave forth sharpened the boy's appetite, and he
ventured to his finger on the breast, which wassbeing
browned, and apply his finger to his mouth. The taste
was delicious! He became bolder, and picked away a
motsel of the breast of the bird; then another; other
bits followed, until none of the breast remained.
Hunger was gnawing at the boy's heart, andie could
not resist the temptation ; so the whole chicken soon
disappeared. His hunger now appeased, he saw his
fault, and, trembling at the prospect of meeting his
-thrifty master, like most boys after doinc, wrong, he
thought of hiding. On entering a closet adjoining the
the room, his eye fell on small bottle, having on. it a
label with the awful word 'poison,' in legible characters.
He feared death much, but his master still more, and in
a minute resolved to end his days; aceorordingly, he
drained the bottle, and was, as he thought, safe from
his master's rage. In a short time the old banker
appeared on the scene, resolved to enjoy his chicken and
glass of brandy and water. Great was his astonishment
to see the spit empty, and find the boy away. On
making a search he found the latter lying on the pantry
floor with the empty bottle, which. quickly brought
before his mind a solution of the mystery. The boy
was drunk, for the bottle contained old Wood's brandy,
which was marked poison,' to guard it from the possi-
bility of being touched by the servants. What the old
gentleman did with the lad is not recorded.—Chanibers'
Book of Days.

articles.title: FRANCE AND ENGLAND.
articles.text:
FRANCE AND ENGLAND.

(Pim the Spectator.)

.ssWill the terrible realities of the American struggle
between men speaking the same language, enjoying
hitherto the most unrestricted freedom of commercial
intercourse, bound together by the closest commercial
bonds—these producers, those consumers, traders,
manufacturers, capitalists—suffice to awaken the com-
mercial school out of its fool's paradise as to the effects
cf abolition of passports, treaties of commerce, interna-
tional exhibitions, and other devices for facilitating the
material "relations of mankind with each other, for
promoting a real unity among them, where moral sym-
pathy is wanting—where some institution, some form
of polity, juts out as a wall betWeennation and nation?
As slavery stands between the North and the South on.
the American continent, so stands the Imperial despot-
ism between France and England, or any other free
People. Till it fall, every mere attempt to pro-
mote material intercourse between the two countries
tends probably but to deepen the bitterness of France.
,The abolition of , passports for English subjects,
whilst these were' retained for Frencii, was felt as
an insult to the nation, and galls Frenchmen every
day to the quick. The benefits of the commercial
treaty are not visible yet in France to the many; its
bischiefe to the few are palpable. The International
rExhibition will:certainly have created more jealousies
Asa kit will have allayed. The very shopkeepers. of
'Paris, the class above all others who have most bene•
fited by late commercial changes, talk freely (though
not, of course, to their English customers) of the
'future war with England. For in truth the old Roman
historian's definition of a firm friendhip—' to will and
mot will the same things'—holds good between nations
as between men. The only true bond of union
between a free people and an oppressed one must lie
the sympathy of the former with the sufferings of the
latter—in their common hatred towards its oppressor.
Now, partly by our fault, partly without our fault,
this :tate of things does not yet exist between England
and France. We are not in general accustomed to dis-
tinguish sufficiently between France, and the tyranny
which weighs on France. Most Englishmen probably do
bate Napoleon lll.—perhaps even Lord Ranelagh
himself at the bottom of his heart (if his heart have a
bottom). But they hate him as the embodiment of
French ambition, not as the oppressor of France;
whilst at other times our statesmen, our journal-
ists, our public spouters, carry even their folly
eo far as to speak of him, or practically to treat
him as our bulwark, our trust, our ally against
France herself. A more stupendous absurdity never
surely entered into the brains of men or one which the
facts more palpably contradict. is it against the
French republic or against the French constitutional
monarehy, that the whole world stands, so to speak, at
4 attention' these many weary years, not daring to
pile arms? Is all history a blank, that despotism,
with its secrecy and promptitude of self-will, should be
c onsidered for one moment a better safeguard for peace
than freedom, with its publicity, its deliberations, even
when most tumultuous? It is our folly and our fault
that we should ever for an instant seem to lose sight of
the distinction between an oppressed nation and its
government—of the deep, vital, and abiding interest
which England has, not in the momentary quietude or
stupor of France—not in her mere material pros-
perity or clatter of monetary speculation but in her
freedom, her unchecked moral development. And let it
again be recollected, that every utterance of England in
praise of the Emperor and his system, in depreciation
of the people whom he rules, as well as every idle
tirade agarnst France not distinguishing between the
two, is sure to be translated, under the official sanction,
in the French newspapers, whilst every condemnation
of the Emperor's own acts, every expression of sym-
pathy with France against him, is carefully suppressed.
Hence, to use a single notorious recent instance, the
seizure of the English papers after the Aepromonte
failure, because they almost unanimously urged the
evacuation of Rome, which France herself longs for,
which it does not suit the Emperor's policy to effect.
F9r one raoment-the hearts of the two nations throbbed
in entire unison—but the wall was there to stop their
hearing each other. Thus, in spite of all official com-
pliments, the two countries are sedulously kept es-
tranged ; France remains ignorant of English sympathy
duction of every
towards her, and is fed from day to day with a repro-
fiippantjournalist's taunt, every silly
piece of national bunkum poured forth by after-dinner
volunteers, which may serve to excite her againsAe.

- THE BIG GOOSBEvatm., OUTDO.—It is known
that at certain seasons of the year our brethren of the
Press, in dearth of news, bring forth a few stock para-
graphs and send them round The best known of these
are the Big Gooseberry and the Child devoured by a
Pig.' But the following, which we (Morning News)
.clip from the Daily Express, eclipses
gooseberry and pig
stories by long odds Suicide Frustrated.—A French-
man resolved to be rid of life, went a little while before
high tide to a post set up the sea side. Ile had pro-
vided himself with a ladder, a rope, a Pistol, a bundle of
matches, and a phial of poison. Ascending the ladder,
he tied one end of the rope to the post, and the other
end round his neck. then he took the poison, set his
clothes on fire, put the muzzle of the pistol to his head,
and kicked away the ladder. In kicking down the
ladder he sloped the Pistol, so that the ball missed his
head and cut through the rope by which he was sus-
pended, he fell into the sea, thus extinguishing the
&trues of his clothes; and the sea water, which he in-
voluntarily swallowed,counteracted the poison; and thus,
in spite of his precautions, he remained .unhanged, un-
shot, unpoisoned, unburned and undrowned.'

articles.title: BEE-HIA-E, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1862.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIA-E, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1862.

MR. MASON ON TILE RECOGNTION
OF THE SOUTH:

The following letter from Mr. Mason is published in
the London organ of the Southern Confederacy. It 'is
in reply to a request from Mr. Boon, the secretary of
the committee of -the Stalybridge meeting, tbr Mr.
Mason's opinion as to the effect recognition would
have in terminating the war; and. also for any oti•ter
information that might strengthen the argumentacf
the speaker in favour of recognition:—
. September 19. IStil.
Sir,—l have the honour to receive your.letre2 of
the 17th inst., informing me of a projected meeting to
be held at Stalybridge, in Cheshire, of the ratepayers
of the town, who 'are to have under consideration the
question of recognition of the Confederate States d
America, and asking my opinion as to the effect that
such recognition would have in bringing about a
peace, and any other information I may deem pertinent
to the subject.
As a citizen of those States I do not feel at liberty to
refuse your request under the circumstances stated,
when, perhaps, otherwise to offer my opinione might be
deemed intrusive.

It is certainly a settled principle of international law
that when a new nation or empire is brought into ex-
istence as a separate and independent power, other
nations are at liberty, without giving cause of offence,
to recognise it as such, and to receive it as an equal in
the family of nations; and to entitle it to such recog-
nition it is only required that sufficient evidence be ex-
hibited of stability and permanence in the new Govern-
ment, coupled with the power to sustain itself in its new
position.
In the case of the Confederate States, I think it may
be confidently submitted that the facts which have
transpired since their separation from the United
States, both in the Cabinet and in the field, come fully
up to such requisitions, it has existed as a perfectly
organised Government, in full and unimpeded opera-
tion, for more than eighteen months; and as to its
ability, to sustain itself, its career in arms against
vastly superior forces may challenge the judgement of
the world. The present population of the Confederate
States comprises about 12,000,000 of people.
I think I may confidently assume as the public
juderoent of Europe, that the sevaration of these States
from the late United States is final and for ever, and
that in no possible contingency—even could the war bs
continued to their extermination—can they ever be re-
stored to the repudiated Union.
Under such circumstances, hew far it may be deemed
incumbent by other Governments publicly to acknow-
ledge the existing fast of such final separation, and thus
te recognise the new power, is for those Governmeut
to determine. Fortunately for us our people have shown
themselves net only self-reliantZbut worthy of that re-
liance, We have fought our battles unaided and alone,
and, until recently, uneheered by the nations looking
en. For the future we have no fears, nor would the
recognition to which you refer be of any value to us
except so far as it might tend to bring the war to a
close—a war to be waged henceforward hopelessly by
our enemy, and at which humanity shudders.
In reply to your inquiry as to what effect recognitioe
of our independence would have towards putting an
end to the war, I have only to say it would at once
and for ever dispel all delusion on the subject in the
United States. So long as it is withheld by Europe it
is taken as an admission in America that in Euroneau
judgment there may yet be a restoration of the broken
Union, and to that extent our adversaries may be en-
couraged to persevere. That I am warranted in speak-
ing a this as a delusion I Trey appeal to the verdict ot
every intelligent Englishman.
Again, you are aware that the war was commenced
and has been prosecuted for the purpose of puffin;
down an alleged rebellion. Our recognition by the
European Powers would be the decree of enlightened,
impartial, and able observers that a rebellion if one
ever existed, had been brought to an end, and there
stood in place of it, as acknowleged by them, a sepa-
rate, sovereign, and independent State, the equal of
any in the line of empire.
It is not in the experience of the world that a war
SO disastrous in its results to those now waging it
against the Confederate States, when they were Made
to understand that it was no longer conducted agairist
alleged rebels in arms, but against an acknowledged
equal political power, could long be maintained.
Such are my views on the questions you have sub-
tmit ed—briefiy, but I hope intelligently, given.
I have the honour to be, very respectfully,
Your obedient servant,
J. M. MAsoll.
TA 'William Boon, Esq., 54, Devonshire-street,
Portland-place, London.

articles.title: MIX IC 0.
articles.text:
MIX IC 0.

A letter from Vera Ortiz of the 18th of September,
in the Constitutionnel, says that letteis have been re-
ceived from the city of Mexico ta the 13th, and for the
first time for several weeks we hear something of what
is going on in the capital
The greatest confusion prevails in the Gcvrnment
since the departure of Doblado, who has retired into
his native State, taking with him 1,000 m la, a v:hole
eonvoy of waggons, and a great part of the archives
of his ministry. No one exactly knows what his
projects are, but the expectation is that he will soon
be seen at the head of a party favourable to the
intervention. The death of General Zarap;oza
an irreparable loss for the Juarist party. He was
the very soul of the army, and had acquired an
authority very rare in this unfortunate country. Uraga,
Ortega, and Comonfort are preparing to dispute the
vacant post, but neither of them is capable of filling it
properly. Articles have been published in the Mexican
journals by order of Juarez, in which the French are
represented as carrying on a completely savage war-
fare, pillaging and burning all that falls in their way.
Those infamous calumnies have caused great irritation
among the troops at Orizaba. Our communications
ith that place are very difficult, not on account of the
enemy, but from the bad state of the roads in conse-
quence Of the heavy rains.
General de Lorencez has published, in an order oi
the day, the following letter addressed to him by the
Emperor :
'My dear General,—' learnt with pleasure the
brilliant affair of the Cumbres, and with mortification
t,he check experienced in the attack against Puebla. It
is the fate of war to see reverses at times obscure the
splendour of success, but that is not a reason for being
discouraged. The honour of the country is engaged,
and you will be supported by all the resources which
you could look for, and of which you may stand in
need. Be to the troops under your orders the inter-
preter of my entire satisfaction at their courage and per-
severance in supporting fatigues and privations, flow-
ever distant they may be my solicitude is always with
them. I approve your conduct, although it does not
Appear to have been well understood by every one. You
did right to protect General Almonte, since he is at
war with the present Government of Mexico. All
those who seek a shelter under your flag have the
same right to your protection. But all that must not
in any way influence your conduct for the future. It
is contrary to my interest, my origin, and my princi-
ples, to impose any kind of government whatever on
the Mexican people; they may freely choose that
which suits them best. All I demand from them is
sincerity in their relations with foreign nations, and
I only desire one thing—the prosperity and independ-
ence of that fine country under a stable and regular
government. I renew to you the assurance of my
sentiments.,
' NazoLEorn'

CAUTION TO HOTEL-KEEPERS. A GENTLEMAN
SWINDLER.—On Friday last a gentleman in appearance
took up his quarters in one of our principal hotels, and
made himself perfectly at home on Saturday, going out
and in quite at his ease. He breakfasted heartily on Sun-
day morning, and before going out ordered dinner against
the hour of his returning, but that hour never came
round, as, to use a trade expression, he sloped,' nobody
knew where, without paying his bill, and leavinr, only a
few well worn articles of wearing apparel and 'a
per-
fumery-case to renumerate mine host for his accomoda-
tion and careful attentions. His sudden departure would
not have been of so great moment had he not purloined
the cash-box of a commercial gentleman staying at the
same hotel. The box had been placed by its owner on
Saturday night, locked, in a leather hat-box in his bed-
room. It was only ma going to remove the box on Mon-
day morning that the owner became aware of its removal.
It contained about £l4O in bills and money.—Duinfries
Standard.

DISASTROIN COLLISION AT SEA. The Hambnrg
steamer, running between Havre and Brest, came into
violent collision with a French barque, called the
Juanita, from Monte Video, on Friday morning, at
about five o'clock, when about six miles west of the
port of Havre. A strong south-wester was blowing,
and intense darkness prevailed. The Hamburg sank
directly. Ten of her passengers are known to have been
lost, and several others are missing. The captain and
mate were savect The total drowned or missing is
stated to be 26. The Hamburg formerly ran between
Havre and Southampton.—Manchester Guardian.
FRESH DISTURBANCES IN GREECE.—According to
information transmitted from Greece to Trieste, fresh
disturbances have broken out at Nauplia, where several
persons were wounded, and among them is mentioned
the son of the Deputy of Argos. Some arrests were
effected. This movement produced considerable excite-
ment at Athens, and large crowds assembled at the
moment of the landing of the prisoners. The armed
force was obliged to interfere and disperse the assem-
blage by poling use of their bayonets. Three pupils
of the university were wounded.

articles.title: CIRCULAR OF N. DROUYiK _DE
articles.text:
CIRCULAR OF N. DROUYiK _DE

_LEUYS.

The Moniteur publishes the following circular, ad-
dressed by 2d. Drouyn de Lhuys to the diplomatic agents
of France abroad:—
Paris, Oct. 18,
_1862._

Sir,—On taking possession of the post to which the
Emperor has deigned to call me anew. I think it useful
to tell you in what spirit I have accepted the mission
which has been confided to me. I need not revert with
you to the anterior acts and proceedings of the Imperial
government in the Roman question. His Majesty has,
however, more particularly manifested his way of think-
ing by a letter addressed to my predecessor, which the
Zoniteur of the 25th September last has made public.
This docunaeht sums up the Emperor's views with an
authority which any commentary could but weaken, and
I cannot do better than refer to it to-day. In
all the phases through which the question has
passed in thirteen years his Majesty's cimstant object,
as he has himself taken care to establish,
•has been
to reconcile the great interests he found divided ; and
the more serious those dissensions ,became the more
the Emperor deemed that his government ought to
labour to appease them, without, however sacrificing
anything of the principles which have been the perma-
nent rule of his resolutions. The policy defined with
such exalted and impartial reason has undergone no
change. It reniains animated by the same sentiments as
hitherto for two causes upon which it has lavished in
equal measure the testimonies of its solicitude. The
Roman question touches the highest interests of teligion
and policy; it arouses on all points of the globe scruples
the most worthy of respect; and in examining the diffi-
culties by which it is surrounded, the Emperor's govern-
ment regards it as its first duty to guard itself against
whatever might seem like precipitation on its part, or
might make it deviate from the line of conduct it has
marked out for itself.
Such is the point of view at which I have placed
myself in accepting the direction of foreign affairs. I
do not think it either necessary or opportune to enter
into longer developments on this head. It will suffice
for me to have summarily indicated, to you the order of
ideas from which I. purpose to draw my own inspirations
for the fulfilment of the Emperor's intentions.
Invariably faithful to the principles which have guided
it hitherto, his Majesty's Government will continue to
devote all its efforts to the work of conciliation which it
has undertaken in Italy, labouring at it with a full
sense of the difficulty and the grandeur of the task, with-
out discouragement and. impatience.—Accept, &c.,
DROUYN DE LiiijicS.

articles.title: LIFEBOAT PROCESSIOIV.
articles.text:
THE LIFEBOAT PROCESSIOIV.

A complete ovation was given on the 20th to the
lifeboat which was drawn, on her transporting carriage,
through the principal streets of the metropolis to the
river side. The lifeboat stood on its carriage at the
western entrance of the International Exhibition all the
morning, and was visited there by a large number of
persons. The boat was built by Messrs. Forrest, of
Limehouse, and the carriage by lir. J. Robinson, of
Kentish-town. The. boat . has a beautiful light and
handsome appearance. Its sides are painted a light
blue and its bottom and keel white, and about 'four
inches from the top of the bulwark is an oval vim or fen-
der, of bright red, all round the boat, to which are slung
loops of rope to assist in saving life in cases of shipwreck.
On the blue bows beneath, on the shield of an heraldic
device, is written, 'National Lifeboat institution,' -while
in the circle round the shield are the words, Supported
by voluntary contributions.' Each side of the boat is
fitted with five rowlocks, and one on each side close to
the rudder. There are ten oars—half of them blue and
half of them white—for propelling the boat, and two
long ones for use, in the stern .rowlocks to assist in
steering or otherwise in the working of the boat. The
stem and stern are alike, with the exception of the gear
for fixing the rudder at the stern. The inside of the
boat is painted white. The head and stern are filled in
with large air cases, and air boxes run round the sides
of the boat under the side seats. Each seat for the
rowers is made to accommodate two men rowing in a
line, and there are raised slabs on the seats, giving them
their exact place for sitting. Just inside, all round the
boat, are lines with floats to assist in saving life. From
the deck leading to the bottom of the boat are six large
tubes fitted with valves on the deck so as to let through
the water that may be shipped, but to let none up from
unaer. A neat, compact, prettily constructed brass
pump is fixed in the boat for emptying her in case of
leakage. Two masts and rigging are provided for
sailing.
The procession was under fhe Management of Cap-
tains Maynard and Brown. It was headed by about
fifty of their men belonging to .the Royal Naval
Reserve, with their colours and their admirable' brass
band. The lifeboat and carri me will leave London in
the course of a week or so for eynemoutla, Northumber-
land, where every winter some dreadful shipwrecks
take place; and this splendid lifeboat is therefore likely
to be of essential service in succouring suffering
humanity in its most helpless state.

articles.title: INDIA.
articles.text:
INDIA.

We have received the Bombay Gazette of the 27th of
Sept. We take the following from its Overland
Summary' :
A large and influential public meeting was held in
the Town Hall, Bombay, on the 17th of Sept., for the
purpose of taking into consideration the best means of
assisting to alleviate the present great distress among
the mill-hands of Lancashire. His Excellency Sir
Bartle Frere, K.C.8., presided, and pronounced the
most effective speech on the occasion. The gum of one
lac and 9,000 rupees (X 10,900 was subscribed on the
spot • the Hon. Rustomjee Jamsetjee and Mr. Corset-
jee spot;
Paruck each contributing 25,000 rupees.
A large committee was appointed, and now at work
successfully in raising subscriptions. The amount
realised to date is about 2,950,000 rupees (L 25,000 By
the present mail the sum of one lac of rupees
(ten thousand pounds) is forwarded to England.
Accounts received from Thibet announce the progress
of revolutionary disturbances there, of such a nature as
to lead to the suspicion that the Nepaul Government
is not entirely unconnected with the actors in them.
A mission is to be dispatched to the Deb Rajah and
the Dhurmo Rajah at Bootan, a medical and four
military officers, with a Ghoorka, guard, accompanying
the representative of the British Government; the
guard to consist of 50 men. What the exact object ot
this mission is has not transpired, but we suppose that
it is of a mixed political and commercial nature. We
are on friendly relations with these rajahs, and trade
between our subjects and theirs would be mutually
beneficial. By latest dates from Cabool, September
3, there had been four battles fought between the
Ameer's troops and those of Sultan Ahmed Jan.
The Ameer was victorious in every action. The
loss on both sides was great. Sultan Ahmed Jan was
shut up in Herat and could not move. The Ameer
had laid siege to Herat, and had ordered his sons and
Khans to erect their several batteries and prepare
mines to reduce and storm the place. A general attack
on Herat was talked of in the Ameer's camp. The
police of the Etawah district have captured a man
named Sheo Churn, who was the senior Suba,dar of the
detachment of the Loodianah Regiment, which
mutinied at Jaunpore on the sth of ?tine, 1857, and
murdered the off;,7.er in command, and Mr. R. B.
Cuppage, of the I.hvil Service. It has been decided
by the Chief Justice of the High Court, Calcutta, that
all pleadings in that court shall be in the English
language. The same rule will probably be adopted in
Madras and Bombay. The Commissioner of Police,
Southern Division, Bombay Presidency, has officially
reported that the circuiation of chupattees has ex-
tended to all the collectorates of the division, with
the exception of Rutnagherree and North Canara.
The magistrates and superintendents of police are
everywhere on the alert, and have taken measures to
suppress the distribution. The Nawaub of Lucknow
has been convicted of forgery by the Commissioner of
Lucknow. He has been sentenced to a fine of 40,000r5.
and to the forfeiture of all rank and title. Captain
Ramsay, the lately appointed agent to the East India
Cotton Agency of Loudon, has applied to Government
for a lease of a certain quantity of ground to be used
for a cotton depot on the line of railway in Berar, and
his request has been granted. The Chief Justice of
Calcutta has nominated Baboo Sumbhoonath Pundit to
the vacant judgeship of the High Court. It is in con-
templation to build a grand arsenal for Central India
on the site of the village of Kirkee, to which the ord-
nance stores of every description from the Poona Ah-
mednugger, and Belgaum arsenals will be removed.

A STRANGE STORY.—The Journal de la Nievre re-
lates the following story A man, named Content, 46
years of age, in comparatively easy circumnances
residing near the Faubourg Saint-Antoine at Nevers, had
a mania for hiding his money, and he had selected a hole
in his stable just over a beam for that purpose. In that
place he had deposited his treasure, amounting to 700 f.
in gold. A few days since he went to see that his
treasure was safe, and wns thunderstruck at finding that
the money had dis Appeared. His suspicions fell on a
cobbler, named Guyot, who resided at a short distance
from him. Arming himself with a loaded pistol, he
went to the cobbler's house, and finding him sitting at
his work, discharged the pistol point blank at him, but
fortunately missed him, the cobbler by some accident
falling at the moment from hio stool to the ground.
Content, thinking he had killed the man, hurried back
to his own house' and reloading the weapon, attemptcd
to blow out his brains, but in his agitation only broke
his lower jaw, the wound of which is not very sezious.

articles.title: FAT-eiL FIRE IN HULL.
articles.text:
FAT-eiL FIRE IN HULL.

About half-past seven o'cleek on Sunday evening the'
most 81:4rtaing fire which has been witnessed in if nil
for a number of year's broke out in the premises
,of
Messrs. John Lee Smith and Co., wholesale grocers, &c.,
High-street. information, was at once conveyed to' the
police-office, and men were despatched with the necessary
apparatus. The premises in which the fire originated
are situate on the banks of the river Hull, and, owing
to the tide being out at the time, an adequate supply of
water could not be obtained on that side. In addition
to this drawb,ick, the wind was blowing a complete gale,
which fanned the flames and caused them to rage with
the most fearful fury. The contents of the building
were most of them very inflammable, consisting in great
part of flax tallow, saltpetre, oils, &e. Ilui dings con-
taining valuable stores surrounded the burning pile on
every side, including a bonded store containing hun-
dreds of gallons of spirits, and great fears were at 'first
entertained for the safety of those places. About
an hour after the fire was discovered the roof fell in with
a tremendous crash, illuminating the heavens for miles
around. Fortunately the rain fell in torrents during
the fire, otherwise the shipping which was lying along
the quay must have become a prey to the devouring
element, as, owing to the tide being out, it was impos-
sible to move them. One unfortunate accident occurred
in a narrow passage in the rear of Messrs. Smith and
Co.'s offices. Several policemen were here directing a
stream from a stand-pipe into the great body of flame,
which was raging in the centre of the premises, whet,
without any previous warning; a wall, four stories in.
height, fell with a tremendous crash. Retreat it so
narrow a place was almost impossible, and six poor
fellows were buried in the ruins. Great excitement
now prevailed, as the flames shot up with- such fury
as to drive all before it, and it was not until the lapse
of several minutes that a force of men could be set to
work to release the men who lay beneath the ruins.
Several brave fellows, and among them some of the
crew of Her Majesty's ship Cornwallis, at length volun-
teered to go to their assistance, but, owing to the dense
smoke which then prevailed, they could not remain in
the place more than a few minutes before they were
driven back almost suffodated, and it was feared that
the whole number would fall a prey to the flames.
However, by the men constantly relieving each other, a
great quantity of rubbish was removed, and at length
they came upon one poor fellow, who turned out to be a
stoker an board Her Majesty's gunboat Ruby. After
the lapse of an hour a policeman was taken out fear-
fully mangled, and his recovery is very doubtful. Two
or three others were subsequently taken out and removed
to an adjoining coffee-house, where medical aid was
procured. About' 2 o'clock in the morning the lifeless
body of Police-constable Itedfearn, 79, was discovered
in the ruins; but, owing to a large beam being
laid across his body, he could not be removed,
as the movitig of the beam would, in all proba-
bility, have brought down the 'remaining portion of
the wall. In addition to the poor fellow who lost his
life, seven are very seriously injured, the recovery of
three of them being very doubtful. The cause of the
fire and the damage done are at present unknown,
although, owing to the nature of the stores destroyed,
the loss must amount to several thousands of pounds.
The premises and stock are insured.

articles.title: DUKE'S ADVICE TO THE
articles.text:
THE DUKE'S ADVICE TO THE

NAVVIES.

On Wednesday the foundation stone of a new viaduct
on the Inverness and Perth Junction Railway, at
Bo wally, near Bunkeld, was laid with Masouic honours
by the Duke of Athole, Grand Master-Mason of Scot-
land. The viaduct is to cross the Tay, in the midst of
a picturesque Highland region, in two spans of 210 ft.
and 145 ft. After the ceremony the Duke was presented
by the navvies (through the contractor, Mr. Gewans),
with a stone cup, carved with Masonic emblems, set on
a marble base. In acknowledging the gift the Duke
said, 'I can assure you, navvies, that nothing could
have been more gratifying to my feelings than to
receive this tribute. When we first heard of the rail-
way coming through this part of the country many
people were much alarmed at -whatthe navvies would do.
(Laughter.) However, when they came, I was so much
pleased, on the whole, with their conduct that I have
endeavoured, I hope to my interest, to be good friends
,vith them.— (Cheers.) All parties connected with me
have given me a good report of them. They have done
as little damage to my property as possible—(laughter)
—and on the whole have •behaved themselves remark-
ably well.—(Cheers.) They have treated the people
of the country in a friendly manner, and, if they
quarrel a little among themselves, it seems to nae
that they rather like it.—(Laughter.) I see among the
faces before me some that I saw lately when I visited
the huts. I endeavoured on that occasion to give
them a short lecture, but I am afraid they have not
profited much by that. (Laughter.) Mr. Gowans has
told us how kind the navvies are to their brethren.
This is no doubt true, but I have been also told that so
long as a navvy has a shilling in t_Docket he won't
do a day's work. (Laughter.) 11 !ma I visited the
huts I advised them not to spend their money so fast,
but I'm afraid they won't take my advice. Their con-
duct, however, towards the country people has been
exemplary, and, if now and then there is something
• wrong, the navvies I believe are not to blame, for there
are people going about the country who are not navvier
at all, but who commit deeds for which the navvies are
blamed. (Cheers.) In conclusion, I will say that I
value this gift more than I can tell, and I hcpe that it
will be handed down as an heirloom in my family, to
show the kindly feelings that have led the navvies to
present it to me. (Loud cheers.)

A SVESTITUTE ron COTtON DISCOVERED IN 1754.—
The following interesting letter, with the paragraph
appended to it, has been published in a Dublin paper :
As the scarcity of cotton is now so much felt, a sub-
stitute for it is very desirable. Can any of your
readers explain if anything be now known relative to
the following statement, as given in the Gentleman's
jifagazine in February, 1754, thus ?—" Scotland.—A
person .of fortune in this kingdom has found out a
method of dressing a common weed so as to produce a
line, strong, even thread, of which a kind of cloth may
be made resembling the-finest muslin. The proper sea-
son for dressing this vegetable is the beginning of
summer." If this vegetable can now be discovered it
may be of -great importance. Relative to the manufac-
tures of that time, it states that, "before the prohibi-
tion of French cambrics and lawns, the greatest value
of those manufactured in this kingdom did not exceed
£30,000 per annum; but since the bill took place, the
manufacture at Glasgow and Paisley only exceeds
£lOO,OOO per annum in. lawns of different sorts, exclu-
sive of lawn handkerchiefs, whichthey have also exported

in great quantities."'
GARIBALDI AND TIIE TRADES OF LONDON.—General
Garibaldi having in letters to friends in England signi-
fied his intention of shortly visiting this country, to
thank them in person for the sympathy manifested in his
behalf, and for the interest taken in the cause of Italian
unity, preparations have already commenced for giving
a public welcome to the Italian hero on his visit to the
metropolis. A preliminary meeting has been convened
of the influential and leading men in the metropolitan
trade societies, to consider the propriety of the trades, as
a body, joining in the proposed demonstration. Should
this course be decided upon, each trade will be at once
called upon to appoint its delegates to carry out the
necessary arrangements, and the friendly societies, such
as the Foresters, Oddfellows, Druids, Old Friends, &c.,
will be also invited to take part in the proceedings.

ANEW REMEDY FOR SMALL-FOX.--The Saracenia
purperca, or Indian Cup, a native plant of Nova Scotia,
which we mentioned some time ago as being the specific
used by the Indians against the small-pox, bids fair to
realise the expectations entertained by medical men of its
efficacy. In a letter addressed to the American Medical
limes, Dr. Frederic W. Morris, President Physician of
the Halifax Visiting Dispensary, states that this saracenia,
a papaveraceous plant, will cure small-pox in all its
forms within twelve hours after the patient has taken
the decoction. However alarming and numerous the
eruptions, he says, or confluent and frightful they may
be, the peculiar action of the medicine is such that very
seldom is a scar left to tell the story of the disease, if
either vaccine or variolus matters is washed with the infu-
sion of the saracenia, they are deprived of their con-
tagious properties. So mild is the medicine to the taste,
that it may be largely mixed with tea and coffee and,
given to connoisseurs in these beverages to drink without
their being aware of the admixture. The medicine has
been successfully tried in the hospitals of Nova Scotia,
and its use will be continued.
GRAND DINNER FORTY OR FIFTY YEARS AGO.—A
prime difficulty to overcome was the placing on your
fork, and finally in your mouth, some half-dozen diffe-
rent eatables, which occupied your plate at the same
time. For example, it would contain, say, a slice of
turkey, a piece of stuffing, a sausage, pickles, a slice of
tongue, cauliflower, and potatoes. According to habit
and custom, a judicious and careful selection from this
little bazaar of good things was to be made, with an
endeavour to place a portio: of each in your mouth at
Oa° came Foment.—Capta Gronow.

articles.text:
THE ).-.ANDYFORD .271CTI?DE1:

• (From the Glasgow Horning, Joupasal.)
The inquiry ordered by the Home Secretary was
opened on Friday by the royal commissioner, George
Young,. Esq., advocate and sheriff of Haticlingtonshirei
in the chambers of Sheriff Sir A. Alison, County-build
ings. Mr. Young arrived in the city on Friday fore—
noon, and, after a conference with Sir Archibald Alison,
proceeded, accompanied by Mr. Fiscal Gemmel and Mr.
Dixon,. one of Mrs. M'Lachlan's agents, to. the house of
Mr. Fleming, 17.„ Sandyford-place, after a minute in-
spection of the premises, returning to the County-
buildings. Instructionshaving, on Thursday last, been
given that all the witnesses to be examined should be
cited to- appear on Friday, the examination of them was
at once proceeded with, in presence of Mr. Gemmel on.
behalf of the crown, and Messro. Dixon, Stracb.an, and
Wilson on behalf of Mrs. M`Lachlan. The examina-
tion lasted till six p.m., and was held with closed
doors,' no one being allowed to enter except those
officially elan-aged in the investigation. Some of the
detective officers, Mr. John Fleming, sea., Mr. John
Fleming, jun., Mary Black or Adams, washerwoman,
Stobcross-street, and. her daughter, the girl Sarah Black
of Adams, George Paton, the milkman, and Donald
M'Quarrie, the milkboy, wita others of the witnesses
examined on the trial, and.all those who have since the
trial come forward with additional items of evidence
were summoned to appear, and were in attendance.

The examinations and cross-examinations as con-
ducted on Friday before the commissioner are a sealed
book. At some little pains we have been able to
collect tte following authentic outline of the new evi-
dence. _ .

The first witness examined was Mr. John Fleming,
accountant, St. Vincent-street. -He was under exami-
nation, for up wards of an hour. We have no informa-
tion as to the nature of the evidence given by this
gentleman, or by his son, John Fleming, jun., who was
next examined for close on an hour. Mr. Stewart,
jeweller, residing at 16, Sandyford.place, was next
examined. His evidence was a repetition, to some ex-
tent, of what has already appeared in our columns.
Mr. Stewart's evidence is an important corroboration of
Mrs. M'Lachlan's statement. On the night of the
murder (Friday evening), Mr. Stewart returned to
his house about half-past 10 o'clock p.m. His
family had that day gone down to the coast,
and about 11 o'clock he retired to rest. Imme-
diately thereafter he fell asleep. He was arous,d
from his sleep by a scream', as of a person in dis-
tress. He got up and looked around him, but did
not examine his watch. He distinctly noticed that
there was about the same degree of light as when he
had gone to bed. It might have been immediately
after he had fallen asleep, but he is certain it was
before one in the morning. His reasons for affirming
that this occurred before one o'clock will be remembered
by our readers, and need not be now r: peated. Mr.
Stewart's impression at the time was that the scream
that awoke him proceeded from Mr. Fleming's house,
and immediately on hearing of the murder he associated
the two. When the murder was discovered he intormed
Mrs. Stewart that if the truth would ever be made
known as to when the first blows were struck, it would
be found that this was not at four o'clock, as repre-
sented by old Fleming, but:some time betwixt 11 and 1
o'clock.
After Mr. Stewart, a witness named Miss Mary
M'lntyre, a dressmaker, was examined. Her evidence,
as will be seen, is of vital importance; and, taken in
connexion with Mr. Steware's, and the evidence of
Mrs. Walker and Miss Dykes (with which our readers
are familiar), seems to place beyond question that Mrs.
M`Lachian has told the truth when she stated that she
was not in Mr. Fleming's house when the first wounds
were inflicted on the deceased.
Evidence of Miss Mary M'lntyre, milliner and dress-
maker, No. 77, Port-street, Oranstonhill.
I was in the habit of sewing in the house of Mrs.
Service, No. 8, Sandyford-place. I had been sleeping
there at night for some time while the family were in
London. They returned on Thursday, the 3rd of July
last. I was sewing in the house of Mrs. Service on
Friday, 4th July, and on the following Saturday, Mon-
day, and Tuesday. I slept in the house during that
time. After my sewing,e as done on the Friday f went
down to my house in Port-street to see my brother about
some business he had been engaged on during the' day.
I left Mrs. Service's house for the purpose about nine
o'clock, and, after being some time in my own house, I
set out to return to No. 8, Sandyford-place. I event
up Elderslie-street. At Cranstonhill-street there
is a spirit shop, which, as I passed, I observed had
just closed, as I saw under the door the lights still
earning within. This attracted my attention, because
I had not thought till I saw this that it was so
late, and by this circumstance I saw that it was after
eleven o'clock. This spirit shop is on the south of
the Dumbarton road. 1 usually take about eight or
ten minutes to go from any house to Mrs. Service's. I
went straight up Elderslie-street. When I came near
to the lane behind Sandyford-place, I saw Mrs. Walker
and Miss Dykes, both of whom I was familiar with by
sight, standing at the close mouth near the lamp upon
the pavement. As I was near the cornmeof the lane, and
just at the small shoemaker's booth on the west side of
the street, a little south:of the mouth of the lane, I saw a
woman go into the line. She came down the street
from the east corner of Sauchiehall-street, and turned
round quickly into the lane. At the same time a gentleman
passed her and looked hard into her face, and then held
straight down the street. The woman had on some
light grey cloak or shawl, but I can't say as to her
bonnet or her gown. When I came up to where Miss
Dykes and Mrs. Walker were standing, I heard them
remarking on the woman who had gone along the lane.
I heard them say the words—' In there at this time of
night,' which 1 understood to mean that they were
wondering rhat she was that went in there at that time of
night. It passed through my mind at the time that they
would perhaps wonder what I was doing, or who I was, out
at the same hour. I passed close by them, and went round
the corner into Sauchiehall-street, opposite Sandyford-
place. I was walking rapidly, and arrived in a minute
or two at the carriage entrance leading into Sandy-
ford-place, nearly opposite Mr. Fleming's house,
No. 17, Sandyfbrd - place. There were two or
three ladies and a gentleman with them, and also
two young men all standing at the opening, talking
of something that had attracted their notice. As I
came up, one of them said, I heard —,' but I can-
not say what it was that the person speaking
said had been heard by them. I understood that it was
something that had struck them. Another person of the
party said, I think it came from that house where the
i light s,' pointing up to a house where there was a light
in the front area windows. I think there was no light
but in the area, and no light in the houses on each side
of the one in question. The house the light was in I
am quite sure was No. 17. I went back repeatedly
since; and, from examination of the place, I am sure it
was No. 17. The light came through the white blinds.
I stopped to listen, but I did not hear anything, and the
ladies went on towards Charing-cross, and the two
young men towards Royalecrescent. I followed them
westward, walking rather slowly; but I had just
gone a few steps, when just opposite No. 17, I
heard • something which made me stop again. It
was a distinct moan, as of some one in great dis-
tress. It came, I think, from those lighted win-
dows. I thought so at the time, and at first I half
thought of going up to see what it was; but from the
character of the sound I was a little frightened, and,
instead of going up, went straight on to Mrs. Service's.
The sound 1. heard was a low, wailing moan, as of pain;
and although it was not long continued nor repeated, it
was quite distinct. After 1 had stood for a minute, I
went on, and Mrs. Service let me in. I mentioned the
circumstance on Monday night
.to Ann Campbell, Mrs.
Service's servant, when some one came in with neva
that there had been a murder in Mr. Fleming's, in No.
17. I said, when I heard this that if the murder had
taken place on Friday night, I would have said that it
was what I had heard at No. 17 on that night. I
mentioned the matter frequently after that, before
the trial and after it, but I did not think it
of any consequence to mention it to the authorities.
After I mentioned it to some friends, I was strongly
advised that it was my duty to state all I knew. I
have ascertained from Ann Campbell that she remem-
bers distinctly the conversations on the Monday and
Tuesday I had with her on the matter. She was ex-
amined before Mr. Young regarding what I have stated
to-day. My brother David, and also two servants of
Mrs, Service's sister—Mrs. Macfie—were present on the
Monday night when I mentioned what I had heard;
but these servants are now in Islay, and I don't know
whether they remember the circumstance or not.
Ann Campbell, who is referred to in Miss M'lntyre's
evidence, was next examined.
Mrs. Walker's evidence was next taken, and acquires
additional importance in respect of the preceding testi-
numy, as, in conjunction with that given by Miss Dykes,
it puts the identification of Mrs. M‘Lachlan with the
Party seen by Miss M'lntyre beyond question.

A painful sensation has been produced amongst the
habitual British residents in Rome by the accidental
death of Mr. Shepherd, jun., son of the geravt of the
Anglo-Roman Gas Company, last week, on the occasion
of the opening of the central railway station in that
city. Private letters state that Mr. Shepherd fell from
a bridge or, platform, and sustained injuries which
produced his death, after a lingering agony of three
days.

Arras, the brother of the Archbishop of Bourges. He
held the legations of Ducal Saxony, Florence, Parma,
and Turin, and.lastly that of Berlin. He is personally
known to the Pope, to whom at the time of his exile at
Gaeta he was several times dispatched en missions by
the lqiniftter for Foreign 4,.fr‘kira.

METROPOLITAN CATTLE MARKET.

OcToßzu 20.—The total imports of foreign stock into
London last week amounted to 81,909 head. In the cor-
responding week in 1861 we received 9,501; in 1800,
12,558; in 1859. 8,395; in 1858, 3,609; in 1857, 4,d0;
and in 1856, 4,210 head. There was rather a large sup-
ply at foreign stoek on sale in to-day's market, the time
of year considered, and its general quality was tolerably
good. Sales progressed slowly, at barely late rates. The
arrival of beasts troth up from our own grazing districts
was seasonably extensive as to number, but rather defi-
cient in quantity. Prime breeds commanded a steady sale,
at prices quite equal to Monday last, the top figure being
4s. Bd. per .81bs. Otherwise, the beef trade was in a
sluggish state, at Thursday's decline in the quotations of
2d. per Sibs., and a clearance was not effected. From
Lincolnshire, Leicestershire, and Northamptonshire we
received 3,000 shorthorns, Bz.c.; from other parts of
England, 80(1 various breeds; and from Ireland, 1,000
oxen and heifers. There were no fresh beasts in
the market from Scotland. We were tolerably well,
but not to say heavily, supplied with most breeds of
sheep, which came to hand in fair condition. Generally
speaking the mutton trade was rather active, and the cur.
rencies realised on this day se'nnight were fully sup-
ported. Downs and the best half-breds changed hands at
from ss. 6d. to ss. Bd. per 3 lbs. Calves—the supply of
which was moderate—moved off slowly, at Thursday's
quotations—viz.,
.from 3s. 10d. to ss. per 8 lbs. The bulk
of the supply was composed of foreigners, in good condi-
tion. Prime small pigs commanded a steady sale at very
full prices. Large hogs were firm, with a moderate de-
maud.

HATES THE ASSASSIN.—Hayes-hunting is still carried
on by the constabulary in various parts of Ireland, and
affords exciting exercise, though there is little chance of
the pursuers getting on the trail of the murderer. With-
in the last few days they have beaten every cover in the.
counties of Tipperary, Waterford, and even Down,
where he was likely or unlikely to be concealed. The
places searched included the underground pits of the
collieries at Earlshill, Tipperary, in which a large party
of constabulary, headed by John Monaghan, Esq.,
continued searching for several hours.

THE DISTRESS IN THE COTTON
DISTRICTS.

PAST LANCASHIRE CENTRAL OPERATIVES BELIEF FUND.

We earnestly hope that the working classes will
lose no time in contributing to this fund. We would
impress upon our readers that the smallest sums will be
of great use in aiding this charitable object. If every
reader of the BEE-HIVE would contribute a penny or
twopence per week, either at their Workshops or at
their Society Rooms, and forward it to this office, the
total amount raised would be large, and many suffering
fellow workmen relieved. In the above district alone
there are 69,000 operatives out of employment, and
26,000 working short time. Will our readers help to
relieve the wants of these, their fellow creatures, dur-
ing the coming winter? They will; and the contribu-
tions they forward to the BEE-Ilivn shall be a proof of
