articles.title: STJ NIMA.RY. FOREIGN.
articles.text:
STJ NIMA.RY.
FOREIGN.

AMERICAN papers inform us of an angry
struggle in the Northern States between the
Democrats and the Republicans respecting the
State elections. Commercial and monetary
matters are also becoming dull, heavy and even
threatening. Gold had seen at 29 premium,
and then fell to 274, although it is believed here
that 29 was again attained before the depar-
ture of the steamer.
Severe fighting has again occurred in the
South and West. The Confederates had at-
tacked Corinth, bnt were repulsed • after a
sharp engagement, with heavy loss on both
sides. General Price led the Confederates
against the Federalists under General Rosen-
cranz. Figures are not given, but four to five
thousand men of both armies were probably
killed and wounded in the attempt to gain
Corinth, and in its defence.

A battle has been fought near Perrysville, in
Kentucky, between General Bragg, the
Confederate leader, and General Buell, who
commands the Federalists. We have only
Buell's statement, and from its cautious tone
we may infer that he gained nothing, but he
lost two thousand men in killed and wounded;
and among the former, it is said, two of his
generals. This battle was fought on the Bth,
current.

Intelligence has been received from New
York to the evening of the 11th, and the city
was startled by the information that General
Steuart, who leads the cavalry of the Confe-
derates on the Potomac, and is ger: erally at the
beginning of all mischief to the North, had
passed the Federal armies many mix' es to the
West, rode through a slip of Maryland, entered
Pennsylvania, seized Chambersburg, w:th five
hundred horses, found at the railway eation,
and while respecting all private property,
made very free with public property. Gem eral

Steuart's invasion of Pennsylvania may only be
a foray for the purpose of seizing stores, or he
may have some other purpose in view. It may
have been observed that the Washington
Government have not published General
ll‘Clellan's report of the battle at Antietam,
and the subsequent day's transactions. South-
ern papers now supply a remarkably red ver-
sion.

They say that the Confederate army Tested
on the ground of Antietam until the evening
of the day following the battle before they
began to cross the Potomac. The greater part
passed over safely, but an attempt was made
by General Burnside on Saturday the 21st Sep-
tember, to cross and seize some batteries sta-
tioned on one point by General Stonewall Jack-
son. The assailants were enveloped by a large
force under Jackson and destroyed.
One Southern journal says that four bri-
gades of the Federals were caught in this trap,
others make the number fewer; but as the
prisoners are put at one thousand five hundred,
and the Federalists drowned and slain at a
larger figure, the blow may have been severe.
General Bragg advises the North Western
States to make peace for themselves, offering
to guarantee the free navigation of the rivers;
but in the meantime this good advice is likely
to be rejected both in the North and in the
West.

Yellow fever on the Mexican coast had
proved a bitter enemy to the French, and the
Mexicans continue to promise a fierce recep-
tion to the invaders, for whom reinforcements
had arrived, but rains prevented them from
leaving Vera Cruz._

A ra- ail. from China brings intelligence of
many deaths from cholera in the northern pro-
vinces; more fighting in the central portion of
the empire, and dull trade
_everywhere.

Herat in central Asia is besieged by Dost
Mohammed, but our Eastern Government con-
sider the present dispute a private quarrel
among the Affghan tribes, with which they
are not required to intermeddle.
The nobles of Poland have petitioned the Em-
peror of Russia for certain reforms, which he is
unlikely to concede to them at present. The
petition may be considered in the light of a
notice that Poland lives.

All Italy is agitated under the refusal of
France to part with Rome; and a large
party in France distinctly express their
opinion that Italy should have its capi-
tal. They only hold Napoleon's opinion
when he was a member of the French
Republican Chambers. Ratazzi, the Italian
Premier, will be obliged to resign, un-
less he can adopt more decisive measures than
he has yet taken to deliver himself from the
imputation of being a deputy from Paris.
The Prussian representatives are now dis-
missed, and the King, along with the nobles,
have carried their point and spend the peoples
money without the sanction of the Lower
House. It is an unpolitic proceeding; but
the Germans only protest,

articles.title: COLONIAL.
articles.text:
COLONIAL.

Contradictory intelligence comes fro m
British Columbia, but the contradictions
originate in the fact that all immigrants are
not successful; while provisions are extremely
dear, and the cost of living is enormous.

Australian papers state-that the gold quartz
in Victoria will maintain the present mining
operations for fifty years. Provisions are now
cheap there, and with the exception of house
rent, living in Melbourne is cheaper than in
our English towns.ss

TheB-outhAustralians propose to grow cotton,
and employment is said not to be abundant in
that colony, while wages are comparatively
low.

The letters and papers from India justify the
expectation of a continued current of cotton
ships to our ports from the present date to the
end of February', or the commencement of
March next.

articles.title: DOMESTIC.
articles.text:
DOMESTIC.

The most terrible storms of the year have
been experienced round our coasts during the
last and present week, resulting in a great loss
of property, and a much more lamentable loss
of life.

Consols have varied slightly since our last,
and are quoted at 93i. Corn has maintained
the price of last week, notwithstanding large
arrivals at nearly all our ports.
Employment in every department, except
cotton, has improved, but the sufferings in the
cotton districts increase. We repeat the
warning that the local rates and general sub-
scriptions are entirely inadequate for their task,
and that the Government neglects a duty by
not interfering in behalf of this population, by
way of loan, chargeable on the rates for a
number of years.
Certificates to the patient endurance of the
operatives, read or spoken at public meetings,
are agreeable, and so far satisfactory, but their
case demands more than "good words." The
nation should not endeitvour to take the
smallest share of this loss and suffering; but
rather to relieve the weak from a burden that
rests on them; only because we forget na-
tional duties and responsibilities.

articles.title: OCCUPATION OF ROME.
articles.text:
THE OCCUPATION OF ROME.

A NUMBER of the citizens of London, who
desired to express ther goodwill to GARIBALDI,
were refused by the LORD MAYOR permission
to meet in the Guildhall, because our chief
magistrate disliked any reference to the French
occupation of Rome. The Mayor of Bradford
declined to call a meeting of his townsmen to
address GARIBALDI, probably from the same
reason. A meeting was held in Newcastle, and
official notice was taken of language employed
there. Open air assemblages in the London
Parks have been suppressed by Sir RICHARD
MAYNE, because they were liable to interrup-
tion by an organised mob of bludgeonists. On
the same principle the Commissioner of Police
should issue his proclamation against gold
chains and watches being carried through the
streets on the persons of his subjects, because
the owners may, be robbed of their jewelry and
watches. People should not present bludgeon-
ists or ticket of leave men with temptation.
Even meetings in schoolrooms for the peaceable
discussion of political questions have been as-
sailed at Birkenhead. Dr. GRANT, of the
Roman Catholic diocese of Southwark, advises
his flocks not to break the heads of men who
happen to differ from their pinions, and he
beseeches employers to watch the conversation
of their men, and to prevent the discussion of
irritating subjects. Sir GEORGE B3WY:ER and
the OTIONOGHUE apologise for, or defend, the
conduct of the persons who interrupted the
Hyde Park meeting; and some of the Dublin
journalists are collecting subscriptions to re-
ward the ringleaders in this war. The march
of events leads apparently to a rough road.
Loris NAPOLEON has dismissed M. THOITVENEL,
who had become restive at the appearance of
the Roman question. The EMPEROR has given •
M. THOUVENEL'S late office of Secretary for
Foreign Affairs to M. DRIJOYN DE Dins, who
being a conservative in other respects, is also
conservative of the position at Rome. A step
of this nature causes alarm in Italy, where it is,

obvious that the Government cannot secure
Rome for a capital within any reasonable time.
LOUIS NAPOLEON should not maintain the pre-
tence of keeping the affairs of Rome -under the
management of his Foreign Office, for at would
be more discreet and honest to place them in
the keeping of the Minister of the Interior.
The French soldiers are at home in Rome, and
the French Goverment should create a depart-
ment of the Tiber.

Some time ago the Times ackised the Italians
to claim Rome; but being 44 all things by
turns, and nothing long," it now urges them to
acquiesce in the policy of NAPOLEON, and wait
for justice on time. Is the leading paper also
in the conspiracy? An amusing weekly
journal was recently published in London, for
the purpose of drawing money from the pockets
of foreign gentlemen, who paid for its support
to their different objects and pursuits. It was
subsidised directly or indirectly by France, and
even extracted money, according to common
report, from Washington. The Times cannot
have taken to this trade, yet its present advice
to the Italians in favour of standing by, for the
tide, is suspicious. NAPOLEON, it says, is in
his sentimental mood, and he must be gratified.
He has decided to support the Pontiff in pos-
session of Rome, and although he acts from
good nature, and neither with common pru-
dence nor sound policy, he must be allowed to
discover his error by experience. It will not
do to be hasty and ill-natured. Arms are out
of the question with the proprietor of six
hundred thousand bayonets. Horrida bella
were the resorts of the Romans in old times,
but now they would be scattered before the
French like Kybiles. The Italians must, there-
fore, make a virtue of necessity, and be quiet
. and reasonable expectants of a good time
coming; when BRENNus 11., alias NAPOLEON
will relent and find some other senti-
mental subject for the exercise of his good na-
ture upon. Like some of the monsters of
antiquity he needs an occasional victim. Rome
is as good as any other place—let him have
Rome. If he would take Mecca, his choice
would be more convenient for the Romans,
but he has not inclined to Mecca, and so the
men of the Tiber must abide their destiny.
This is the argument of the Times, and it is ,
equally good for any other city, as for Rome,
Mexico:or Southampton, Berlin or Brussels; for
if it be a good argument other nations might
disarm and permit the man of destiny to settle
all disputes to his own satisfuction. Every
thing comes to an end. With that consolatory
thought the Italians ina,y look patiently for the
end of the French occupancy of Rome. The
EMPEROR may adopt some new notion, or take
some nem? whim. A short time may serve to
satisfy him of his present toy. Now, however,
the child of fortune must have his way.
The occupation of Rome by the French is an
Italian question. While it exists Italy is de-
based and dependent. Thirteen years have not
served to accomplish French objects in that
capital. Another thirteen years would not
accomplish the purpose. France holds Rome
to over-awe both the Italians and the Pope, and
will not quit Rome until the place be no longer
tenable by its legions.
The business belongs to historical retribu-
tions. The annals of nations are full of them.
So long as directly or indirectly nations endea-
vour to influence their neighbours, they are
liable to catastrophes of this character. Italy
had its good times when Italians held Gaul and
Germany, and Gauls and Germans now alter-
nately hold Rome. The Gauls are opener in
their possession than the Germans were, but
in reality Rome has been occupied by some
foreign power for a long time.
We are differently situated in this country
and in its possessions, and here at least we may
be permitted freedom of speech and thought,
but the encroachments of two different powers
an organised mob and an ambitious policeman,
endanger our privileges. A determined stand
is necessary against both usurpations. We
can neither havt. the Mayne law, nor the Roman
law, thrust upon us. Freedom of speech has
been so dearly earned, that it must not be
parted from because some foreign gentlemen do
acts that will not bear to be spoken of. The
people must care that while they are amused
with "sensations," and "rope-dancing," and
other luxuries, they do not allow themselves to
be roped up and made powerless. A small chink
may drown the land. These small chinks, such
as the bludgeon business in Hyde Park, and the
Mayne proclamation in consequence of that
event, are far more dangerous to freedom than
could be any act, proposed by any Cabinet to
any Parliament, for the suppression of discus-
sion among the people, and their dangers are
enhanced when the Syrens of the press chaunt
the praise of apathy as one of the virtues, and
sing "Oh be patient," or" There's a good time
coming," which never seems to come. The good
time is the present time for doing what is right,
and keeping what is right. We can never
have a better time for asserting privileges, than
the day of their danger. •

articles.title: COTTON AND ITS PROFITS.
articles.text:
COTTON AND ITS PROFITS.

A public meeting was held in the Town
Hall of Bombay, on the 17th September, to
adopt measures for increasing the Bombay
subscription in aid of the Lancashire operatives.
The money subscribed in Bombay was increased
to £25,000, of which £lO,OOO were remitted
to London by the last mail. Two Parsee mer-
chants gave £2,000, with an explanation that
the amount was part of their profits realised
from the sale of cotton. The profits made from
sales of and speculations in cotton by dealers
and merchants of Liverpool, London, and other
of our towns, have been calculated at twenty
millions sterling, within twelve months. This
estimate may considerably exceed- the reality,
but the gains have been very large. Even
if we compute them at five or ten millions, this
division with the afflicted, adopted by these two
Parsees, would relieve the existing pressure on
the rates and the relief funds. One tenth of
the money gained would not be an excessive
rate on profits. From five millions it would
produce five hundred thousand pounds ; from
ten millions, ten hundred thousand pounds;
and from twenty millions, twenty hundred
thousand pounds. Each sum of one hundred
thousand pounds represents rather less than
the amount of wages lost in each week. We
can thus understand how a tithe from the
profits made on cotton, during the crisis, Would
enable the operatives to pass through the
gloom of the approaching winter.
The payment cannot be demanded as money
due. It is only a conscience tax, and if the
men who have the means will not part with
the money the law cannot enforce its payment.
They may assert that they ran all the risk, 9,nd
the assertion is true, but a tithe of the pro-
ceeds would leave them nine-tenths of the
windfall. Many of them may have already
subscribed to the relief funds more, perhaps,
than this rating on their profits; some of them
probably more than all their profits and we
believe this statement to be true of several
gentlemen to whom the public have only to
express gratitude for duty well performed.
Still, the half million, the million, or the

two millions, which Sanguine calculators say I
would be a tithe of the profits made by the rise
in cotton, without reference to the money saved
by those merchants who had stocks of cotton
goods, and yarns—these one-half, one, or two
millions; where are they? Not yet represented
in our relief fluids ; not as yet paid for the
support of those families rendered destitute by
the calamity to many which has secured great
riches to others; not even due or payable
by those holders, with less distinct notions of
duty than ithe two Parsees of Bombay, who
paid eight per cent of the munificent subscrip-
tion at once raised in that town.
The narratives of this distress received from
the different manufacturing towns not only
describe the patience of the people, but also the
sacrifices of many manufacturers and spinners;
who pay their operatives three days or two
days wages, although their machinery is out of
work. Efforts of this character deserve to be
recorded, for their magnitude greatly exceeds
that of any single subscription. They are
practicable only by old, rich houses, whose
capital enables them to keep their operatives
together, and whose outlay will be repaid in
better times, not in so much money. for several
of them make the advances while declining to
book them as loans, but in that attention and
care for their interests, deserved by men who
meet a great calamity in this manner. Other
spinners may be unable to provide for an out-
lay that is not re-productive, and are them-
selves objects of sympathy; for an idle manu-
factory will consume itself in a few years; but
a very large number are comparatively callous
to the suffering around them; and, enabled by
the profits on their stocks to do without
labour for a time, treat it as any other com-
modity; sugar, tea, or wool: not caring for
what they do not want. But labour is a
perishable commodity; especially skilled la-
bour; it wastes with wasting energy and
health; it perishes with parting life; and even
when it survives tribulation, diverted from one
channel it returns no more; and this character-
istic of labour is overlooked by many of the
manufacturers and owners of property in the
cotton districts, whose riches are fugitive, and
would disappear with the flight of labour, or
the ruin of their trade.

OUR CHARACTER. IN PHILADELPHIA.
Mr. GEORGE FRANCIS TRAIN is acquainted
with England, and England is not altogether
unacquainted with Mr. TRAIN, who came to
London some time ago for the improvement of
our rails, roads, and streets, and occupied him-
self in examining the manners and customs of
the English, and studying their beer, in the
discussion forums of Fleet Street. Mr.
GEORGE FRANCIS TRAIN was unsuccessful in
his speculation for the improvement of English
rails, roads, and streets. We regret that cir-
cumstance, because the omnibuses on our
streets are jerking and shaky vehicles, as con-
trasted With those large boxes owned by Mr
TRAIN, that passed so easily along his tram •
ways; and we sincerely wish that the latter
could have been made consistent with the plan
of. the London streets, and the safety of their
numerous vehicles. Mr. TRIM returned to
the States an angry man, and if he had made a
foolish speech regarding us and our "belong-
ings" on the channel, from the deck of the
steamer that carried him away from his new's
shop in Fleet-street, •we could have forgiven
it; but the man has bad stuff in him whose
anger takes more than three months to cool.
Mr. TRAIN was petted in this country by a
knot of persons who drank their beer and
smoked their pipes, and allowed him to talk
nonsense to them, in some of the public-houses
in Fleet-street, where the evening visitors ar-
range the politics of the world. We are not
astonished that Mr. TRAIN has mistaken one
of these jolly clubs for a club of tha Jacobins,
and supposed himself capable of alarming the
nation, for his friend Louis Napoleon, de-
cidedly the superior intellect of the two, made
a similar mistake.
In the days of other years, Mr. TRAIN
agitated in a different style. We then had the
pleasure of receiving from the gentleman a
card of invitation to a champagne something—
breakfast, lunch, dinner, or supper. As we
did not find it conirenient to drink his cham-
pagne, we of course can refer to his doings
without a spark of gratitude; although even
at that time considerable quackery appeared to
gather round his railways or tramways, and
indeed round all his ways.
After his return to the Federal States, Mr.
GEORGE FRANCIS TRAIN became an agitator in
favour of the Democratic party who are not now in
office; and he found that attacks on the Britishers
rounded off periods advantageously, and led to
great applause. Abuse of England seems to go
down favourably in the Northern States, and
we regret that fact. Perhaps it may be equally
popular in the South, but the meetings are not
reported. Mr. TRAIN discovered that Mr.
CASSIUS CLAY and others were doing a good
thing, and he determined to run them off the
line. He addressed a meeting in Philadelphia
on the character of the English, and displayed
some fertility of invention. The English are,
he says, a nation of liars, and he has told them
so to their teeth, and designs to return and tell
them it once morp to their teeth. Great ap-
plause followed this announcement. These
Pennsylvanians rather like to hear a bad
character of the people from whom they
were chiefly descended. Occidental nations
have a worse taste in such matters than
oriental. Nothing cimld be more disagree-
able to a man or woman of Asia than
to be told of ancestral lies or other misdeame-
flours. Americans appear on the other hand
to rejoice in hearing of their ancestor's follies
and sins. The English are a nation of liars,
as Mr. TRAIN has told them "to their teeth,"
and as he intends to come over and repeat to
them. We advise him to re-consider his inten-
tion, All the English are not philosophers.
Some of them might be inclined to resent the
imputation, and if Mr. TRAIN has any regard
for his own teeth he will not keep his word.
Men may repent them of rash promises. Next,
"the English," he said, "are a nation of cow-
ards "—(gaeat cheering). All liars are cow-
ards; so we are prepared for the con sequence
of our sins. Britain has been saved in its
difficulties by the instrumentality of Irish
soldiers, as MT. TRAIN says, and undoubtedly
the Irish are good soldiers; and yet their
greatest achievements have been effected when
they fought along with our "English cowards."
The heart of ELIEU BURRIT would have been
delighted to hear of our pacific character.
Amcng us, according to Mr. TRAIN, no need
of olive leaves or a peace society exists.
As a nation of cowards we will not in-
terfere with American quarrels. All that
is said and written of our plans of in-
tervention must be trash. Cowards will
not endanger themselves even for the sake
of cotton. So the Philadelphians, being forget-
ful of ancient or modern history, cheered this
piece of news, and we hope instructed their re-
presentatives to insist, on the assurance of
TRAIN, that the money being paid for iron ves-
sels to keep out the English was lost; as

cowards that they are, they would not go in '
through an open sea.
The English were next described as a nation
of drunkards, and the epithet was drowned, as
became drunkenness, in cheers. As we have
been accustomed to call ourselves by that sort
of name, we need only to remark that the Ame-
ricans, if they have forsaken our "cowardice,"
and" lying," have retained our "drunkenness."
[hen the English are necessarily "a nation of
paupers" being a nation of" drunkards," and
while lamenting our "pauperism," we remark that
we have not yet employed that abominable
noun "repudiation." Even Mr. TRAIN con—
descended to omit " dishonesty " from the cata-
logue of English crimes. " Repudiation "
would have formed a delicate subject for dis-
cussion in Philadelphia, where people are al-
ready accustomed, to the thing. "Paupers "
but honest, "cowards, liars, drunkards," worse
than "slaves," bad-looking, with women whose
hands and feet are too large ;—Mr. TRAIN is an
aristocrat, and has been in China, and knows
the proper shape of female hands and feet—
such is the summing up of English character
given by this adventurer to a " Philade]phic"
audience; fond, be it observed, of "lying
oracles," friends of Delphos by name, and
therefore natural admirers of the "oracle" or
orator TRAIN'.

Our national position is described as very
low—" a province of France," and the cheapest
conquest we must have been that France has
ever made, for we do not even remember the
circumstance. Consols among us are worth-
less. They don't fetch 931, at three per cent.
&ock Exchange quotations are old almanacs
not reliable. GEORGE FRANCIS TRAIN spoke in
that dark parlour of Fleet-street, and our
securities became waste paper.
Like Dr. TAYLOR, GEORGE FRANCIS TRAIN
believes in the prevalence of private poisoning;
and he has a fixed opinion that Viscount
PALMERSTON operated on the late Prince
ALBERT; and Philadelphia cheered this view of
the past; while the Premier's purpose has also
been disclosed to Mr. TRAIN, Viscount PAL-
MERSTON wants the Crown; wants to found a
dynasty; practises treason, and makes no
secret of his purpose. This wonderful old man,
drawing nigh eighty years of age, and standing
alone in the world, without a relative of his
own family, is to be met and checkmated by
Mr. TRAIN, who, bad republican as he must
be, has long entertained the idea of playing an
O'BRIEN on the British throne.

We are distinctly obliged to Mr. TRAIN for
his attentions, bnt we have no desire for any
change just yet, and when this people have a
vacancy in their dynastic relations being
"liars," "cowards," "drunkards," "paupers,"
inhabiting a province of Mr. TRAIN'S friend's
kingdom, the place will hardly be worth ac-
ceptance by any O'Brien with a chronology or
a genealogy lost in the mist.
The amazing impudence of this man's lies
would be amusing if his audience had not been
pleased with them. Gross and wanton attacks
on this country are popular in the States, and
parhaps their popularity has done more than
any other cause to elicit a slight current of
counter-feeling here. People do'not like to be
abused even at a distance of three thousand
miles. Still as the style pays the orators and
writers, and pleases the Philadelphians, while
cannot materially injure us, retaliation
would be very foolish.

Consols hive fallen one-fourth since GEORGE
F. TRAIN- delivered his Phillipic against us,
but a coincidence is not always a consequence.
Our coasts have also been swept by storms
since that night with 'PRA,IN in Philadelphia:
but we do pot believe that they originated in
this unlimited vituperation.

articles.title: GENERAL GARIBALDI.
articles.text:
GENERAL GARIBALDI.

Representatives of the Trades' Societies in
London, met at the office of this paper on
Wednesday, and agreed, as will be observed
from the report, to recommend the trades to
join in welcoming Garibaldi to this country;
and any demonstration of this nature, justly
due to the man, will be effective and popular.
We rejoice to learn that the statements re-
specting the health of Garibaldi, in some of the
continental journals are exaggerated. He is
weak, but his friends do not consider him in
danger, and he has been removed to a con-
venient residence in a healthy locality.

BILL POSTERS' AssocinTroN.--The annual meeting of
the Bill Posters' Association took place on Monday
evening, at the house of Mr. James Bettye, the Granby
Hotel, Bradford, on which occasion a dinner was pro-
vided. After the cloth had been drawn, Mr. Cooper, of
Stockport, was called to the chair; Mr. Sheldon, of
Leeds, occupying the vice chair, and after transacting
the usual business of the association, a number of loyal
and patriotic toasts were drunk. Mr. J. Bentley, of
Bradford, the treasurer, in proposing Success to the
Bill Posters' Association,' expatiated at some length on
the advantages to be derived from their union. Several
other toasts pertinent to the objects of the association
were ably given, and warmly responded to, by other
delegates. The proceedings were interspersed with
sem-0 and recitations, and an agreeable evening was
spent.
THE FRENCH OCCUPATION OF ROME. —A public
meeting of the working men of Marylebone was held
on Monday evening at the Cleveland Institution,
Cleveland-street, Fitzroy-square, Mr. Nicholay in the
chair, for the purpose of protesting against the French
occupation of Rome. The meeting was a very united
one. The first resolution was moved by Mr. Wash-
ington Wilks, declaring that the occupation of Rome
by the Emperor of the French was a violation of the
principles of non-intervention, and ought to be put an
end to. The resolution was seconded by Mr. Mackay,
and carried with about half-a-dozen dissentients. A
second resolution was adopted—' That her Majesty's
government be memorialised to use their best influence
with the French government to withdraw the French
troops from Rome. Mr. Nicholay, in returning thanks
for a vote passed to him for presiding, said a movement
was going on amongst the ratepayers of Marylebone
for a requisition to the vestry to grant the use of the
Court-house for a further meeting on the Roman ques-
tion, and he had no doubt that the vestry would grant
the use of the building for that purpose.
How £lO STOLEN WERE RECOVERED* AND How THE
NORTHERNERS GOT A SOLDIER. —ln July last, Chris-
topher Wagner, a German, who occupied apartments
at 40, Sun-street, robbed a fellow•lodger, named Alex-
ander Miller, of £lO, and absconded. Application was
made to the Detective Police Station, and the case was
placed in the hands of Cousens an ingenious officer of
the force. Couzens obtained information that the man
'wanted' had taken a steerage passage for New York,
in the name of Carl Gubt, in the ship Constantine, on
the 26th July. Under these circumstances the idea of
recovering the thief was abandoned, as under the
Extradition Act the amount involved would not pay
expenses. How to recover the money, therefore,
next became the question, and the ingenuity. of
Couzens, aided by one of the detectives on the other
side of the Atlantic, proved instrumental in doing
so. Couzens wrote a letter to a New York
detective, distinguished for his shrewdness, named
Farally, informing him of the ship in which
Wagner would arrive, and instructing him when he
got possession of his man to 'bounce' the money out of
him. Couzens' letter went by the mail boat, and of
course arrived before the Constantine reached port.
On the arrival of the latter vessel at New York,
Farally was in waiting to receive Herr Wagner, whom
he charged with having stolen £lO, for which, he said,
if he did not refund, he would be sent back to Liver-
pool for trial. The latter was a contingency the
accused was glad to avoid at all sacrifice, but £1 38. 61.
was the whole of the money he was possessed of. The
ingenuity of Mr. Family assisted him to avoid the
penalty of a criminal prosecution in England. The
Northerners' wanted soldiers; the bounty was good;
the £lo.could thus be raised,with a balance in favour
of the recruit. Wagner enlisted, receiving a bounty of
eighty dollars, out of which he paid the amount de-
manded, which was at once transmitted to Couzens
and by him handed over to Miller.

PARIS, Oct. 23 (Evening.)
La "ranee, of this evening, says :—lt appears certairb

articles.title: PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT.
articles.text:
PROROGATION OF PARLIAMENT.

Yesterday morning the ceremony of proroguing par-
liament to Nov. 13, took place in the House of Lords,
in the presence of those of the officials who are in town
at this dull season of the year. The house itself pre-
sented the dullest possible aspect. The throne was
covered up so closely that not a bit of it could be seen,
while all the benches were similarly cared for, giving
the place the appearance of the large room of a gentle-
man's house, the owner of which was out of town for
the season.

_MR. COBDEN ..42VD TIIE MAN-
CRESTER CHAMBER OF COMMERCE.

Yesterday, in the Manchester Chamber of Com-
merce, Mr. Cobden, M.P.. delivered an important
speech, pointing out the enormous evil to this countiy
occasioned by the existing state of International and
Maritime Law, which he declared was mainly main-
tained by the Government of Great Britain, and
urging, from the example of the success of the Corn
Law League, the formation of some association to place
pressure on the Government to procure the abolition
of the blockade of all commercial ports by belligerents,
and the exemption from capture of all vessels of com-
merce not actually engaged in the conveyance of muni-
tions or contraband of war. Mr. Cobden spoke for an
hour and twenty minutes.

articles.title: LONDON TRADES' COUNCIL.
articles.text:
THE LONDON TRADES' COUNCIL.

We have received the following minutes of the last
meeting of the Council from the secretary, with two.
letters, one of which, however, must stand over until
next week.

At the meeting of the London Trades' Council, at
the Bull Inn, Old Bailey,-on Monday evening last,
Mr. Goddard, bookbinder, in the chair, the following
business was transacted :

The first question discussed was the condition of the
operatives in Lancashire, and how the Trades' Societies
could best render them sure and permanent relief.
Many useful suggestions were offered, and two letters
on the subject were read; one from the East Lancashire-
Central Relief Committee, the other from our late
Secretary, Mr. Howell. The, following is an extract
from the Lancashire letter :---

SlB.,—Will you kindly bring the above subject before
the Executive of the Metropolitan trades at the earliest
possible opportunity? Hundreds of honest and upright
workmen are starving in these districts for tho want of
adequate support. In very many cases within our
knowledge, members of unions have suffered from the
malice of employers on Relief Committees. Hoping
you will do something for us soon, JOSEPH PEACOCK,.
Hon. Secretary.'
After a careful consideration of the contents of these
letters, it was proposed by Mr. Murray and seconded
by Mr. Tremlett, that a special meeting of the council
be called on Monday next, for the purpose of taking
into consideration the best means to be adopted in
order to bring the united power of the Trade Societies
to the assistance of the distressed cotton spinners..
Carried unanimously.
The next question was a Political Paper, addressed
to the Council by the members of the Silver Cup So-
ciety of Carpenters and Joiners, in answer to which I
am instructed to say that the members of the Council
individually sympathise with its general tone and senti-
ment, but, as a Council, begs most respectfully to
acquaint its promoters that it is not within the province
of the Council to move in agitations entirely politi-
cal, and that a meeting of members of Trade Societies
will be held at the Brown Bear, Broad-street, Blooms-
bury, on Tuesday evening next, at eight o'clock, to
which the members of the Silver Cup Society, and all
other earnest reformers belonging to any Trades So-
ciety are invited to attend, hen a plan will be sub -
mitted to the meeting, upon which the whole of the
members of Societies can act together in one common
union, for the express purpose of obtaining a compre-
hensive measure of Reform during the coming session
of Parliament.

The next business was a deputation from the Gazi-
baldian Demonstration Committee. After hearing the
statements made it was proposed by Mr. Murray. and
seconded by Mr:Dawson, that a deputation from the
Council attend a meeting to tie held at the BEEHIVE
Office, respecting the Garibaldian Domonstration. -
[I beg to inform the trades that Mr. Coulson
brought credentials from the Bricklayers' Society to
the Council with a note expressing satisfaction with the
explanations given to their body by the Council in
reference to a mistake in the publication of certain
minutes]. GEORGB ODGERS, Secretary.

WOOD v. IRON.—THE DISPUTE BETWEEN
THE IRON PLATERS AND THE SHIP-
WRIG
The following letter appeared in the Devenport
Independent on the 11th inst.:—
TO THE EDITOR OF THE DEVONPORT INDEPENDENT;
SIR,—In perusing your paper of the 11th inst., I
saw there reference made to the two platers who were
diseharged last week from Keyham Yard, for refusing
to level plates for the shripwrights to fix and rivet
together. Your informant says that the two men
attended the Admiral's office on Tuesday morning,
when the cause of the dispute was investigated, which
was not exactly the case; for when they came before
the Admiral and gave him their reason for refusing to
do the work, he told them he was not prepared to dis-
cuss the subject with them, hut their refusal to perform
the work given them would lead to their discharge
from the service. The men told him that they felt
justified in pursuing the course they had taken, and
were quite prepared to leave. Now, sir, I think that
every right-minded man, when he understands the
cause of their leaving, would say they acted quite
right in so doing. Was it reasonable ta expect them
to level plates—the most difficult and laborious part of
the work—fur a number of men of quite a different
branch of trade to fit and rivit them together, that
part of the work being comparatively easy
when compared with the former? They were
quite willing to do that or any other work
in their branch, it matters not hew laborious
it might be if allowed to complete it. Now, sir,
if shipwrights can build iron ships (which some are so
ignorant as to say they can) as well as platers, why do
they send the plates to Key ham-yard to be levelled by
platers, and then compel the men to do it or leave their
work? They woulduaost gladly perform the whole of
the work if they were capable. There is a specimen of
their iron shipbuilding in her Majesty's ship the
Triton, now at Keylfam-yard, which they have been
working on for the last four months putting some new
plates in her sides. One plate cost the country £6
for labour alone, which it done in a contract yard, a
plater would receive 7s. 6d. for, and pay the men that
help him their wages out of that sum. Ide not find
fault with the men, for they may be very clever at their
ewn branch of trade nor do I suppose that platers
would do better as shipwrights, but to discharge two
men who oiily wanted, their rights and would not allow
themselves to be made tools of for other people's use is
a great injustice. But with them it matters not about
the price of work, as the country has to pay for it,
which the officers of the dockyard quite understand;
for, in pleading the cause of the shipwrights, they are
advancing their own interest; bat how different would
it be if they had to pay the cost out of their own
private purse. Then it would be the shipwrights
instead of the platers that: would have to leave; but I
am happy to say that the two discharged platers have
employment at Northfleet in the county of Kent, at
iron ship building, where they will not be troubled
with shipwrights. A MECHANIC.

In reference to the dispute that occurred between
the iron platers (employed at Keyham) and the ship-
wrights of the dockyard, noticed above, we have been
given to understand that already the two iron platers
that left their employment have, through the publicity
given to their case, received applications from New-
castle, Birkenhead, Northfieet, Chatham, and other
places. The wages offered to this class of artisans
range from 7s. to 102. per diem. Application has been
made for four iron platers to proceed immediately to
one of the above places from this locality, but two only
can be supplied, viz., the two men who left their em-
ployment at Keyham last week. It appears that
neither the men nor the society, which is determined
to support them, are desirous of offering captious
opposition to the authorities. And should it be re-
quired, the men have expressed their willingness to per-
form the work given them, providing they are allowed
to finish the work they begin. But they say they do
not consider themselveljustified to prepare the heaviest
portion of the work, ',and allow the ght s to
have the lightest, and ultimately to reap the praise
for suocessfully performing the whole of the work,
when in reality they have only done the least part of
it. The boilermakers deprecate the idea of a strike,
but are, it seems, determined to leave their employ-
ment individually, whenever they may be called upon
to do work similar to that which has led to the present
dispute. The funds of their society were never in a
more flourishing condition than at present. From
what we can gather in reference to the boilermaker's
case, it appears that they do not object to the ship-
wrights attempting to do a portion of their work.
But if it is proved, by ocular demonstration, that they
are incapable of performing and finishing that which
is given them to do, it only seems fair that the
boilermakers should be allowed to finish the work.
The fact of there being a great demand for the iron-
platers, is a proof of the importance of this particular
branch of the trade to the future success of our iron-
side ships.

THE MANCHESTER STONEMA.SONS' LOCK-OUT.—This
lock. out has now lasted four weeks. About 400 men
were locked out owing to the dispute, nearly 300 of
whom left the town obtaining work elsewhere. On
Fridly last, the employers succeeded in obtaining the
services (?) of twelve men belonging to the black
brigade,' who were placed to work at; the Assize Hall.
They have advertised for 300 more, and it is just
possible they may obtain them; the business, however,
is very brisk in the stone branch of the building trade;
no man need, from necessity, accept employment at
Manchester during the dispute; and those who do,
therefore, must be rotten and unprincipled at heart—
slaves who delight to hug :their chains. The Man-
chester justices, under whose direction the Assize Hall
is being built, met last week, and approved the action
taken by the employers. Of course they did.; what else
could be expected?
THE COTTON OPERATIVES IN BRISTOL.—The great
Western Cotton Works being about to be closed, thereby
entirely throwing out of employ 1,600 workers, the
Mayor of Bristol convened a meeting on Monday, the
result being that nearly £2,000 was subscribed, the list
being headed with £5OO by the well known firm of
Finzel, the eminent sugar refiners, and besides the
other mercantile firms and the gentry, the working
men are swelling the list—the men at Messrs. Slaughter
and Co., engineers, promising £lO per fortnight—in
fact, every effort is bAng made by all classes to raise a
noble sum for the distressed cotton operatives.

AN ADDRESS
From the Members of the Silver Cup' Society'ef
Carpenters and Joiners, to the London Trades'
Council and Fellow Unionists in London, on the
Necessity of Combining the Study of Political with
Social Questions has just been issued, from which
we take the following extracts, fully coinciding
with the views expressed:—
'We feel a grave responsibility resting upon us in
coming forward as the pioneers of this movement, but
we consider the matter to be of vast importance to the
future welfare of the toiling millions of our land, and
believing it to have been already too long delayed, and
feeling confident of the assistance of our fellow union-
ists in this great cause, has emboldened us to issue
this address; for, after mature deliberation, the con-
clusion has been forced on our minds that the Trades'
Council, to be useful and successful, should study not
only to preserve the Social Rights of the Trades, but
should take a wider, a more comprehensive view, and
endeavour to upraise, instruct, and elevate the work-
ing classes, by advocating their Political Rights and
privileges, equally with their Social Rights; for on
this, we believe, hinges the ultimate success of those
Social requirements for which we have all been so
long battling. We believe that body to be eminently
fitted to take up Political matters, with profit to
the Council and immense benefit to the Trades.
We find other important towns in Great Britain have
taken the initiative--forming their Trades' Council
into a Political Society—taking as their basis Political
Reform. We know, by sad experience, that laws
vitally affecting the best interests of the working
classes—and frequently to their injury—are con-
stantly being introduced by the Legislature of this
country, a Legislature in which we are not repre-
sented, for we have no voice in the making of the
laws, or in the election of our so-called representatives.
It will be fresh in the recollection of the Trades of
London that a case occurred about a year since, by
which the Council had an excellent opportunity of
proving the utility of the Trades' Council ccusidering
political questions; and the result of their joint action,
we are pleased to remember, was very successful—we
refer to the Government interference with the rights
of labour, by supplying Sappers to perform the work
• of artizans at Chelsea Barracks. This direct interfer-
ence was resisted by the Council, by their calling
together, in a few days, the various Trad.es, and ap-
pointing a deputation of fifteen, who waited on the
Secretary of State for War, the result being that the
Sappers were withdrawn.
'As a Trades' Society we have no Political Union,
which we deena.to be highly essential, and the Council
appears to us to be peculiarly fitted for the accomplish-
ment of that great object, having within its means the
power of drawing large bodies of men together in the
shortest possible space of time. We, therefore, trust
we shall have the active co-operation of the Council,
and our fellow unionists in accoriplishing this desir-
able end. The Extension of the Franchise is a question
'which sooner or later must occupy the deep attention
of the working classes. And if they are in earnest, if
they desire the amelioration of their class, they must
show pressure from without, and no opportunity can
rnore favourable than during the recess for the
Council to take steps for the attainment of this object.
by suPPorting and backing up with petitions, and
public opinion,
those few honest statesmen who have
courage
House in the nineteenth century, in the
Britleu of Commons, to speak of reform, even
though they receive only a sneering laugh in reply.'
WILLIAM PETHERBRIDGE, Chairman.
WILLIAM HIBBARD, Secretary.

articles.title: CORRESPONDENCE
articles.text:
CORRESPONDENCE

TRADES' UNIONISTS AND POLITICS.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
SIR,-The desirability of trades unionists advocating
the enfranchisement of the working classes has for
some time been freely discussed; and the fact has
been evidenced, that all who have written on the
question desire the end to be obtained, only differing
as to the means to be employed. It is, therefore, quite
time some practical effect was given to the opinions
enunciated ; time that talking and writing ltd to
working and decisive action. We believe that for the
last fourteen years the desire for political power has
sunk deeply into the minds of the masses, and
that there exists scattered up and down our land
ample materials, which, if gathered up and nation-
alised, such an effort could be made as must ensure
success. To gather together the scattered elements,
to concentrate the now isolated Efforts is, then, the
great object to be achieved. And who so fitting for
the purpose as the trades unionists, with their stern
experience and practical knowledge of the value
of a calm and close combination at present applied
only to economic considerations. But there are
other and still higher duties devolving on us; for
while we are trades unionists we are also citizens.
and, as such, have duties to perform, duties which, if
neglected, imperil the state. Is it not, therefore,
possible while conserving the principles of our unions,
to form an association which shall be available for
working out our political freedom? The writers of
this, with many others, believe it is, and also b.lieve
that those who in their unions successfully apply the
principle of combination, are the best fitted to esta-
blish and work such association, and that without
neglecting- their union, or turning them into political
clubs. With this object, the committee invite all
union and non-union brothers, who have a sincere
desire to obtain the complete enfranchisement of our
order, and who are prepared to work, work, work—
earnestly, persistently, and gratuitously—to meet for the
purpose of establishing an association to carry out the
above objects. The meeting will be held at the Brown
Bear, Broad-street, Bloomsbury, on Tuesday evening,
October 28, at eight o'clock punctually.
On behalf of the Preliminary Committee,
GEORGE ODGERS, HOR. Sec., pro. tem.
6, Park-lane, Kensington, W.

THE MASONS' SOCIETY AND THE 'BEEHIVE.'

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
Snt,—As a member of the General Society of
Operative Stonemasons, I feel deeply humiliated at the
result of the voting of the members upon the Bristol
Proposition.' Your paper nobly supported the
London masons durinE their strike against the hour
system. The Masons' Society more than any other have
found the benefit of a working man's paper, and I feel
shame that your exertions lave not ratt with a better
return. Though defeated, your friends are not dis-
couraged, and the proposition will be again placed
upon the paper at the proper time; and, I trust, with
a result more creditable to the Society at large.
October, 22. AN OPERATIVE MASON.
[We have been too long connected. with working
men to experience any surprise, though we confess to
feel pain, at the result alluded to by our corre •
spondent. It is this indifference of working men to
their own interests, and their ingratitude to those who
work on their behalf, that tends so much to keep them
in their present degraded position. Working men are
the only c!ass of society who neglect those who
advocate their cause. The aristocracy and middle
classes always well repay those who most zealously and
honestly work for them. We are, however, consoled
by knowing that tlere is yet a large body of work-
men who do sympathise with and support their friends.]

ORGANIC REFORMS.
TO TILE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sra,--In—your leading article in last Saturday's
paper I find this language, 'The sanatory and social
reforms, essential to the well-being of our state, will
not be speedily accomplished without organic reform in
the legislature.' You spoiled this, otherwise, sound
philosophy, by the. introduction of the adverb. Speedily
accomplished implies that the reform will be accom-
plished, though at a distant period. Sir, is this possi-
ble? If a concern, whether private or public, has been
brought to ruin by the conduct of the managers, is it
probable, is it possible, that a change for the better
will ever take place while those who have produced the
evil retain their power? The evils which afflict our
country are caused by the law River. The power of the
law giver, according to his opinion and practice, is
unlimited. There is no responsibility, however he
may abuse the power, and whatever may be the con-
sequences resulting from the abuse. It is in vain to
expect a change for the better, while the cause exists.
The duty of every Editor of a paper friendly to the in-
dustrious classes should be, to airect the attention of
his readers to this point, and to endeavour to apply the
proper remedy.
One of the means to obtain this end is to report the
different meetings through the country, held for the
Purpose of producing a real reform in the House of
Commons. I believe there are millions of men in the
United Kingdom who perceive the evil of the present
system, and are anxious to apply an efficient remedy.
But there is no organ, so far as my knowledge goes, to
collect public opinion and to bring it to bear on the
authorities. Men are stimulated to activity by the
conduct
.of those engaged in the same work, and they
become izirt when they perceive no movement around
them. It is better,' as Curran said, to hear occa-
sionally of the waves, than always to
inhale the thetlie pedsa.tsihlenntgial effluvia of stagnant waters.'
When the Bristol
_reformers see an account in the
papers of meetings in different parts of the country,
when they
Bee that the cause is progressing, they
become doubly active from the hopes based on the pro-
bability of success. The same feelings must be excited,
and what is better perpetuated, in other reforms when
the great cause appears to progress.
What is become of One of the Hive?' More than a
month has elapsed from the date of his letter. I am
afraid that he is so deeply immersed in the honey,
that his wings are clogged. I dare say he is much
more pleasingly and profitably engaged than are the
poor weavers of Lancashire, brought to their present
miserable state by that system of which he is an
Advocate.
I hope that the secretaries of the different Reform
Societies will furnish you with full reports of meetings,
and particularly with the resolutions entered into at
those meetings. B ILISTOLIAN.

day the quarterly court of the governors of this insti-

Mr. Symonds, V.P., in the chair. It was stated in the
report that at the last election nine boys were admitted

18s. 51., independent of the lodge property; being

FORESTERS.
ASYLUM FOR FORESTERS.

_
To THE EDITOR OF THE BEE HIVE.—For the past
year there has been much talk regarding the build-
ing of an asylum for disabled and aged Foresters. The
plan I should submit is very simple, but would be
quite as successful. In the London United District
there are 34,000 financial members, and if a resolution
was passed that every court in the district should pay
to the district fund the sum of one shilling per mem-
ber, to he paid from the funds of the court, it would
bring in, as a commencement, £1,700, which sum
would purchase freehold land and build 12 four-roomed
houses, capable of holding 24 residents; the cost of
building would be about £l,OOO, leaving £7OO to
purchase the land. The next question is, now we
have got the building and 24 residents, what is to be
done with them? for we cannot place them there to
look at the bare walls. I would propose that every
member in the district should pay to the fund 6d. per
annum, which would produce £B5O, which would
amount in seven yeas to £5,950. I should also pro-
pose that every new member should pay is., con-
sidering for the last seven years we have initiated
3,000 new members per annum; this wont I produce '
£1,050, and 6d. per annum from each of them would
produce £2,100 in seven years. Casting the above
sums together it would produce in seven years the
sum of £9,110; the above would allow the residents, in
addition to the 3s. 6d. per week allowed by the courts
to members that are incapable through blindness,
paralysis, or loss of limb, the sum of 4s. per week,
which would amount to in seven years £1,75C; and in
seven years it would cost £i,050, or £l5O per annum,
to find the residents in fire and light, repairs, and all

incidental expenses, leaving a- balance, without
interest, in seven years, of £6,310 ; with which sum
we should. be in a position to build. 12 more houses,
and the same every seven years. I may also state
that a special meeting, in connection with the above,
will take place at the Court House, of Court Trafalgar
1,539, the White Horse Tavern, Fann-street, Alders-
gate-street, City, on Monday, Oct. 27, when the above
will be fully discussed.

THOMAS HOOD, Sec., 1,539.
67, Charles-street, City-road, EC.

GENCE.

THE ROCHDALE EQUITABLE PIONEERS. The com-
mittee, in their report for the quarter ending Septem-
ber 16th, say that the condition of the society is every-
thing that could be expected, especially considering
the continued depression of the cotton trade in this
district. The profits this quarter amount to £4,422
12s. 21-d., which, after paying interest on capital
invested and allowing £97 193. for the educational
department, will give a dividend of 2s. sd. in the
pound on members' purchases, and leave a balance of
£2B 2s. Bd. The directors call attention to the cash
account of the Co-operative Relief Committee. The
applicants for relief have greatly increased since the
commencement of the distress, until about 1,320
persons are now receiving relief from this source; and
to meet the necessity, the three co-operative societies
in Rochdale are at present giving £23 per week. The
library now contains nearly 5,000 volumes, to the
privilege of which all members of the society are
entitled, free of charge.
COWPEN DISTRICT CO. OPERATIVE PROVIDENT SO- I
CIETY.—The fourth quarterly meeting of the above so-
ciety was held in the house of Mr. Thomas Ruther-
ford, Buffalo Inn, Cowpen Quay, on Saturday. Mr.
Henry Henderson, president, occupied the chair. The
report, read by the secretary, Mr. Thomas Dixon, was
unanimously adopted. It stated that notwithstanding
the great depression which has characterised the coal
trade in the district for the last three months, there
has been an improvement in the receipts of the society.
The committee recommend a dividend of 2s. in the
pound on all members' purchases, after paying 5 per
cent, per annum on all paid-up shares. The following
are the business transactions of the society since its
establishment :—First quarter's receipts, £554; second
ditto, £747; third ditto, £1,075; and this quarter,
£1,363. The receipts for goods sold is £1,308, and
members' contributions, £5,5. The profit, after all ex•
penses are deducted, is £103; the capital of the society
,is upwards of £4OO. The number of members is 145,
12 new members having entered last quarter.
HULL CO. OPERATIVE AND MUTUAL ASSURANCE SO-
CIETY (Ltiarren).—The quarterly report of this society
just issued, states the receipts for the past quarter
have amounted to £2,456, being an increase over the
previous quarter of £486, and that the present receipts
of the society are at the rate of £12,000 per annum.
The profit on the quarter is £334, which, after paying
interest on shares, and allowing for depreciation of
fixed stock, will give a bonus of 31. in the pound to
each member. The number of new members during
the quarter has been 98.
HULL CO-OPERATIVE PROVIDENT COMPANY (LI-
MITED). —This wor iing man's company having removed
its central store from Dock-street to the extensive
shop No. 67, Lowgate, held its October quarterly

adopted unanimously; and it transpired that several

days the company had been in Lowgate. The share-
holders resolved most emphatically to stand by the
company in its extended undertaking, and to inau-
gurate the opening of their new central store by a tea
meeting.
BRISTOL EQUITABLE AND INDUSTRIAL CO-OPERATIVE
SOCIETY. —The quarterly general meeting of this
Society was held at the School-room, Sussex-street,
Dings, on Tuesday evening. The chairman reviewed
the amount of business transacted at the several stores
of this society, and the decided progress which had
been made, stating that the society was in every sense
a success. The committee, in their report, recom-
mended that a dividend of 5 per cent, per annum on all
paid up shares, is. Id. in the pound on members' pur-
chases during the past quarter, and 6-td. on those of
non-members, be declared, which was carried nem. con.;
this result being highly satisfactory to all present.

THE HYDE PARK RIOTS.—John Mahony, the young
'man charged with assaulting several persons in Hyde
Park on Sunday, the sth of October, was brought up

twice for the attendance of a witness named Bailey,
who, on a person in court being pointed out to him,
now said he could not swear he was the person he saw
the prisoner striking on the ground, as the person he
saw was lying on his face; he was sure, however,

had been out on bail, ad should call upon him to find
two housekeepers in £lO each, to keep the peace for
six months.

articles.title: MARY LEBONE.
articles.text:
MARY LEBONE.

GARIBA.LDI RIO ---- —William Worrall and James
Wood, bricklayers, were charged with drunkenness
and disorderly conduct in John-street, Edgware-road.
Police-serjeant Dibben, 11 D, deposed that he was
called to the Laurie Arms, John-street, and on his
reaching there he found a mob of over a hundred Irish
and other per_sone. The disturbance was very great,
fighting going on in all directions, and foremost were
the prisoners and a companion of theirs, whom he
observed were very drunk. They and their companions
were calling out that if any one spoke against the Pope
they would kill them. Finding they would not go
away he sent to the station for assistance, and on its
arrival he took the two prisoners, and handed one over
to a brother officer. On the way Worrall knocked
witness down and Wood kicked him several times.
Mr. Mansfield rebuked them for their assault upon
the officer, and fined them each 405., with the alter-
native of imprisonment for one month with hard
labour.

articles.title: WORSHIP STREET.
articles.text:
WORSHIP STREET.

Charles Crange, a man of middle age, was charged
before Mr. Leigh with having unlawfully and by
violence endeavoured to force one Joseph Hartman to
depart from his employment —Mr. Joseph Glbbons, a
silk manufacturer in the Kingsland-road, stated that
both men had been in his employment. The evidence
went to show that the complainant and defendant
met in the street, that defendant charged the
other with having spoken words disrespectful
to him, and asked him what right he had to go to
work under the regular price of remuneration. The
complainant answered by asserting that he had a
privilege to do as he liked, upon which defendant
stuck him with his fist in the mouth, and after-
wards gave him a black eye by a second blow.
Mr. Leigh, in dealing with the case, said that intimi-
dation under any circumstances was not to be tolerated.
Workmen had a right to form themselves into a society
for the purpose of fixing a scale of wages if they chose;
but, in so doing, they had not the right of dictating to
any other workman what he should or should not do
with reference to it. Occasionally the acceptance of a
price lower than ordinary might save a family from
the workhouse or starvation. The powers of the Act
extended to an imprisonment of three months for the
offence in question. In this instance the order would
be for a third of that time, namely, one month, with
hard labour.

articles.title: HAMMERSMITH.
articles.text:
HAMMERSMITH.

Mr. Joseph Good, a gentleman, was charged with
being drunk and incapable, at eleven o'clock on
Sunday night, in High-street, Notting-hill. In
answer to the charge, the prisoner said it was an un-
intentional mistake on the part of the constable who
took him.—Mr. Ingham (to the constable) : How do
you know the prisoner was drunk ?—Constable: He
could not walk.—The prisoner: Quite true, I could not
walk.—Constable: He smelt strongly of liquor.—Mr.
Ingham: Was it from water or, milk ?—Constable:
From gin, sir.—Mr. Ingham: Could he talk rationally?
—Constable: He talked like a drunken man. When I
inquired for his name, he told me he was Lord John
Russell.—Mr. Ingham thought the evidence strong,
and fined him ss. for being tipsy.—A. gentleman then
stepped forward and said he had known Mr. Good for
twenty years and never saw him under the influence
of drink. He thought the constable had made a
mistake. The witness made an observation in a low
tone of voice, upon which Mr. Ingham placed his hand
upon his head, and said that accounted for it, and dis-
charged the prisoner.

GREENWICH.

SYMPAEHY WITH GARlBALDL—Christopher Sykes,
of 2, Thompson's-buildings, Redcross-street, Borough,
was charged with being drunk and creating a disturb-
ance in the public strests.—Police-constable 124 R
said: On Sunday afternoon a large number of persons
assembled on Blackheath and in Greenwich Park, for
the purpose of holding a demonstration meeting in
favour of Garibaldi. The mob, however, dispersed,
and in the town the prisoner raised a cry of 'Down
with the Pope!' and 'Up with Garibaldi! ' A large
number of persons collected, and, biting to persuade
the prisoner to be quiet, or to go away, he took him
into custody.—Mr. Train : There does not appear to
have been any violence occasioned by your silly con-
duct, but be careful in future. You are now fined 53.,
and in default you will be committed. to the House of
Correction for seven days.

articles.title: DESTRUCTIVE FIRES
articles.text:
DESTRUCTIVE FIRES

FIRE AT KILBURN.—On Saturday night a serious
fire occurred on the premises of Mr. J. Day, a beer-
shop and refreshment-house keeper, situate in the
Canterbury-road, Kilburn. This building had a
frontage of between fifty and sixty feet, expensively
fitted up, and was adjoined on one side by the premises
belonging to Mr. Richard Richards, and on the other
by the private residence of Mr. M. Foltham. The
damage is thus officially returned by Capt. Shaw to the
various fire-offices forming the London brigade :
Canterbury-road, Kilburn: Mr. L. Day, beershop-
keeper, &c., house of 55 feet frontage and the contents
about two-thirds destroyed; insurance unknown at
present. Ditto, next door, Mr. Richard Richards, roof
of front house burned off and part of roof of workshops
destroyed; the rest of building and the contents
damaged by fire, water, &c.; it is unknown whether
this sufferer was insured. Ditto, Mr. M. Faltham
(private), contents and the building damaged by
breakage and water, consequent upon hasty removal of
the furniture, &c.'

SERIOUS FIRE AND Loss or LWE.—On Monday
morning the aged inmates of the 111arylebone Alms-
houses, St. John's-wood, were considerably alarmed by
the noise of a policeman's rattle. The poor people
rushed out into the street, some almost in a state of
nudity. A few seconds showed that the fire had com-
menced in the house numbered 9, in which resided a
female named Mary Smyth, aged 82. l'or any one to
attempt to enter the place was then an impossibility.
The firemen were unable to get the flames extinguished
until the building and contents were destroyed, bilt the
tire was prevented from reaching the adjoining houses.
As soon as the ruins were sufficiently cooled search
was made for the poor woman, and after some time her
charred remains were found. How the catastrophe
occurred at present remains a mystery.

DESTRUCTIVE FIRE IN' BISTIOPSGATE.—About eleven
o'clock on Wednesday night a fire, accompanied by
great destruction of property, broke out on the pre-
mises of Mr. George Udell, cabinetmaker and bedstead
manufacturer, Skinner-street, Bishopsgate. Before
any of the engines arrived, the whole of the extensive
range of workshops were in flames, and all hopes of
saving them or their valuable contents were at an end.
Some of the engines had by this time arrived, but
before • they could be brought into play the fire had
seized on the large stock of valuable wood kept in a
yard at the rear of the burning warehouse, which speedily
fell a prey to the flames. The efforts of the fire-
men were now directed to save the dwelling-house, in
which they were aided by a side gateway leading down
to the wood yard, separating the house from the ware-
house. By dint of great exertions they at last suc-
ceeded, and, by cutting down some old sheds, they
prevented a further spread of the fire. The house and
its contents were much damaged, and the whole of the
warehouses and workshops, with the manufactured
stock and raw material, were entirely destroyed, to the
amount of over £l,OOO.

THE .ACCIDENT ON' THE LONDON;
(~'HATHA.iIf, AND DOTER _RAILWAY.

The coroner's inquiry into the circumstances at-
tending the death of William Reed, engine-driver,
who was killed by an accident which happened on
the London, Chatham, and Dover line, near Teynham,
on the 13th inst., was resumed on Monday by Mr.
Hills and a respectable jury at the Fountain Inn,
Sit tin gbo lune .
Several witnesses were called, the effact of whose
evidence was to show that the engine got off the line
through some defect in the way. Some of the
witnesses stated that the engines called Crampton's
patent had a damaging effect on the line, and it was
shown that the line at the spot where the accident
happened was frequently out of repair.
Colonel Yolland said he attended by the instructions
of the Board of Trade. Ile would not say what had
been the actual cause of the accident, but he would Say
what his opinion was from the evidence he had heard.
He thought the evidence had been truthfully given.
He believed that both the first and second rails
spoken of by Mr. Mills had been forced out by a
heavy lurch of the engine, and probably the carriages
got off after they had passed the spot. He did not
think that one key being out would have caused the
accident.
The jury, after deliberating an hour, returned the
following verdict :—' We find that the deceased, Wm.
Reed, came to his death by accident; and we believe
that the engine left the rails in consequence of the de•
fective state of the road, which we consider mainly
attributable to the use of the engines called 'Cramp-
ton's patent."'
The Comner said that was equivalent to a verdict of
accidental death. He would take that opportunity of
stating that no sort of imputation rested on the de-
ceased Witham Reed. His character had been beyond
reproach, and he had been the best driver in the
company's employ.
Mr. Martley said he might state that the Govern-
ment were making those arrangements respecting
their engines which would most conduce to the safety
of the public.
The inquiry then terminated.

articles.title: ROBBERY AT Tifg LINCOLN POST-
articles.text:
ROBBERY AT Tifg LINCOLN POST-

OFFICE.

On Saturday last considerable excitement prevailed
in the city when it became known that Mr. George
been apprehended on a charge of embezzling a letter,
Robinson, the son of a former resident of Lincoln, had
the property of the Postmaster-General. On Monday
the accused was brought before the magistrates, and
the following facts were given in evidence :—From the
numerous cotnplaints made from the Lincoln district
of the los° of letters containing valuables, the Secretary
of the General Post-office in London instructed Mr.
Charles D. Style, the Inspector of the Missing Letter-
office, to come down to Lincoln, and he accordingly
did so. On Friday, the 17th inst., he posted at the
pillar latter-box, at the corner of Sillon-street, a letter
in a pink envelope, containing coin, and directed to
Buford, near Nottingham. Upon receiving certain infor-
mation, he went to the post-office atLincoln, with Police-
constable Crocker, attached to the General Post-office,
London, and saw the prisoner. He told him that he
was an officer from London, and that he wished to ask
him a few questions relative to a letter which had not
reached its destination. He told him that he had
posted on the previous day a letter containing money,
and addressed to Basford, Nottingham, and enclosed
in a pink envelope, and which had not reached its desti-
nation. In reply to the inquiry of what he knew about
this letter he said that he had never seen it. He was
then requested to empty his pockets, and was searched
by Police-constable Crocker, but nothing was found on
him. The police-officer then accompanied him to his
lodgings, but nothing was found; but uprin searching
Robinson more closely a letter was found secreted
between his chest and his shirt front. The officer
asked him what it was, and he replied, It is a letter
that I had given me to forward a few days ago, and I ,
omitted to do so.' When asked what he had donel
with the money (as mention was made of a post-office
order) he did not reply. The Post-office Inspector
then saw him, and to him the prisoner said, I have
not got the money, I have spent it, but I am going to
get £6O from the bank.' The letter found upon him
was addressed to John Donlan Read, near Mollieau,
county Galway, Ireland, and contained written in-
structions for a post-office order for X 2 10s.
.The Brox-
holm postman said that he received the instructions
for the post-office order at North Carlton one day last
week, and he placed the letter and money, as was
usual, upon the counter, Robinson being close in front
of it. The magistrates remanded the prisoner for
further examination till Monday next, and an applica-
tion for bail was refused.

LONDON GENERAL OMNIBUS COMPANY.—The award
of Mr. Barstow, the arbitrator in the long-pending
suit between the late Metropolitan Saloon Omnibus
Company (Limited) and the London General Omnibus
Company (Limited) has been delivered, and is in favour
of the latter company.
DARING SHOP ROBBERY.—A young man of short
stature, having the appearance of a watchmaker, went
into the shop of Mr. Baker, Cranbourne-street, Lei-
cester-square, on Tuesuay night, at six o'clock, and
asked to look at a gold watch. The moment he got the
watch in his hand he ran out of the shop and got cloar
off with his booty. Mr. and Mrs. Baker were in the
shop at the time.
MILITARY RIOTS IN EDINBURGH—TWO serious dis-
turbances have occurred in Edinburgh, between borne
soldiers belonging to the 25th Borderers and the city
police. Some ill-feeling had been caused by the arrest
of several soldiers, and on Thursday about a dozen of
them attacked a couple of policemen with their belts
but were held at bay, and, on the arrival of reinforce-
ments of police, had to retreat, with the loss of several
prisoners. The following night they marched up
towards the police-office, howling and hooting, knock-
ing down a policeman on the way, and attacking
others, without the least provocation. The policemen
at length made a sally from the office, and captured
one or two of the rioters. The row then grew fiercer,
the shopkeepers were compelled to put up their
shutters, and the disturbance was not quelled until the
arrival of a picket of soldiers, who gathered in the
stragglers. Several of the policemen were seriously
l injured.

LITERATURE.

The Negro Prince ; or, the Victims of Dahomey. By
Capt. Livingstone. London: Ch. H. Clarke, 13,

Paternoster-row.
This is a work of thrilling interest, and destined,
we think, to become very popular. Nothing can sur-
pass the picture here drawn of the early splendour
and high civilisation of Northern Africa, in which the
opening scenes are laid. The descriptions of Afrie.an
scenery are vividly beautiful, while the atrocities of
the Da.homian court are portrayed with great power
and beauty of language. The fiendish cruelties of the
King of Dahomey and his Amazon warriors make the
soul shudder and call aloud for prompt and energetic
action on the part of civilised peoples. The horrors of
slavery are graphically unfolded in connection with
the histcry of the Negro Prince and his consort. We
hope the book will attain a large circulation.

TIIE _DRAMA.

THE PRINCESS'S.

This house opened on Monday evening, under a new
management. So short a time has elapsed since the
termination of Mr. Harris's season, that the new lessee
would certainly have acted wisely if he had taken a
little more time for preparation. However familiar
artists may be individually with a play, it is quite im-
possible that it should be satisfactorily performed until
they have had fair opportunities of rehearsing toge-
ther; and the representation of Sheridan Knowles's
play, Love,' afforded strong evidence of the absence
of this desideratum. In simple justice the company is
a good one, and when its members have a better chance
of making their ability manifest, we have no doubt
that they will deserve and .earn the patronage of the
public.

THE LYCEUM.
