articles.title: .ACCIDENT ON THE WEST MIDLAND
articles.text:
.ACCIDENT ON THE WEST MIDLAND

_RAILWAY.

An alarming but not fatal collision occurred on
Tuesday night, near Evesham, on the West Midland
line—the down express train from London, which
leaves Paddington station at 6.30 p.m., running into a
lot of trucks that had been by some carelessness left
on the line, unguarded by danger signals, although
the express train was known to be due. The train
does not stop at Evesham, but passes that station at
the usual express speed, and is due at about 9.5
p.m. The train was a few minutes behind time,
but IN as proceeding at the usual rate, and had
passed Evesham station I,y about 200 yards, when
the passengers wtre suddenly thrown together
in confusion, some receiving bloody noses and others
being badly bruised. The effect of the collision,
was to dash the trucks (three in number) Linto
splinters, scattering the debris over the line and.
breaking down the telegraph wires. Two of the wheels
of one of the trucks had in an extraordinary manner
got under the forewheels of the engine and become
firmly fixed in it, and it was thought that the engine
would have left the rails and run off down an embank-
ment but for these wheels holding it upon the
.line..
At the place where the collision occurred there is an
embankment leading over some low lands adjoining
the river Avon; and had the train gone a little fur-
ther and run off the rails, it must have fallen bodily
into the river, which was much swollen by the late
rains and is always deep at this place. The escape of
the passengers was, indeed, miraculous. The engine-
driver, who was the worst hurt, received a severe blow
on the chest, but his wound was not serious. In about
an hour a fresh engine was supplied at Evesham, and
the train proceeded. How the trucks got on the line
of course the authorities cannot yet say, but the fore-
man porter at Evesham, who has the management of-
the shunting of trains, has been taken into custody,
and will be examined before the magistrates.

articles.title: ATTEMPT fiD ROBBERY AND
articles.text:
ATTEMPT fiD ROBBERY AND

HURD AR .

A serious charge was investigated before the magis-
trates sitting in petty sessions at Solihull, on Monday
last. The prisoner is Thomas Woodward, a married
man, residing near Solihull Lodge, a character well
known to the police, having so frequently been before
the Solihull magistrates on various charges of felony
and receiving stolen property. On the present occa-
sion he was charged with breaking and entering the
dwelling house of Thomas Castle, a public house
known by the sign of the Boatman's Rest,' situated
at the drawbridge, near Shirley, with the intent to
commit a felony; also, atthe same time and place, with
assaulting with intent to murder the wife of the said
Thomas Castle. It appeared from the evidence that
about eight o'clock on the 15th inst., Mrs. Castle,
hearing some noise upstairs, went to see what it was,
and perceived a man in her bedroom, whom she iden-
tified as Thomas Woodward, attempting to open a
drawer, in which was a considerable sum of money.
She, holding a candle in her hand, spoke to him, end
said, Why, here is a rogue in the house.' He then
struck her a violent blow over the right temple with
some heavy instrument, dragged her into another
room, and beat and kicked he in a dreadful manner.
The husband, hearing her scream, ran upstairs to her
assistance. The thief, no doubt hearing him approach,
at once discontinued his brutality, and escaped along
the landing-place into a room, and through a window
to the canal side. The prisoner, about two years back,
was the tenant, if not the owner, of the public-house.
At that time he let it to Thomas Castle, the prosecutor
in the present case. In June last Mr. and Mrs. Castle
gave evidence against him in .a case of horse-stealing,
and again on his trial at the sessions in July, on which
evidence he was convicted. A ladder was found on
the towing-path, about forty yards from Castle's
house, and in the direction of Woodward's, which no
doubt was the one used for the purpose of the robbery.
The ladder was sworn to be the property of the pri-
soner. Mrs. Castle was in a very weak state, and had
to be conveyed very quietly in a car to give her evi-
dence. In the bed-room were found a dark lanterst
and three picklock keys, all newly-constructed articles.
The prisoner was committed for trial.

AN UNFORTUNATE ACTRESS.—The Nouvelliste
_Rbuen announces that Mme. Defreysoles, well known as
a clever actress, and who was performing at the
principal theatre in that place, was on Friday suddenly
seized with madness. She had played the night before
in the Testament de Gmsar Girodet, and was greatly
applauded. Some time after her return home, at about
two in the morning, she went down stairs and, proceed-
ing to the post of the suspension-bridge, asked for
medical aid, saying that she felt ill. The °Pier de sante
on service perceived at once that her mind was wavering,
and had her taken home. The unfortunate lady then
barricaded herself in her apartment, and opening the
window spent her time in alternately approaching it and
drawing back, so that several persons of the ranghbour-
hood who had collected on the news of her madnessi,
were afraid she would precipitate herself on the pave-
ment from the third storey. At last, the police being
informed of what was going on, ordered a carriage to be
brought, and succeeded in carrying her off to a lunatic
asylum. Her fixed idea, it appears, was that she was to
be poisoned by the smell of flowers, and all her efforts
were made to guard against such a death, but what
determined her sudden attack of madness is not known.
SUDDEN DEATH OP A FOOTMAN OF THE QUEEN'S.—
On Saturday last an inquest was held at the Town-
hall, Windsor, before Thomas Marlin, E.q., coro-
ner for the borough, touching the death of George
Golding, who has been ten years in the Royal estab-
lishment as footman to her Majesty. Charlotte Ledger,
of St. Alban's-street, said that ehe was acquainted with
deceased, and had some conversation with him at the
castle the day previous to his death, respecting hie
health. Ho was then packing his things to go to Os-
borne to attend on her Majesty on her arrival there from
the Continent. He complained of weakness and debility,
but no pain. Witness considered he was not fit to take
his duty, but he said he wished to go. Saw him again
this morning about nine o'clock, when he seemed in
goad spirits. On going up the steps in the Castle-yard,
he complained of shortness of breath; walked with him
in front of the Military Knights.houses, and when
nearly opposite to the Castle stores he suddenly fell
down, and died in a few minutes. Afterwards the body
was conveyed to the stores, where it now lies. Other
witnesses were examined in corroboration of the above
facts, and the jury returned a verdict, 'Died by the
visitation of God.' Deceased was in his 38th year, and
has left a widow and four young children.

President Lincoln returned to Wc..shington on as
oth. While in Frederick, Maryland, ho deliveredtao
following address
In my present position it is hardly proper for me to
make speeches. Every word is so closely noted teat it
will not do to make trivial ones, and I cannot be ex-
pected to be prepared to make a matured one just no‘r
If I were as I have been most of my life, I might;
perhaps talk amusing to you for half an hour, and it
wouldn't hurt anybody; but as it is I can only return
my sincere thanks for the compliment paid our causo
and our common country.
At the railway station of the same city he said.:—
'Fellow Citizens,—l see myself surrounded by
soldiers, and a little further off I note the citizms ot
this good city of Frederick, anxious to hear something
from me. I can only say, as I did five minutes ago,
it is not proper for me to make speeches in my presuat
position. I return thanks to our soldiers for the good
service they have rendered, for the energies they have
shown, the hardships they have endured, and the blood
they have so nobly shed for this dear Union of ours;
and I also return thanks not only to the soldiers, but
to the good citizens of Miryland, and to all the good
men and women in this land, for their devotion to our
glorious cause. In say this without any Malice in my
heart to those who have done otherwise. May cur
children and our children's chiidren to a, thousand
generations continue to enjoy the benefit's conferred
upon us by a united country, and. have cause yet to re-
joice under those glorious institutions bequeathed Us
by Washington and his compeers! Now, my friends,
soldiers and citizens, I can only say once more—
farewell.' •

General 31‘Clellan had issued the following orders
to his army respecting the emancipation proclama-
tion:—

Head-quarters Army of the Potomac Camp,
near Sharpsburg, Maryland, Oct. 7.
General Order No. 163.—The attention of the
officers and soldiers of the army of the Potomac 13
called to General Order No. 139, War Department,
September 24, 1862, publishing to the army to Presi-
dent's Proclamation of September 22. A proclama-
tion of such grave moment to the nation, officially
communicated to the army, affords to the General
commanding, an opportunity of defining specifically
to the officers and soldiers under his command the
relation borne bee all persons in the military service of
United States toward the civil authorities of the
Government.
The Constitution confides to the civil authorities
legislation, judicial and exclusive, the power and duty
of making, expounding, and executing the Union laws.
Aimed forces are raised and supported simply to sus-
tain the civil authorities, and are to beheld in strict
subordination thereto in all respects. This fundamen-
tal rule of our political system is essental to the security
of our republican institutions, and ahouldbe thoroughly
understood and observed by every eoldier.
The principle upon which and the objects for which
armies shall be employed in suppressing the rebellion
must be determined, and declared by the civil autho-
rities, and the Chief Executive, who is charged with
the administration of the national affairs, is the proper
and only source through which the news and orders of
the Government can be made known to the armies of
the nation. Discussion by officers and the soldiers con-
cerning public measures determined upon and declared
by the Government, when carried at all beyond the
ordinary temperate and respectful expression of opinion,
tend greatly to impair and destroy the discipline and
efficiency of troops by substituting the spirit of political
faction for that firm steady, and earnest support of the
authority of the firm,
which is the highest
duty of the American soldier. The remedy for political
errors, if any are committed, is to be found only in the
action of the people at the polls.
In thus calling the attention of this army to the
true relation between the soldiers and the Govern-
ment, the General Commanding merely adverts to an
evil against which it has been thought advisable during
our whole history to guard the armies of the Republic,
and in so doing.he will not be considered by any right-
minded person as casting any reflection upon loyalty
and good conduct, which has been so fully illustrated
upon so many battle-fields. In carrying • out all
measures of public policy this army will, of course, be
guided by the same mercy and Christianity that have
over controlled its conduct towards the defenceless.
By command of Major. General ld'Clellan.
JAMES A. HARDEE, Lieutenant-Colonel,
Aide-de-Camp, and A.A.A.G.

To Major-General,M'Clellan, Commanding, &o.

General,—Your report of yesterday, giving the

land are creditable alike to the troops and to the officers
who commanded them. A grateful country, while
mourning the lamented dead, will not be unmindful of
the honours due to the living.
H. W. Halmtcx, General-in-Chief.

FRESH BEEF FORTY YEARS OLD.—The Nourelliste
of Hamburg says :—'At a banquet just given at
Tronisoo, in Norway, a dish of fresh beef was served
which had been found last summer in some tin cases
buried at Spitzbergen. According to indisputable indi-
cations these cases were placed there by the Parry
expedition in 1526. The meat was perfectly fresh, and
bad not contracted any bad smell.'

articles.title: ADDRESS TO T 111; AROHBISHOP lIINAIE OF CANTERBURY.
articles.text:
ADDRESS TO T 111; AROHBISHOP
lIINAIE OF CANTERBURY.

The following address to the Most Rev. Dr. Longley,
Archbishop designate of Canterbury, and Primate of All
England, is in course of signature amongst the elergy of
the Archdeaconry of York, and will be presented to his
Grace in the course of a few days :
We the undersigned clergy of the Archdeaconry of
York are unwilling that your Grace should quit the
diocese without some expression of our regret at the loss
of one whose wisdom, kindness, and self-denial we have
largely experienced, and so gratefully acknowledged-
We trust, however, that the change we ourselves lament
will conduce to the general welfare of the Church. We
rejoice that by your elevation' under God's providence,
to the Primacy of All England our national Church will
receive the benefit of the mature experience acquired
during an active episcopate of twenty-four years in the
Northern Province. We pray that the blessing of God
may ever rest upon you, and that his grace may guide
you in the discharge of the high functions of that office
to which you are now called; that you may long enjoy:
health of body and vigour of mind, and that you may
be the honoured instrument of promoting what we are
assured is the dearest wish of your heart, the glory of
God, and the eternal good of man.'

articles.title: AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.
articles.text:
AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS.

(From the Mark Lane Express.)
The week opened with a thoroughly wet day, and the
wind from the S S.W. to the south. Monday morning
proved fine, but the day wasthreatening, and some showers
were experienced towards evening. Not much progress
vas made in wheat sowing, except on the lighter soils.
ruesday as a remarkably fine day, wind S.S.W., warm
and breezy. This proved a most favourable day for
autumnal tillage, which progressed extensively. The
land was in fine order for the reception of the seed, and
the quality of the grain good,-with numerous varieties in
nearly all our counties, each season bringing out now
names and favourite sorts. Thus far amongst the red
the 'nursery' has had the run, and the demand for it con-
tinues good, while as next, Browick," Spalding,'
Golden Drop' and 'Burwell.' Amongst the white,
Tauxton Dean' is a good deal inquired for; the Chid
barn, Rough Chaff,' and 'Earl Dude.' From Lincoln-
shire onthis day it was remarked, 'The weather continues
very favourable for wheat sowing, which has now com-
menced in this district.'

Wednesday was in places a fine warm day, barometer
29.70, thermometer 67 deo.'s., with slight rain in the
afternoon, and in the westa great deal in the morning:
but much work accomplished in a satisfactory raacner.
From Scotland it was stated, that 'harvest in the '
Lothians and neighbourhood was about completed; wheat
promising a poor return • spring corn generally better,
although samples brought forward have been various
and of irregular quality.'
Thursday was a very splendid autumnal day; cool, ther-
mometer 56 degs. ; clear and breezy; wind N.W. Every
advantage ought to be taken of a fine day, for the changes
are very sudden, and occasionally heavy falls of rain take
place._

- Friday was wet, with-a stoppage to field-watk ; and this
continued. on Saturday, which proved a miserably wet
day from 10 a.m. 5 p.m., wind having veered to the
northward, and thermometer down to 50 degs. On the
whole, the fall of rain this week has been greater than
during the past, and more than was wanted for pushing
on the work of the farm.

The moist atmosphere so continuous is m.uch against
the condition of new wheat, and the samples brought
forward are in a miserable condition. This is sadly
against making fair prices, so much so that some farmers
have determined to bring out no more, keeping it in the
straw under drying winds to improve it, and with a hope
that prices may then be better. The delivethes are,
Tartly from this feeling, and from the occupation of the
farmers, falling off, and until seed time is over there
'will be no increase.

Barley, on the contrary, is taking favour, and fine
malting qualities are,tending upwards, the proportion of
such being small, perhaps only one-third of the whole
crop. The mailing season, with the present ternperat ure,
will now set in fairly, and a more general demand may
be looked for. The intermediate qualities' however,
must be resorted to, or sufficient will not be found for
thetrade ; and so for the present this article is the most
promising to the agriculturists.

articles.title: LT. GLADSTONE OX SLAVERY.
articles.text:
LT. GLADSTONE OX SLAVERY.

The following letter has been addressed by the secre-
tary of the Chancellor of the Exchequer to Mr. L. W.
Moore of Northampton. It is in reply to a letter from
Mr. Moore, written after reading Mr. Gladstone's New-
castle speech, and making some inquiries as to the sen-
timents of the right hon. gentleman in reference to
slavery :

'll, Downing-street, Whitehall, Oct. 17.
Sir,—l am desired by the Chancellor of the Ex-
chequer to aclinowledge the favour of your letter of the
13th inst., and .I am to say that he hopes that the policy
of this country will never be directed, to the support or
encouragement of slavery; but in viewing the conflict
which now rages in America, we must all, Mr. Glad-
stone thinks, wish it wore in our power, by friendly
means, to stop the effusion of human blood.—l am, Sir,
your obedient servant, Culuixs L. Rxillg.
Mr. W. L. Moore.'

I)EATEI OF CAPTAIN GERALD FITZGERALD KING.
WO regret to announce the death of the above gallant
officer, of the 13th Regiment of Light Infantry, which
occurred near Aden, on the route to join his regiment in
India, at the early age of 33 years. The deceased, AN ho
was the youngest son of the late Hon. and Rev.
Richard Fitzgerald King, entered the army as ensign
Nov. 3, 1840; lieutenant, Oct. 14, 1842; and captain
June 26, 1855. He landed with his regiment in the
Crimea on the 30th June, 1855, and was present at the
battle of the Ilchernaya, and also at the siege and. fall
of. Sebastopol, for which he was rewarded. with the
medal and clasp.
Lieutenant Robert Sterne, who hasbeen appointed. by
the Board of Admiralty to the command of the Psyche,
2' paddle-yacht, at Portsmouth, was acting rage of the
Sampson, 6, in the Mediterranean, from Oct., 1852,
until promoted to lieutenant Nov. 13, 1854, and was
present at the bombardment of Odessa and destruction of
Redout Kaleh in 1854. He served. as lieutenant in the
Euryalus 51, in the Baltic and on the North American
Station, from Feb., 1855, to the spring of 1857 ;in the
Renown 91, in the Mediterranean, from Nov. 1857, to
Jan., 1860; in the Argus, 6, on the last-named station,
from Jan., 1860, to paid off, Aug., 1861; in the R,oyal
Adelaide flag-skip, at Devonport, from Sept., 1861, to
Feb., 1862; and in the Russell, 6.0, at Falmouth, from
Feb, 1862, to the present time.

DrATII OF JUDGE RADCLLPEE.—With great regret
we announce the death of Joseph Ormsby Radcliffe,
Esq., LL.D., Q.C. Dr. Radcliffe had for a considerable
period, laboured under a serious disease, to which. he
finally succumbed, after much pain, on the I.Bth. Ile
had rallied slightly, and was able to be present at the
funeral of the late Lord Primate; but having caught
cold upon that occasion, unfavourable symptoms re-
turned, and his recovery became impossible. Dr. Rad-
cliffe discharged his onerous duties as Judge of the Con-
sistorial Court with independence and ability, ,and was
much respected by the profession. As Vicar-General of
the provinces of Armagh and Dublin he exhibited the
same high qualities of mind, and will be deeply regretted,
no less by all who came into contact with him in his
public capacity than by his personal friends.—Dublin
Evening Mail. -
INDIAN ANTIQUITIES.—The London Review, in noticing
a work by Mrs. Speicl on military life in India, says,
'The eaves of Ellora occupy a prominent place among
the rock-cut temples of India. Local tradition assigns
them an antiquity of 7,000 or 8,000 years'; but recent
research has led to the conclusion that they range, with a
few exceptions, from the 6th to the 12th centuries of our
era, Dnd that they were constructed not only at different
periods but for different forms of faith. In the caves of
Ellora, for instance, there is a Buddhist group, consisting
of a monastery, a relic-shrine, and "shales,' or college-
halls, in which neophytes received instruction. Next to
the Buddhist excavations come some of the Brahmanical
period, and beyond these the " Jaina," or Jaina and Bra-
hmanical mixed, the most modern and least artistically
carved. Each of these groups has its own distinctive pecu-
liarities; the Buddhist temples are especially interest ng.
"Their form," says Mrs. Speid, "is not only similar to,
but actually identical with that of the Norman Church of
the eleventh or twelfth century."'
INTOLERANCE PENISEED.—A young man named
James Moriarty has pleaded guilty, at Tralee Petty
Sessions, to an indictment charging him with having
committed a wanton and malicious assault upon Mr. C.
Harold, of Killorglin, at a fair on the 11th August last.
The attack originated in a feeling of vindictiveness ex-
cited in the minds of the peasantry against the prosecutor,
because he held prayer meetings in his house, and brought
up as Protestants certain children over -whom he was
appointed guardian, but -whom the priests wanted to
bring up in their Church. Mr. Coppinger sentenced
him to three years' penal servitude, a punishment which
marks the determination of the magistrates to put an end
to the system of coercion attempted to be exercised
against persons on account of their religious opinions.
COUNT BERNSTORFF. --- His Excellency Count
Bernstorff, who left London in July of last year, in order
to assume the office of Minister of Foreign Affairs in
Berlin, and who resigned that post lately on account of
some differences o? view with the majority of his
colleagues about the internal affairs of Prussia, arrived
on Saturday last with his family at Prussia House,
Carlton-house-terrace. His Excellency now resumes
his former diplomatic functions at the British Court, with
the rank of ambassador.

articles.title: EXECUTION OF CAI7IE.RINE WILSON.
articles.text:
EXECUTION OF CAI7IE.RINE WILSON.

On the 20th Catherine Wilson, who was sentenced
to death by Mr. Justice Bylea, at the last sessions .of
the Central Criminal, Court, for the murder of Maria
Soames, was executed in front of Newgate.
Fourteen years have elapsed since a woman was
executed in Middlesex, and as might have been antici-
pated, a vast crowd ,of persons assembled. From
Smithfield to Ludgate- bill there waa•a dense Mass of
human beings, and at all the windows in the Old
Bailey from which a view of the scaffold cOuld be'
obtained were well dressed people, many Of whom had
provided themselves with opera glasses which were
levelled at the miserable woman when she came forth
from the prison to die. "
Shortly after seven o'clock the two Sheriffs, Alder-
Man Lawrence and Mr. Hugh Jones, who Were accom-
panied by Mr. Deputy Farrar and Mr. Mackrell, the
Under-Sheriffs, arrived, and ascertained that every-
thing that could be- done had been done by the
authorities of the prison. At a quarter before eight
o'clock a procession, Consisting of the Sheriffs, Under-
Sheriffs, the Rev. ohn awls, the Ordinary of Now-
gate, Mr. Jonas, the governor, and Mr. Gibson, the
surgeon, went to the bedroom of the convict, and then
'brought her to the room in which the pinioning was to
be performed. There she was met by Calcroft, who
commenced the operation of strapping her arms.
While this was being done she sat on a form
and was slightly, but very slightly, agitated.
The female warder, who accompanied her, asked her,
whether she could do anythin g more forher, and having
been told that she could not, she kissed her and lefte
IVIr. Jonas, the governor then asked her whether slut
would have some brandy, but she declined. Heeled
a glass of water to her lips, and she drank a little,
after which he said to her 'The last moment' has
arrived, do you wish to- say 'anything?' She replied,
feebly, 'No I am innocent.' She then rose from her
seat and followed with unfaltering step the- Ordinary,
who; as the procession moved across the yard, read
the burial service .of the Church of England. From
the prison she ascended the steps leading to the gal-
lows without betraying any emotion. The white cap
was draw over her eyes, the rope was put round her
neck, her legs were tied, and the bolt having been
withdrawn, she fell heavily, and died apparently with-
out a struggle. There was very little groaning or
noise on the part of the mob.c
Only one person has visited the convict since her
trial. This was a Mrs. Williams, who resides in
Loughborough-road, Brixton, who was a neighbour of
Catherine Wilson when she resided at Boston. The

interview lasted only about ten minutes, and it was
very, evident that the convict had no desire to prolong
it. On Saturday last two women called and desired to
see her, but on their names being taken in she said she
had no desire to see them.
The convict attended the ordinary chapel services on
Sunday. She has been respectful in her conduct, and
atteniive to the religious instruction which has been
afforded to her, but she nas shown no further sign of
contntion. Nothing has been said by her which can
he construed into an acknowledgment of her guilt;
indeed, her last words were a declaration of her inno-
cence.

On Monday morning, at four o'clock, a special mes-
senger arrived at the Governor's house from the Post.
office, with a letter addressed to Catherine Wilson,
The Governor at once opened it, and found it to con-
tain two tracts on religious subjects—a species of lite-
rature which has been very freely offered to her by
well-meaning people out of doors.
Catherine Wilson, alias Constance Taylor, waSTOrn
about the year 1817. Her parents' name was Crane
and, they lived at Surfleet, a little village near Spalding.
Her father was a carpenter, and in the latter part of his
life was an inmate of .one of the Bede-homes of the
town. There were two other children, one of whom,
an idiot, died two
.years ago. The parents have. been
dead about twelve years. The first thing that rendered
her notorious was a robbery which she committed
when only fourteen years of age, the circumstances
being of a very base and heartless character. She had
gone to the house of a friend as a child visitor, and
whilst there committed a theft. The servant was sus-
pected, taken in charge, and convicted of the theft, the
evidence against her being that of the child, who, on
being subsequently examined about the rebbery, con-
fessed that she committed it, said fixed the crime upon
the servant. After this she left her home and went
to live at Spalding, where she led a loose life. She
then went to Boston, andthere became acquainted with
a highly respectable master mariner, trading from that
port, and by her plausibility and her apparent. respec-
tability, she induced him to marry her, and for some
time they lived in comfort, but she returning to her old
mode of living while her husband was at sea, he
abandoned her on his return. After this she went into
the service of an eccentric old seafaring gentleman, of
the name of Mawer, who died, under very suspicious
circumstances after a few hours' illness, it was said of
cholera, and other. property worth X5O a year. She
then made the acquaintance of the parties named in
in the cases recently before the public. In 1856 she
lived with a young sum named Dixon, • who was sad-
denly taken ill with violent vomiting and purging.
His symptoms were exactly the Same as those exhibited
by Mrs. Soatnes. The woman stated that he died of gallop-
ing consumption, but upon the body being
,opened hre
lungs were found to be perfectly healthy. About the year
1859 she was in the habit of visiting a Mrs. Jackson, who
resided at Boston,alid who drew from the bank a sum of
£l2O, which the convict knew to be inherposaession. She
was taken ill with the same symptons, and died in
four days. After her death the money was nawhere
to be found. Upon that occasion the coneict produced
a promissory note, apparently signed by two persons
residing at Boston, for the amount which was missing,
but it was proved that those signatures were forged.
In October, 1860, she was connected with a Mrs. Atkin-
son, who resided at Kirkby Lonsdale, but who came
to live with the convict at her residence at Kennington.
Mrs. Atkinson was in possession of a considerable sum
of money.. On the 19th. of that month Mrs. Atkinson,
was taken ill, with violent retching and purgingeand
in four days she was dead. In 1851 she was living
with a man named Taylor, and he was attacked in the

_
same manner as the others, but remedies were applied,
and ho recovered. In the earlier part of the present
year she was tried at the Central Criminal Court for
an attempt to murder, by the administration, a
sulphuric acid, a roman in whose house she was
residing, when, notwithstanding a summing up greatly
to her disadvantage by Lord Chief Baron Pollock. the
jury acquitted her.
The body, after banking an.hour, was cut dOwn, and
buried within the precincth,nf the )ga6i.
Amongst the minor Incidents 'connected. With the
proceedings may be mentioned the fact that a clergy-
man called upon the governor, and requested to see the
convict in order that he might afford her spiritual COD-
sOlation. The governor introduced the rev. gentlenn.n
to the ordinary, who did' not seem disposed to allow
his spiritual duties to be interfered with After .some

conversation, the rev, gentleman adinitte4 that: 'Li
i s
main object n wishing to see tho prisoner VMS.
obtain somo inform ton on which to Write. an. article

_
for a periodical with which be was connected, and
upon, this tidraission his services were declined:.

CVRIOUS EFFECT PILODUCED BY LIGHTNING.:—:The
Messager de Bayonne gives an'aceount of an extraordinary
effect of electricity produced last week in the village of
St. Esteve near Perpignan. About one in the morning,
while M. Gaily, the Mayor, and his family were in bed,
they were aroused from their sleep by a tremendous
clap of thunder, accompanied. by heavy rain. The
lightning had fallen in the garden of a house about MO
yards from them, but, FM -the storm did not appear to
have touched their house, and had soon afterwards
passed away, they, again composed themselves to sloop.
On getting up in the morning, however, they. were
astonished at the effects which had been produced by
the lightning. All the doors and windows, beth. on the
ground and first floors that of the dining-room, which
led into the garden, and of the kitchen, which opened
into the street, were covered with patches of a substance
like melted tin or silver, and round all the edges were
shining streaks of the same kind.
CONVICTION UNDBB. ;EHE Nzw POACHING AcT.—On
Saturday last, at the Shire Ilall, Nottingham, an im-
portant case was heard before Lord. Belper and a full
bench of magistrates. Three men, named William
Terrey, Anthony Denham., and John Palmer, were
charged with being at Arnold, near Nottingham, on the
loth of October, with a number of note, rabbits and
game in their possession. Sergeant Blasdall said about
5 o'clock on Wednesday, morning last he and police-
constable Ilill were out watching at Arnold, when they
met the prisoners Palmer and. Denhamanda man named
Wood (who was not now in custody.) Their appear.
ance being suspicious, the policeman stopped and searched
them, finding upon their persons game pegs, driving
lines, &c., of which they took possession. Palmer swore
at witness, and said he was robbing them on the high-
way. The Pegs and lines were wet, and appeared as if
they had been just used. Witness let the prisoners go,
saying he should summon them on a future day. A few
minutes after wards witness saw Terry (who was coming
towards them) place a bag by the side of a hedge.
Witness secured the bag, and Hill held Terry. They
found four rabbits in the bag quite warm and a large
net. Lord Belper said the bench had resolved to con-
vict the whole of the prisoners. In default of paying a
tine of 305., Terry would be committed for one mouth's
imprisonment, with hard labour. Palmer and Denham,
having been previously convicted of poaching, would be
committed for two month's imprisonment, with hard
labour, in default of paying a fine of £3. An order was
then made for the game to be sold and the nets and pegs
destroyed, according to the provisions of the Act.

articles.title: 7.1H.E .EQUINOCTIAL GALE.
articles.text:
7.1H.E .EQUINOCTIAL GALE.

• During the whole of Sunday night, and up to an ad-
vanced hour on al onday morning, an alarming gale
rand over London. The wind, which blew from
ISP.S.W., began to increase in violence shortly after five
o'clock in the evening, and reached its greatest pressure
between nine o'clock and eleven o'clock p.m., as regis-
tered by the anemomear of the Meteorological Depart-
ment of the Board of Ti7ade. It, was accompanied by a
heavy fall of rein. The scene in the different
thoroughfares, particularly at Dulwich, Peckham, and
Camberwell, was truly alarming. The vast accu-
mulation of water on the high land rushed down the
hills with great form, overflowing, the market and
other gardens, and uprooting and, destroying vege-
tables and shrubs. The low-lying lands adjacent to
the Eastern Counties Railway below , Stratford were
completely covered with water, and considerable
damage was done to property,. several sheep being
drowned in the vicinity of Tottenham. In some in-
stances the roadways in the neighbourhood of Greenwich
were so inundated that they 1% ore almost impassable,
the water rushing into the basement of the houses, and
doing much injury. At Sydenham two immense trees by
the force of the wind were snapped in two, and falling
upon a brick wall levelled about 3011. of it to the
ground, carrying away also a large conservatory
attached to a dwelling-house. In the Anerley-road a
lofty stack of chimneys was blown from its position,
fercing in the roof of the house, but fortunately not
injuring any persons. In the same locality the side
wall of an unfinished house was forced Jo ,vn with a
terrible crash, leaving the remaining portion of the
structure in a most dangerous condition. Between 10
.and 11 o'clock a loud crash was heard in the Camber-
well-road, and it was ascertained, that a range of lofty
chimneys had been blown from the roof of a house,
falling upon some out-premises, which were also
destroyed. The gale continued to range up to
an early hour on Monday Morning, when much
more injury, was done bath to
,persons and property.
The river during the gale presented. a most alarminr,
aspect, it being almost impossible ibr small craft Co
remain afloat. Between Battersea and Nine Elms two
sailing barges came into co lision, and great injinl was
done to both; and below Putney a barge laden,kith
timber struck against another, and shortly, afterwards
'filled and sank, the man on board having a narrow
escape. At Battersea, Lambeth, and other low-lying
places, the water at high tide was forced over the banks,
deluging many warehouses in the lower floors, and,
destroying a vast amount of property. The shipping
in the Peal ,sustained • a. deal of damage, the loss of
spars and, injury to rigging generally being most exten-
sive. Three vessels broke thair anchorage, and came
into violent collision, one, the Sisters, having her bow
greatly datnaged, and her rigging injured. A small
steam-tug was cast adrift, and before. it could be pre-
vented ran into a bargeovhichwas stove in and quickly
sank.

The effects of the gale have been most disastrous at
sea. In the Downs, where a large fleet was anchored,
Lloyd's agent reports two ships to have gone down at
their anchors and the fate of the crews uncertain. The
ship Elizabeth, bound to Belize from London, is also
said to have foundered, and it is faired with some of her
crew on board. She broke adrift during the gale on Sun-
day night, and came into violent collision with two
ships called the Wellington and Ambroisine, which
were lying at anchor at her stern. The bark Trio, from
Saffi for London, suffered, so severely from the fury of
the storm, and the sea breaking over her th a she went
down at her anchors; but providentially the crew are
reported to have been able to save themselves in the
boats. A large fleet of disabled vessels have put back;
some have gone into Ramsgate, and others have re-
turned to the Thames. The schooner Charlotte, from
Oporto to London, in coming up Channel, had her
commander washed overboard. The Cupid, belonging
to Goole, was in collision with, the ship City of Pekin
off Folkestone, and foundered. Off Beechy Head the
Wesleyan schooner, laden with stone from Portland to
London, was struck by a heavy sea and had to be aban-
doned-

PORTS3COTTII, Monday, 6.30 p.132.—Th0 gale Of last
night reached its highest point here about midnight,
when the wind considerably moderated, and. daylight
. this morning broke with a clear atmosphere, and the wind
getting into N.N.W. A strong breeze prevailed during
the whole of yesterday without rain up to 5 p.m. when
a rain squall passed over from N.N.W., but was of short
duration. The wini is now N.Vir., strong. The ships
at Spithead had their topgallant masts down and yards
pointed to the wind. The lowest point reached by the
barometer last night was 28.90, from which it rose again
to 29.35 by 10 o'clock this morning, and now has reached
2912.

LEEDS, Monday Afternoon.—This part of Yorkshire
was visited with a severe storm of wind,. rain, and hail
on Sunday night last. The temperature was very low,
and there was a constant fa 1 of rain, with occasional
squalls of wind during the greater part of the day. The
storm increased in the evening,7 and continued the
greater part of the night. In Leeds many houses and
buildings were more or less injured, buthappily no lives
were lost.

GVAT YAIDTOUTII, Oct. 2dt—A storm of great
violence raged off the Norfolk coast last night and this
morning. No loss of lifa has yet been reported, but
the Hannah Booth, of Plymouth,. is on shore at Caistor,
having been abandoned by the crew, who succeeded in
saving themselves through their boats. The Integrity.,
of Hartlepool, also sank after having struck on the Bar-
ber Sand; in this instance also. the crew were saved.
The John, of Hartlepool. has been brought in here
derelict, and the Cambria, of Shields, has also been
assisted in, much damaged, having got on the Scroby.
The wind blew tremendously last night from the S.S.W.
--fortunately neither upon the Scroby, the d nagerous
and fatal sands in the offing, nor upon the shore, other-
wise, no doubt, immense damage and loss of life would
have taken place, as there were no lass than SOO to 900
sessels at anchor in the roadstead:

•
SUNDERLAND. Monday Afternoon.—A violent hurri-
cane burst over Sunderland this morning. The
weather had been uns4tled throughout the greater part
of yesterday, and about nine o'clock in the evening a
heavy fall of rain: commenced, accompanied with gusts
of wind, By half-past eleven. it blew a• gale from
W.S.W. In tli,e River Wear two vessels broke adrift,
hat they were secured without having received match
damage. Outside the town a large portion of a foundry
which was being built has been thrown to the ground;
and a portion of the roof of a newly-built house fell
into the bedroom occupied by the children. No injury
to life or limb has, however, as yet been reported. Th..
hurricane began to abate about two o'clock, and as the
wind kept ranging to W.N.W., it gradually died away
to a calm by daybreak.
SIIIELDS; Monday Afternoon.—Between 9 o'clock last
night and 1 this morning the coast was visited by one
of the most terrible storms from the W.S.W. that hal
been experienced here for many years. At about a quarter
past 12, when' it tvas at its height, it blew a perfect
hurricane' and.the amount of injury that has been done
in our harbour is'something fearful. Mercifully the
wind was off shore. If it had blown upon the coast no
ship could have kept off, and our coast would have been
sh own with wrecks. About o'clock last night lights
were flashing' in the offing., indicating that vessels were
off the port, and a powerful steamer took out a number
of sea pilots, and got them aboard these vessels. These
ships were subsequently blown off the land, but there is
no special cause of anxiety with regard to. them. A
large bark, the Clarendon, was towing round from Hull
to Shields in the height of the gale. While off Souter
Point -the towline broke, and the steamboat, the Van-
guard, had to abandon her. Some 'anxiety prevails
with regard to this ship, as she had but few hands
aboard. The force of the gale has been most seriously
felt in the Tyne, however, down the reaches, by which
the wind swept with the: greatest fury. Above Bill
Point a number of vessels are sunk, and a large amount
of mischief has been done by factory buildings in that
neighbourhood falling, and below that point to the bar
of the Tyne the banks of the river are strewn with
wrecks.

LT"EnrooL, Monday Afternoon.—Liverpool and the
vicinity were visited on -Sunday night with a heavy
gale from the north-west: The gale somewhat abated
on Monday morning, but towards afternoon the wind
considerably increased in strength. The weather was
exceedingly cold, and heavy showers of hail fell at inter-
vals. There have as yet been no serious disasters

reported in the Mersey, but it is apprehended that some
casualties may have occurred outside the port. Last
nipt the American ships Wisconsin and Carrier Dove,
both lying off Seacorabe, in the Mersey, came into
collision in consequence of the former dragging her
anchor and drifting against the Carrier &ye. The
_

steam-tug Universe succeeded in towing the Wisconsin
into the George's Basin, where she now lies; she has
lost her mizennaast, spars, &c. The Molocka, from
New York, drifted to Bootle Bay, had to cut her masts
away, and was towed back to the river. Telegrams
received in Liverpool announce that the bark North-
umberland, from Dalhousie, had been driven from her
moorings in Lime, Fleetwood, and gone ashore, and that
the Ann E. Hooper, from Baltimore, had been wrecked
near Southport. This morning the Southport and
Lytham lifeboats had gone out to her. One boat left

BRADFORD, Monday.—For some days the weather
here has been exceedingly boisterous and wet, the wind
blo nag from the south-west. Last night, about ten
o'eloel, a terrible storm came on from the same quarter.
The tempest was preceded by an extraordinary fall in
the barometer. During some hours the wind blew
with th.e force of a hurricane and at intervals there
is ere heavy showers of rain and hail. About midnight
.an immense chimney at the Horton dye works was blown
down.

The stations upon this line are now ready fer' traffic,
though some few days will yet elapse before they are
brought intduse. That in Farringdon-street is a very
commodious one, and is situated about a hundred yards
• from the foot of Holborn-hill. The railway runs in an
open cutting from this station parallel with the New
Farringdon-street, until the mouth of the tunnel is
reached near Coppice-row. This tunnel is about 600
yards long, and terminates at Frederick-street, Bagnigge-
wells road. There is then an open cutting to the tunnel
mouth at King's-cross, where there are two branches
connecting with the Midland and Great Northern
Railways. The retaininr, walls are fine specimens of
brickwork, carefully finished, and the mouth of the
tunnel has considerable architectural decoration. The
station at Kling's-cross is a few feet below the
Burnie° of the road. At the station there are -two
wide platforms ; and sPanning a width of about
ninety feet, and sustained by girders of openwork, is the
station building itself, containing booking-offices,
waiting-rooms, parcels-offices, &c., and communicating
With the platforms by stairs and landings in duplicate,
one set ' serving for arrivals, the other as departures.
The station is 'covered by an elliptical wrought-iron
roof, with sufficient glass to preserve an agreeable but
not a glaring light. Passing under the New-road the
first station is one at Gower-street. The platforms here
are under the footpaths-of the road, and with the rail-
way are spanned by a huge arch of forty-Ave feet open-
ing. The sides'of the arch are perforated with openings
at intervals of ten feet: these openings are continued
into the forecourts or gardens of the houses, where,
area-like, they emerge, and are covered with glass,
the whole having the appearance of windows • with -
elongated reveals, lined with glazed white earthen-
ware tiles. Thus both direct and reflected rays of light,
impinge upon. each platform and completely light
the whole superstructure. Ingress and egress to the
stations are effected by Means of booking-offices
placed on the north and south sides of the EustOn-road,
in the gardens of the houses, and by wide exit and
entrance stairs leading from booking offices to platforms.
The effect of this station, and' its numerous intersected
and intersecting arches, is novel in i4s appearance and
imposing in its effects. Portland-road station is the
next one. It is above ground, and occupies the site of
the once verdant oval enclosure near Trinity Church.
One booking-office here suffices, and the 'lighting and
ventilation are effected by a- pair of domes, and by open-
ings in the crown of the arch. The communication
with the platforms is by stairs and galleries across the
line, which, sustained by trelliswork, has a light and
pleasing effect. The station at Baker-street, which is
the next one, is similar in almost all respects to that of .
the Portland-road. The station at the Edge w are-road,
though of somewhat smaller dimensions, is not unlike
that at King's-cross. It spans over the line and plat-
forms, and is covered by an elliptical arched roof of iron
and glass. The brickwork is faced with Ransom's
patent stone, of which the ornamental parts of all the
bridges is formed. At the Great Western Railway the
station is very conveniently placed, and is on a level
with the Paddington station.—Observer.

articles.title: DESTRUCTIVE FLOOD NEAR
articles.text:
DESTRUCTIVE FLOOD NEAR

C.ARLISL.E.

A seriousl disaster occurred at Holme Head, near
Carlisle, on Friday, which resulted in part of Messrs.
Ferguson Brothers' siiesia works being washed away,
and the effect of which will be to throw out of employ-
ment the hands at several mills. Until about two
months ago there was a bay in the river Caldew, at
Hearne Head, from which part of the river was diverted
into a mill race, to supply about half a dozen mills of
different kinds with water power ; but, as some of our
readers may remember, heavy rains in the beginning or
middle of August undermined and washed down the bay,
and the milloWners had to resort to the erection of a
temporary embankment to turn the water into the old
dam course. On Thursday last heavy rain fell in Carlisle,
and towards evening there was a severe storm, which
flooded the rivers till they overflowed their natural
banks: As-the waters of the•Caldew rose it was found
necessary to strengthen the temporary embankment,
and by this means the Water was held in check for a
time; but during the night the river rose higher, the
' rain falling in torrents, and the wind blowing a strong
gale,. and by six o'clock on Friday morning the em-
bankment was submerged. In half an hour longer a
head- 20 yards long was made in it, and as a pile of
stones on the south side of the river (the ruins of the
old bay) diverted the current from that side' the
stream poured through the head with great fury,
and dashed against the otter walls of the silesia
works of Messrs. Ferguson Brothers. A stone wall
on which a public footpath was constructed, formed
an outwork which strengthened their premises, but
the power of the water was so great that the
large foundation stones w ) soon hurled out of their
places and rolled down the torrent. This protection'
having at length been washed away, it became evident
that the building near the stream must fall. It was a
brick erection, two stories high, used as a. store-room
and damping-room. Men were set to work to clear
.the goods out, and before their work was- completed
they were warned to leave the building. They had
scarcely done so when down fell-the gable end and
part of the side wall with a great crash into the raging
waters. On man had a 'narrow escape from drowning,
but there were no lives lost. About leAt pieces of
silesia were precipitated into the river, but most of
them were eventually dragged out lower down the
stream. The storm had now abated, and with the
falling of the river further danger passed away. The
hands employed in about half a dez,tn mills along the
dam”course will be thrown out of work,. and it is
feared that it will be a long time before the water can
be brought down the course again.

MURDER OF THE CAPTAIN OF THE' CONFEDERATE
lirAa SHIP SUMTER. LIVERPOOL, Saturday. A
telegram was received here to-day from Gibraltar, and as
the source is respectable we place it before our readers:
The second officer of the Sumter yesterday, (Oct.
16th), murdered the captain at Gibraltar. He has con-
fessed his crime, and is under arrest.
THE NEW ORGAN OX THE PAPACI7.—SOMe of the
speakers at the London. Tavern disclaimed any hostility
to Catholicism, and pretended that the outcry for the
evacuation of Rome had nothing to do with 'No
Popery' feeling, and ought not to be offensive to Catho-
lics. Surely they could not expect the Catholics to
believe them. The feelinc, in this country in favour of
the evacuation of Rome has a religious origin.; the sup-
port which the Ministerial policy in. Italy has so gene-
rally obtained is dictated by religious beliefs and preju-
dices. The Ministers themselves deal with the question
from a purely Protestant stand-point; they are always
denouncing the Papal Administration, and treat with
the utmost contempt all the remon,strances of the Catho-
lics. Although so large a part of the population of the
empire is Catholic, no consideration is shown in the
treatment of this question for Catholic feelings.Korn-
iny Herald.

-EXTRAORDINARY ESCAPE OP a. BOY FRO3I THE FURY
OF A BULL,—On Sunday morning, as the ten o'clock
fast train on the Notth Kent line was maring Erith
Station on the way to Stroud, the engine-driver saw ,a
boy, of about twelve or thirteen years of age, being
pursued by a bull from the adjoining marshes. The
boy, got on the line, calculating that ,the aninial would
not venture on the metals. He judged wrongly, how-
ever, for the animal dashed over the fence, and had just
reached the down metals, when the noise of the whistle
caused. it to hesitate for a moment and incline its head
towards the engine, and, at the instant, it was struck
on the right shoulder by the near beer, and the guard-
iron in front having entered the body, tore it up in a
manner that death must have been instantaneous. The
engine passed on uninjured, and the boy had been fox
tunately delivered from his danger. _ _ '

GALLANT RESCUE OF A CREI.-011 Friday morning,
during a furious storm, a merchant vessel laden with
stone and bound for Titchfield from Portsmouth, became
a total wreck on these dangerous shoals called the Wool-
sners, lying outside of Langstone Harbour, a: few miles
to the eastward of Portsmouth. She grounded hard and
fast, and parted amidships, the upper part of the masts
and rigging appearing just above water. To these the
crew clung, almost in despair, and remained in that
perilous position for more than five hours, almost without
hope of rescue. The Coast-guard boat, manned by
Coast-guard boatmen, put off tp %he vessel, but were
compelled to return on account of the imminent risk they
ran of being upset. At length one poor fellow slipped
from the mast almost insensible and would assuredly
have been drowned had not three gallant boatmen of
Hayling Island, at this critical juncture put off. These
men in their little boat pulled stoutly towards the ship.
Several times they were given up for lost, the waves
having to all appearances overwhelmei them. But pro-
videntially they reached the barque, rescued the crew,
and gained the shore in safety amidst the plaudits of the
bystanders. The man who slipped from the mast has
continued insensible, and doubts are entertained as to his
recovery. On the same day the annual meeting of the
Hayling Island Agricultural Association was held at the
Royal Hotel, on the beach, Mr. Y. Casher, who witnessed
the bravery of the boatmen, proposed that a subscriptioD
should be entered into for the gallant fellows. The
appeal was responded to in a most liberal manner.

The last great horticultural show at Namur was the

NEW YORK, Oct. 10 (Evening).—Desperate ghting
occurred on the Bth and 9th inst., at Perrysville, Ken-
tucky; between 'General Bragg and General Buell's
forces. The-Fe4ral loss is reported to have been 2,000
in killed and -wounded, two generals and a large number
of officers being among the former. The accounts re-
ceived are very confused, some stating that the Confede-
rates remained in possession of part of the field, while
others, on the contrary, affirm that the Federals drove
them seven miles. The result of the engagement
appears from present accounts to have been indecisive.
A general battle was, however, expected on the follow-
ing day. Confederate General Morgan has been routed
by General Dumont, at Frankfort, Kentucky. The
Confederates have evacuated Lexington, and are moving
in the direction of Cumberland Gap, pursued by tile
Federals.

Istiw YORK, Oct. 10 (Evening).—General M'Clellan
has issued a eongratzlatery general order to the troops
for their Conduct in the battles of, South Mountain and
Antietam. He states that the Federal triumph is evi-
denced by the capture of 14 guns, 15,000 stand of arms,
and 6,000 prisoners. A large 'Republican meeting has
been held. in New York, at which the Democrats were
strongly denounced as sympathisers with treason. The
Federal Governmenthas aband one d the negro colonisation
scheme. The Ministers of the Central American Republics.
had protested against the scheme being carried out in
Central America. General Bragg has issued. a procla-
mation urging the North-Western States to exercise
their State sovereignty and make a separate treaty of
peace with the, Confederates. as the Federal Government
refuses to conclude a general treaty . He declares that
the South will never interfere with the free navigation
of the Mississippi and concludes by making a vigorous
appeal to the•peOple to desist from a-war s, Oh, he says,
can only, after greater sacrifices. terminate, in a. treaty
of peace.

NEW YORK, Oct. 11 (AI or g.)—*—Tb e Confederates,
under General .Stuart, have again crossed. the Potomac,
at Hancock, into Maryland. They pushed forward
across the country, and yesterday occupied Mertersburg
and Chambersbmg, in PennSYlvania. Their force is
estimated at 3,000 men, their advance consisting of 1,000
cavalry, and sir pieces of artillery. The. inhabitants of
Mercersburg and. Chambersburg had no means of resist-
ance. The Governor of Pennsylvania is however,
sending troops up the Cumberland Valley. The
news has created the greatest astonishment in New
York. The latest reports state that the engagement
at Perrysville, Kentucky, on the 9th instant, was short
but desperate, when the Confederates broke and retreated
south, with the Federals in full pursuit. The corres-
pondence published in the New York journals repre-
sents the fighting at Corinth en the 3rd and 4th inst. to
have been very severe. The Confederates succeeded in
reaching the main public square of Corinth, but new
batteries were opened upon them, and they retreated.
The Federal pUrsuit was continued as far as Ripley,
Mississippi. The Federals have captured a battery ou
the St: John's river, 'and cut off the retreat of a Georgia
regiment. An engagement has occurred near Suffolk.
The Confederates were driven acme 13l ckwater river.
A Federal brig has been chased by a Confederate steamer
supposed to be the Ovieto, in the. Gulf of Mexico. The
steamer Leopard has arrived at Nassau from Charleston.
A resolution has been introduced in the Confederate
Congress authorising the Secretary of the. Treasury to
purchast, or impress one million bales of cotton at a fixed
price, and also to send agents. to Europe to sell this
cotton. The resolution, also proposed. the repeal of all
laws prohibiting the export of cotton from ports occupied
by the enemy, when such cotton is purchased by foreign
Governments or subjects. •

Forty thousand men have enlisted in the Federal
navy.
THE COLLEEN BAwN.—Ellen Hanky, the Colleen
Bawn,' was drowned in the Lower Shannon on either
13th, 14th, or 15th of July, 1819. Her boAy was washed
on shore at a place called Money Point, and it was in-
terred in Burrane churchyard, which is about a mile
distantfrom Money'Point. The spot wheie the body was
buried was unmarkedby any tombstone, until fecently ;
but Mr. Reeves, on whosepropertythe Burranechurchyard
is situated, has just erected an Irish cross to the Colleen's
memory. It bears the simple epitaph—' Colleen Bawn,
July'l9! Some Irish papers have made Mr. Reeves'
act ridiculous by calling the tombstone magnificent.'

. -
I PATENTS AND PATENTEES.—It is not long since a num-
ber of men, more or less prominent, were declaiming
against patents and urging their entire abolition. In-
ventors, we were told, were not entitled to monopolies,
and really needed no protection. Sweep away the
patent laws,' said Sir William Armstrong and his
disciples, and the prestige of successful invention will
sufficiently reward the inventor.' It ii not exactly shown
how an inventor was to realise a fortune from an unpro-
tected invention, nor was it, indeed, shown in what

'prestige' really consisted. Sir William said in substance,
if not in so many words, Look afme; lam an inventor;
I have succeeded without protection.' But he was not
an inventor, and his success has come rather through for-
tune and worldly wisdom than through the recognition
and appreciation of his merits by the public at large.
The so-called Armstrong gun is ne more his invention
than it is that of Lord Dundreary, and it is now more
than questionable whether, if Sir William had really in-
vented it, it could do him any great credit. There were
circumstances which placed him in a good position with
the late Sir Benjamin Hawes, and a premature knight-
hood and a fat contract are the r.esults. Sir William has
no right to speak for inventors. Ho is not of them, albeit
he has shown great aptitude in assimilating inventions,
and respectable mechanical skill in working them into
shape. Even the mazy failures of Ihe Elsw-iok and Wool-
wich guns do not disentitle Sir William to the rank of a
first-class mechanical engineer, but an inventor he is not,
and, indeed, his famous attack upon the rights of inven-
tors was inconsistent with any notion to the contrary.—
Engineer.

AN INFURIATED Ox.—Great alarm and excitement
were created on the 21st in the Bageigge-wells-road,
Gray's-inn-roed, and Meeklenburgh-square, by the ap-
pearance of a bullock in a most infuriated state. The
foot passengers in the route the animal took had the
greatest difficulty in effecting their escape from being
gored. After overturnirE several barrows, the owners
of which had abandoned, he rushed furiously at a
lad who was endeavouring to effect hie escape near the
Bagnigge-wells Tavern, and threw him up; fortunately
the home only penetrated his dress, leaving a slight scar
on his thigh, but the lad sustained a severe contusion by
the fall. The furious beast then turned off, and, crossing
the Gray's-inn-read into John-street, Bedford-row,
followed by a number of men and boys, he there knocked
down two men, and rushed at great speed into Doughty-
mews, where he entered the stables of Mr. C. Case,
omnibus and cab proprietor, tearing up a manger with
his horns, and the ostlers-had the greatest difficulty in
getting the horses out of danger. He then turned into
Mr. Case's dwelling house, where he tore up the banisters
and did other damage, but was at last captured by the
lasso and taken to a corner of the yard, where he was
chained up in security.
A Royal warrant, issued by command of her Majesty,
laying down the rules and regulations under which
medals and annuities for long and meritorious service
will in future be issued to the non-commissioned officers
Of the army, has been promulgated, with the view of re-
warding distinguished and meritorious services and of
promoting good conduct in the army. The Royal warrant
directs that a certain fixed sum will be granted in an-
nuities to sergeants who, shall be entitled to receive and
wear a silver medal bearing on one side the Royal effigy
and on the other the words for meritorious service,' the
name and rank of the sergeant being inscribed thereon.
A silver medal, bearing on ttle side 'for distinguished
conduct on the field,' will, in certain cases, where
specially recommended, be issued to sergeants, with an-
nuity, in lieu of the before-mentioned medal for meri-
torious service with annuity, subject, however, to the
conditions and limitations now in force as to the grant of
annuities. The warrant further declares that a similar
medal be granted, without annuity or gratuity, to
sergeants, corporals, and privates of the army, when
specially recommended by the General Commanding-in-
Chief, and appointed by the Secretary of State for War,
for individual acts of distinguished conduct in the field
in any part of the world.
, THE GOVERNOR OF TASMANIA.—A bill some time
eince passed the Tasmanian Legislature altering the
sum Payable to the Governor of Tasmania for allowances
and contingent expenses. This bill has been submitted
for her Majesty's consideration. The Duke of New-
castle has 'written to the Governor of Tasmania, stating
that whilst her Majesty would be advised to assent to
any measure for such prospective reduetions as any of
the Colonial Legislatures might deem necessary, it would
not be considered competent for such Legislature to
curtail eithei the salary or the allowances to which a
Governor was entitled when he was selected by the
Crown for the administration of the Government.
SOMNAMBULISM—The
Courrier de l' Isere relates an
extraordinary
instance of somnambulism in a young
workman at Grenoble. Two nights ago, while fast
acleep,aurent, now in
he left his house, descended towards the Qual doSaint-L
construction, and after walking
about amongst the stones and rubbish, went on board a
boat moored alongside, end then passed along the narrow
planks which served for carrying the materials to the
lauding-place. He afterwards proceeded to the suspen-
sion-bridge, and jumping lightly on one of the iron cables
effected the perilous ascent to the top of one of the lofty
constructions on which the wires are drawn. He there
sat for a few Minutes, turning his head right and left, as
though looking at the number of persons who in breath-
less anxiety were watching his movements. ,He after-
wards descended by the same dahle, walked along the
Parapet of the quay, and returning to his lodging entered
h bed in safety.

articles.title: LANCASHIRE DISTRESS.
articles.text:
LANCASHIRE DISTRESS.

MANSION-HOUSE COMMITTEE.

On the 21st the Lord Mayor received the munificent
contribution cf £lO,OOO, the first instalment of a tam
of about £2a,000 subscribed by the inhtbitants of
Bombay assembled in public meeting, at which his Ex-
cellency Sir Bartle Frere, the Governor, presided, and
which was largely attended by all classes of the com-
munity, both native and European. The remittance
was accompanied by a letter from Mr. Brooke, one of
the honorary secretaries, explaining that, in consequence
of the great increase in the destitution in the cotton
manufacturing districts, the Committee of the Bombay
Chamber of Commerce had deemed it a fitting occasion
upon which the sympathies of all classes of the com-
munity should be enlisted, and hence the meeting. The
money has been forwarded to the Lord Mayor, with the
reiniest-that he will apply it at his discretion in the re-
lict of the prevailing destitution.
Mr. Cu.bitt wrote the following reply:—
'Mansion-house, Oct. 2/.

Sir,—ln my 'mu name, and on behalf of the Mansion-
house Committee for tie relief of distress in the cotton
districts, ever whom I have the honour to preside, I beg
to offer our united thanks to his Exceth-ncy the Governor,
to the Committee of the Chamber of Commerce of Bom-
bay, and to the numerous contributors by whose.generous
aid we are put in possession of the munificent donation of
£lO,OOO. This emphatic demoNstration of sympathy.
from Bombay will be gratefully appreciated in the suffer-
ing localities; the large amount will enable us materially
to augment our immediate distribution and tl,e no le ex-
ample thus set cannot fail to have a beneficial influence
throughout the wide extent of the British empire.
'lhave the honour to be your obedient servant,
WI-m.lAm Cufarr, Mayor.'
H. Brooke, Esq., &e.'

articles.title: PRESTON.
articles.text:
PRESTON.

At the weekly meeting of the relief committee, held
on Monday night, it was reported that 7,596 cases, com-
prising 30,855 persons, had been relieved during the
past week, at a cost of £712 2s. Bd., being an increase
of 202 cases, 1,129 persons, and an expenditure of
cf.:34 I@s. 2d. over the preceding week. 259 young
women had been employed at the Great Shaw-street
sewing-room, at a cost of a 2s. A considerable in-
crease in the number of sick cases relieved by the com-
mittee, more than 600 having received assistance from
the sick kitchen. The medical officers report that about
80 cases of fever have been attended to by them, and
energetic steps are being taken to arrest the further
progr,ess of this fearful malady. The visitors in con-
nection with the :relief committee are instructed to re-
port all cases of overcroweling'in -dwellinghouses to the
inspector of lodginghouses, as also all houses which
are found in filthy condition, when steps will be
taken to render them habitable. The board of guar-
dians, the borough surveyor, and the relief committee
are all working together in dais matter. A third public
meeting is to be called for the purpose of raising a fund
for the purchase of bedding and clothing. About £B,OOO
will be required to place the people in a condition to
withstand the inclement weather which has set in. The
local subscription list for the week includes a donation
of £l,OOO from the Lord Mayor's Committee, and £5OO
from Mr. Alderman Miller, the latter sum being spe-
cially given for the purchase of fuel. Three hundred
tons of coals, part of Mr. Blundell's gift, will be dis-
tributed in Preston forthwith. The police returns of the
state of employment in the cotton mills alone are as fol-
lows :—Total number of mills in Preston, 87; totally
closed, 34; number of workpeople fully employed, 3,81;
worldno. five days, 736; four days, 2,733; three days,
7,585-; atwo days, 131; and totally unemployed, 12,130.
The usual. number of workpeOple employed in the cotton
mills during ordinary times is 27,196. The above does
not include those -who are out of employment 'through
the btoppage.of the mills, estimated to be about 2,000.

articles.title: BURNLEY.
articles.text:
BURNLEY.

The distress rapidly increases in this district, and it
is expected that both in Padiham, Marsden, Barrowford,
COlne, and also in Burnley itself, a considerable number
of cotton operatives will be thrown out of work in a
' few days. The Burnley board of guardians his gradu-
ally raised its relief to is. 6-kd. per head, including all
classgs of paupers, and the aid given to cotton opera-
tives is generally reckoned on a scalc of is.. er
head. The relief committees of Burnley and Padiham,
and generally throughout the union, keep their relief
entirely distinct from that of the, board of guardians.
The rate of relief by these committees in Burnley
and Padiham is now is. 9d. per head. Recently the
Burnley committee adopted a decision to raise the rate
of relief for 5,000 persons from is. -3d. per head weekly to
is. 9c1., thereby encountering an immediate increase of
expenditure of .L 125 per week. This increase was
doubtless adopted in. the expectation. that the committee
would receive external assistance, as well as that
the local subscriptions in. Burnley • would, at a
very early peiiod, receive a large augmentation.
The board have been justified in. the first of these con-
clusions by a grant of £BO9 from the Central Executive
Relief Committee, and one of £3OO from the
Mansion-house Committee. Both the boards of guardians
and the relief committees have established sewing
classes, and likewise schools for youth, and have set on
work able-bodied men in various local improvements
throughout .the distritt. The board of guardians has
now under its consideration the best means of providing
indoor manual work for youth and men during the more
inclement part of the season; and it is proposed to them
to obtain unoccupied warehouses or mills aud to provide
various forms of employment in them, which may .fulfil
the requirements of the law, during a greater part at
least of each day. The distribution of relief in kind in
this district has hitherto been conducted by means of
tickets, which are taken to the ordinary shopkeepers and
are expended on whatever articles of necessity the
family may require. There is, however, under considera-
tion a project for establishing in some parts of the
district cooking kitchens, in which not only soup
will be prepared on a considerajile scale and
distributed there upon the tickets of the relief com-
mittees or 'board of guardians, or sold at a low
price; but in which also coffee and bread may be obtained,
and other forms of refreshment. It is intended by the
projectors to make these cooking kitchens subser-
vient, as far as possible, to the instruction and employ-
ment of young females in cooking, so as to supply one
of the chief defects in the training of factory girls.
The conduct of the working classes throughout East
Lancashire has hitherto in the main been exemplary,
though efforts have not been wanting on the part of
reckless persons to excite dissatisfaction with the reason-
able forms of employment which have been adopted by
the relief committee and the boards of guardians. These
efforts have little chance of success, since the board of
guardians has had the wise forethought to make ar-
rangements with the Poor Law Board that both youth
and men shall in inclement weather be permitted to
exchange outdoor manual labour for work in school. In
every part of the union suitable rooms are now being
fitted up, and masters have been appointed to take
charge of schools for youth and men; and both the
relief committees and the boards of guardians will in-
crease the exteat of these arrangements as far as the
necessities of the case may be found to require—the
intention being that the entire population shall be kept
from the evil consequences of idleness by reasonable
employment on suitable work. •

articles.title: ASIETON7UNDER-LYNE.
articles.text:
ASIETON7UNDER-LYNE.

The Borough Relief Committee relieved last week at
Messrs. Hulme's mill (4774 persons, at a cost of
£209 17s. 6d., and at various mills 2,550 persons, at a
cost of £147 16s. Rd., making a total of 11,324 persons,
at a cost of £357 14s. 2d. As compared with the pre-

the foll3wing grants to sewing classes—viz., to the

netion class, £2O; and to the Wesleyan Methodist class,
£2O. The committee also allowed £2l is. Bd., for
