Mr. Elihu Burritt intends to visit England in the
course of a few weeks.

Lord Stanley was present at the last petty sessions
held in the town of Tipperary, when he saw the follow-
ing specimen of the Tipperary Boys' :—John Mh-Fa,
an ol:c1 offender, was charged, on his own admission, with
burning, on the lands of Kilfeacle, a rick of hay, the
property of Richard Dalton, of Tipperary, and also two
houses, the property
of P. Gleeson, of Kilfeacle. Con-
stable T. Regan proved that Mara came to his barrack
the night previous. and showed him houses on fire, and
on, about three-quarters of a mile
also showed him a rick of hay on fire, and
in
anotherfitsetarnbtinhe being direction,
cautioned he admitted to his having burnt
the hay and houses, and pointed out to the constable
where he threw away the matches. When asked had
he anything to say, he said that it was he who burnt
them, and that he would, only his feet failed him, burn
every house from Kilfeacle to Cashel.' When asked
where he was from, he said, from Tipperary, and that
he was only two days out of Clonrnel Gaol, where he
had. been confined. The total property destroyed is
about 15 tons of hay, a forge, and an outhouse. The
case was returned for trial to the next assizes of Clon-
mel. This is the second instance in the neighbourhood
of Tipperary of wantonly setting fire to farm buildings,
thereby causing great destruction of property.
AN ELECTOR'S ARGUMENT. - The following is a
literal fact, and occurred not a hundred miles from the
good town of Reeding. A member of parliament was
called on by a tradesman from a different part of the
country, for an order for work in a darticular depart-
ment. The tradesman having no personal knowledge
of his desired customer, nor any recommendatory intro-
duction, sent his business card, writing at the foot the
following significant hint: Too (two) votes for
county.'

articles.title: GOLD-DIGGINGS OF CA1211300.
articles.text:
THE GOLD-DIGGINGS OF CA1211300.

Intelligence from British Columbia is conveyed in a
letter from San• Francisco, dated September the 10th.
Within the last week two steamers have arrived from
Victoria, Vancouver Island, which brought late news
from the mines of British Columbia. - The steamers ply-
ing between Vancouver Island. and New Westminster,
brought to. Victoria, between the 23rd and the last day
of August, 168,0JU dols. in gold dust, besides consider-
able quantities in the possession of passengers, not mani-
fested. A much larger amount would have come from
the mines were it not that remittances from Cariboo have
almost entirely ceased in consequence of the dread of
robbery, inspired by the murder and robbery of two men
mentioned in my last letter. This danger has induced
the miners to retain their gold till such time as they can
come down in gangs for mutual 'retection at the end of
the mining season, so that much gold need not be looked
for in Victoria tilt about November. The last two
steamers from Victoria ',-,brought to. San Francisco about
150,000 dole., of which 107,231 dols. was manifested. It
is impossible to ascerta n .the amount brought to this
place, as the passengers carry so much which is not
manifested, and as efforts are made to suppress the
amount carried, with the view of depreciating the pro-
ductiveness of our mines. For instance, some time,back
I knew of 120,000 dots. having been shipped from Vic-
toria by a steamer whose remittance was published on
her arrival in San Francisco at one-fourth of this amount.
This must happen so long as we are dependent upon
American steamers for the carrying trade between this
place and our colonies.
An enclosure from a gentleman who had been travel-
ling in the Cariboo district, says :
At Antler the returns are moderate, the miners not
having got to the bed-rock. Some few claims are doing
well.

Williams Creek is the soul of Cariboo. Here are the
rich deposits. Through the kindness of Mr. Abbott I
saw his men wash up. - The day's returns were 100 oz.
to five men. He informed me that he averaged 90 to
_ _ _ _

100 oz. per day. He has since sold out for 1-f,OOO and
some odd dollars. I had a conversation with Mr. H. N.
Steele; his claim yielded 1,000 dole. to the pan on Wed-
nesday, the 23rd of July. The largest piece of gold
found this season here was found in Abbott's claim-
-11 oz.

Hid a conversation with Mr. W. W. Cunningham.
TheSo.rgest week',s yield was 23,000 dols. At a rough
calculation, his claim has yielded 180,000 dols. this sea-
son. An eighth share sold for 16,000 d.Ue has some
13 men employed by night, and 12 by day; depth of
claim four feet to eight feet.
At claim,
Gulch 300 dole. were taken out of a
hole on the 4th. Claims above are making 30oz. to the
hand per day. Good news has reached us from Lowhee
,and Lightning. But I must conclude, as the express is
waiting. I shall be with you in a week or so after you
receive this.
Provisions at Antler last week were :—Flour, 1 del. ;
retail, 1 dol. 10e. ; beans, 1 dol. ; bacon, 1 dol. 25c.; tea,
3 dols.; sugar, 1 dol. 12.1 C.; butter, 2 dols. 50a. per lb;
yeast powders, per box, 125 dols.; tobacco, 9 dols. 50c. •
dried apples, 1 dol. 25c.; lard, 1 dol. 12,1 e. per lb.; and
you will have Williams' Creek prices.
The Brothers Fenton have opened a first-rate hotel
for Cariboo. We can now get a good meal for 2 dols.
.50e. Formerly we paid the same for a bit of steak *and
a couple of pieces of bread. They are gentlemen much
liked, and are sure of success. Excuse more.

articles.title: MB. GLADSTONE AND THE ROYAL AVA.L RES.ERV.Z.
articles.text:
MB. GLADSTONE AND THE ROYAL
AVA.L RES.ERV.Z.

On his recent visit to the Sunderland Docks, Mr.
Gladstone received a salute from the men of the Royal
Naval Reserve, who, under the command of Captain
Heard, of the training ship Trincomalee,. were under
arms on the roadway opposite that vessel. Before
taking leave of the men, Mr. Glad-tone addressed them
as follows :--‘ My friends of the Naval Reserve, and
especially your gallant commander, I hope you won't
think I use the words of idle compliment when I state
that I have seen nothing in the whole course of my
most deeply interesting visit to the north Of" England
with greater interest or satisfaction than your body
gathered on this occasion. Ido not believe among all
the measures that have been taken by the government
or suggested for the purpose of national defence, a,
wiser suggestion has ever been made, or better mea-
sures adopted, than the incorporation of the Naval
Reserve.. It is a measure in its spirit essentially pacific,
and, at the same time, it is a measure, as we know per-
fectly ,well, from the . experience of last winter, which
has proved to be quite effective. I must not presume
to .make myself a judge of military or naval discipline,
but I have spent some writke on board a Queen's ship,
and I never spent a portion of my life with greater
satisfaction; and. if t may be allowed to say so, I see in
you the indications not to be mistaken of the same spirit
of self-denying discipline and resolution which have
made the name of British sailors so famous throughout
the world. Accept my best wishes for your healtt . and
prosperity, and of my certain confidence that .you have
rendered a great service to your country, as well as
taking the wisest course for yourselves, in becoming
members of the Naval Reserve.'

articles.title: BRITISH COLUMBIA.
articles.text:
BRITISH COLUMBIA.

(From the Weekly Colonist, Aug. 26.)
The following extract from a report received this day
from the Assistant Gold. Commissioner of the Cariboo
district is herewith published for general information.
WILLIA.3t A. G. YOITNO.
Colonial Secretary's Office, Aug. 20.

Mr. Elwyn to the Colonial Secretary.
Williams' Creek, July 13.

'At the time of my visit to Lightning' thei:e were
nearly 1,000 men on that creek and its tributaries,
some engaged in opening out their claims, the ma-
jority pLospecting. Lightning is considered a difficult
creek to work, its waters being affected by every shower
of rain; a rise of .two feet during an afternoon is by
no means an uncommon occurrence. I spite of this
disadvantage, the creek, I am convinced, will be most
extensively worked. At the time of my visit the claim
owners had not commenced to take out gold, and I
am therefore unable to report with certainty as to the
richness of the claims. I have no hesitation, however,
in stating as my firm belief that Lightning will be found
second only in importance to the creek from which I
write. At the Junction of Van Winkle with Lightning
Creek a town has already sprung up, and, unless I am
greatly mistaken, will become the depot for the whole of
the present mining district. The rich lead on this
(Williams') Creek, hitherto only found in Steel and
Co.'s and a few other claims near the town, has at last
been " struck" at a point on the right bank of the
creek, about a mile above where the lead was lost. In
addition to this the lead has also been found at two
points between and in a straight line with the places
above mentioned, showing almost conclusively that the
lead runs the entire distance, and most probably beyond,
as far as the Bald Mountain, from which the creek
takes its rise, a distance of about three miles and a half.
The importance of this discovery can hardly be over-
estimated. I believe most firmly that in a month's time
gold will be taken out of this creek to the value of at
least £20,000 per diem. Such is the confidence men now
have. in Williams' Creek lead that claims in a line with
those lately discovered are selling as high as £BOO,
though unprospected. On Antler Creek the claims are
being rapidly opened and worked with great success. A
great many new creeks, most of them supposed to be rich,
have been discovered since the date of my last report.
I would submit that, as a gold-field,.the prospects of the
country could hardly be better. Many old miners have
stated to me as their belief that British Columbia will
surpass both Australia and California. On the other hand
, regret to report that the great scarcity, and con-
sequent high prices of provisions, is, for the present,
not only crippling every man in the mines, but
forcing very many to return. I fear that few will be able
to pass the winter in Cariboo this year for want of pro-
visions. The present rate of supply by no means equals
the demand, and I am at a loss to conceive how any
surplus stock can be laid in for winter use. By far the
majority of the claims on this creek are in the bank,
and, could provisions by any means be brought up,
claims would be worked (tunnel) all the year round,
and many men unsuccessful during the summer could
then get employment during the winter, months. There
is a report up here that merchants do not wish to send
UP supplies because as yet no money has been taken out
to pay for them. I can hardly believe that an idea so
absurd can have had any weight either with the British
Columbia or Victoria merchants. Not one sack of flour
has been sold in the district this season :without cash
payment. I have the honour to be, Sir, your obedient
servant. 'T. Erimar.'

DIOCESE OF ExmEn.--The Bishop of Exeter has
given notice that after Christmas next ensuing graduates
will be required to give six months' notice of their
intention to present themselves as candidates for deacons'
orders, except such as can produce a certificate of their
having resided with credit for three terms, or two at the
least, at one of the theological colleges of Exeter, Wells,

Bishop intends to hold his next general ordination in the
Cathedral, Exeter, on Trinity Sunday.

The Steele says: 'M. Petruecelli della Gattina,

articles.title: IHE RIOTS AT BIRKIVII-PAD.
articles.text:
IHE RIOTS AT BIRKIVII-PAD.

With reference to the recent disturbances at Eirken-
head, we ,haTe been requested to bring before the notice
Df our readers the following circular, which was ad-
iressed to the Lords-Lieutenant of counties in England,
Wales, and Scotland, on the 7th June, 1861 :
'WAR OFFICE, 7th June, 1861.

Having observed that in several -instances volunteer
corps have assembled under arms for various purposes
unconnected with drill, parade, or rifle practice, I think
it right to inform you that no such assemblies ought. to
take place, exceptwith the approval of the lord-lieutenant,
and that if the number of volunteers who propose to be
present should exceed the strength of one battalion,
previous application must be made to the Sect etary of
State for War for his sanction, in accordance with the
circular memorandum of ihe 6th June, 1860.
'I have also le irnt that in some cases volunteer corps
have been called out in aid of the civil power on the
occurrence of local disturbances, and I have therefore to
point out to you that as the volunteer force is not in-
tended to be employed in this manner, it is inexpedient
to assemble it on any such occasion.
'I desire farther to draw your attention to the impro-
priety of the presence of any armed body at Parliamen-
tary or municipal elections, and to request that you will
give directions to the commanding officers of all volun-
teer corps, within the county under your charge, not to
assemble their corps for drill or any other purpose,
between the issue of a wri; and the termination of the
election in any county or borough in the neighbourhood
of their head-quarters, or during the progress of any
municipal election in any town, to which they may
belong.
I. have, &c.,
(Signed) HERBERT.'

articles.title: BRUTAL .3IUR.DER OF A GIRL.
articles.text:
BRUTAL .3IUR.DER OF A GIRL.

HEEEFORn, Tuesday.

Last night, Mary Corbett, a girl between 16 and 17
years of age, in the service of Mr. Skerrett, farmer, of
Ullinswick, in this county, was sent by her mistress to a
shop at some distance to purchase sonic candles. As she
did not return during the night, a search 'as set on foot
by the parish constable and others, which resulted in the
finding of the body in an orchard. Marks were first
discovered near the side of the turnpike road, along
which the girl would have to Rau, and it appeared as it
two or three persons had ,been there engaged in a
struggle: From this spot footmarks were somewhat
indistinctly traced across some fields into an orchard,
where they discovered the body of the poor girl in such
a state underneath a tree as to lead to the conclusion
that her person lied been violated. Her neck bore
marks as it she had been strangled, the ribbon of her
bonnet, which was on, having been pressed into the skin
of her neck, while her mouth was lull of blood. The
authorities were at once informed of the sad event, and
the Herefordshire constabulary force having been put
into operation, two men, named George Hope and Wm.
Wenner, one of whom is a returned convict, were at
once suspected a being connected in some way with
the offence. The body was removed to the Prince of'
Wales public-house, where Mr. N. Lanwerne, the coroner
for this division of the county, will hold an inquest on
Thursday next. The men suspected had been drinking
at a public-house in the neighbourhood.

The wheat and corn crops of the North-Westem

AN UNFEELING Warn.—At the inquest upon the
body of a man named Soames, who committed suicide
at Boxley (from fear, it was supposed, of some proceed-
ings which had been instituted against him by his wife),
it was stated that the wife discovered her husband
hanging shortly after he committed the fatal deed; she
made no statement whatever in the matter, excepting to
tell her children to say nothing about it, in which, how-
ever, she was not implicitly obeyed, for the son, on
meeting a person named Parker, told him of the circum-
stance, and the man broceeded to the cottage at once,
and cut Soames down, when, though quite dead, his
body w.as still warm. The coroner severely reprimanded
the wife for her unwomanly and unfeeling conduct in
the case.-3faidstone Jou,tal.'

ACCIDENT IN LEITH ITARDOUR..—AH accident whrch
nearly proved fatal took plaee on Saturday. A merchant,
having happened to lose his way in North Leith, wan-
dered down a narrow, lane leading from Coburg-street
to the harbour, and not being aware that he was near
the water, he walked over the quay. His cries for help
were heard by Constable Elriek, who was on duty in the
neighbourhood, and others and they hastened to his
assistance. The constable in his eager desire to save the
gentleman fell into the wate), and both had to struggle
for their lives. It being about haaf-tider a mint bank
near was uncovered, and it they succeeded in reaching.
Here they were compelled to remain till more assistance
was procured, and ultimately they were drawn out with
a rope in a sad condition from the water and mud. The
gentleman did not receive any cut or bruise, but the con-
stable sustained a severe injury on one of his legs, which
has rendered him unfit for his duty since the accident.

SIR RICHARD MAINE AND THE RIGHT OF MEET-
ING.—Taking the text of the edict issued by the chef de
service, as he would be termed' in Paris, it seems to be
very premature to conclude that all speeches, lectures,
preaehings, and meetings in Hyde Park are prohibited
by the authorities. Indeed, the form of prohibition
strikes us as being either in excess or deficiency. It
either forbids too much or too little. We cannot quite
understand the source and authority of the prohibition.
Either the Ranger of the Park or the Commissioner of
Works is entrusted with the custody of the park, and
from him should have issued the special directions of
what should or should not be done in the park. With
the Commissioners of Police, under the Home Office,
rests the duty of preserving the peace, and Sir Richard
Mayne is concerned, not m ith the moral, but only with
material interests. Crowds, not the causes of crowds,
are under the cognizance of the police. With the Home
Secretary, if with anybody, rests the duty of pronounc-
ing what sort of meeting is, by its subject matter, likely
to endanger the public safety. But Sir Richard Mayne
seems to have undertaken the duties of the ranger,
Board of Works, and the Home-office all at once, and
to have administered none of them Successfully. As we
read his proclamation, it does not forbid all meetings
and speeches, but only such meetings as are held 'for
the purpose of delivering and hearing speeches, and for
the public discussion of popular and exciting topics.' If
any speaker or preacher chooses to say that his oration
or assembly is not connected with any popular or ex-
citing topic, is he to be permitted to speak? Or is the
chief officer to be the judge of what is or is not popular
and exciting ?—Saturday .Review:

articles.title: WORKING HEN'S COLLEGE.
articles.text:
THE WORKING HEN'S COLLEGE.

On Monday evening the forthcoming session of the
Working Men's College, in Great Ormond-street, was in-
augurated by an address from the Principal, the Uev.
Frederick D. Maurice. The hall was crowded oy the
students and their friends. ,_ _ _ _ _ _

The Rev. Principal commenced his address by remark-
ing that they were now beginning the eighth session of •
the college, as it had been established in the year 1854.
lie was glad to see so large a gathering for the purpose
of celebrating the beginning of another year. Several
circumstances Jiad happened in the course of the year
which had given him considerable encouragement. He
was especi,dly glad of the sv.deess which had attended
the classes during the vacation, when the teachers had
been absent from London. The result showed that the
stadents themselves were beginning to understand how
to manage the classes. That circumstance gave him
great satisfaction, and the more so when he recol-
lected that they were deprived of the valuable
services of Mr. Ruskin. Mr. Maurice then went on
to describe the kind of work done in the college,
remarking that the instruction given was not of
a superficial description. The teachers had not
cared to produce showy results; they wanted to send
men into the world able to do good substantial work.
In so far as the college showed the fruit of training
men to be good and brace citizens, it would be success-
ful in securing its object. If any other test of success
than that was required, the teachers would be obliged at
once to decline it. They would say they could not do
it. Every teacher would tell his students that he would
degrade them by attempting to make them showmen, or
by giving them something merely to sell in the market.
They wanted to make the students good sound men, and
anything less than that was insignificant. Mr. Maurice
then referred to the volunteer movement in connexion
with the college, observing that, although it might in
some degree interfere with the ordinary studies, yet the
general result would be beneficial. Passing from this
topic, he observed that it gave him, great satisfaction to
know- that the students were becoming teachers of one
another. Mr. Maurice then glanced at the history of
the college, and said there were many matters which led
lidm to look with something of solemnity on the begin-
ning of another session. • Having stated that he would
conduct the Bible classes on Wednesday evenings, he
concluded a brief address by giving certificates of pro-
ficiency to several students.
• 141 r. Thomas Hughes then delivered a short address.
lie had, he said, found the social life of the college
valuable to him in many respects. He had gained much
ne insight from his connection with it. The great
object of the college was to make the stud, nts upright,
righteous, and brave citizens of their country. The
importance of that great object had been more brought
home to him in his connection with the college than in
his connection with any other educational establish-
ment. He wished that side of education was more pro-
minently kept in view in other colleges. Al r. Hughes
having expressed his pleasure at the efforts which were
being made by the students of the college .to spread
education in the eastern part of London, said he was
extremely glad that Mr. Maurice had recogni,ed the
importance of the. volunteer movement. He (the
at eaker) had strong convictions that the proper way of
defendieg a country was by citizen soldiers.
The proceedings terminated in the customary manner.

articles.title: LOVE AND SUICIDE.
articles.text:
LOVE AND SUICIDE.

An inquest has been held-at the Reservoir Inn, Osier-
street, Birmingham, before Dr. Birt Davies, on the
be ly of James Ebenezer Boon. The only witness ex-
amined was W. H. Boon, jun., of 66, Grant-street, clerk,
who said that the deceased was his brother. He wds
18 years of age, and was also a clerk. Witness last saw
him alive on Thursday morning at about half-past eight
at 66, Grant-street, where he also resided. They had break-
fast together, and deceased afterwards went to business.
Witness had reason to know that he returned to dinner,
but he was not seen again at his own house after that
time. Witness and his parents suspected that deceased
had drowned himself from a letter which he hAd written•
to a young lady on Thursday night. The letter was in
the handwriting of the deceased. The reservoir was drag-
ged on Saturday morning by witness and two police-
men, and the body was found at the spot indicated in
deceased's letter, namely, on the west side of the reser-
voir. He was quite dead and cold, and appeared to
have been in the water for some time. Deceased had
appeared to have a good deal on his mind for the last
fortnight or three weeks. He had complained of severe
pains in his bead, and had hardly ever answered other-
wise than with a nod of the head when spoken to. On
Thursday, when asked by his mother about some
business he had been transacting, and when told to
speak out,' he said, Oh, mother, don't bother me; I
cannot tell if I do.' Deceased had been paying his
addresses to the young lady to whom he wrote the
letter before referred to ; but their parents wished
to keep them apart for a couple of years, on ac-
count of their youth. The folio ing is a copy
of the letter, the name and address of the young
lady, however, being omitted: 2, Waterloo-
street, Birmingham, Oct. 16, 1862.—My dear, precious,
darling Lizzie, &c:, &c., &c., &c., &c., &e. As this is
the last letter I shall ever send you, please bear with
me an& comply, with my last request; but first let me
explain the object of my writing to you. You know
that for five years and upwards I have loved with.a
worshipping love. I have adored you—looked to you
as my 'pole star,' my guiding and guardian angel—
have seen in you, and you alone, that spark that caused
me to love you more than my parents nay, even mole
than God Himself. And, believe me, I die uttering a
blessing upon you. When I am out of the way
you will be happy again. God knows it is time
I were, but to-night—" I have done the deed! Didot
thou not hear a noise ? " I know this act will cause
some consternation, but that I cannot help. Now,
firstly, I want you to break the fact to "my mother."
for before the letter reaches you James will be dead,
dead, and tell her that I shall be found in that Deep
Bay where the little:bridge is in the (our) " retreat"
(Reservoir.) Secondly, that I may be buried with your
locket over my heart where it has been so long, and let
the withering curse of God and angels, men and devils,
restupon, and my " niarrowless bones" for ever encircle,
him or her who dares to remove it! Thirdly and lastly,
that you will forget the foul specimen of humanity that
has led you astray, and return to the embraces of your
mother from whom.. I took you ; and now may God and
angels ever keep you from the sins of this wicked world
is the prayer of him whose onlY fault was "loving you
too well"! Adieu ! adieu! adieu!—Sames E. BOON.'
No further evidence was adduced, and the jury, after a
brief consultation, returned a verdict to tbe effect that
deceased drowned himself while in a state of insanity.

SUSPECTED INCENDIARY FIRE AT UPTON, CHESHIRE.
—On the 20th five Stacks of valuable farm produce were
destroyed by fire at the Snow-park farm, near the vil-
lage of Upton, Cheshire, occupied by Mr. James Kerr,
There were 25 large stacks of produce about the premises,
but at such distances apart as to prevent the spread of
the conflagration. The fire is believed to have been the
work of an incendiary, as the hay was in excellent con-
dition, and this conclusion is strengthened by the fact
that on the night of the Birkenhead riots .a fire occurred
at a farm at Greasby, after the, discharge of some Irish
labourers.

articles.text:
FEDERAL ROMANCE.

Writing to 'gr. Lincoln's Government after the battle
of the 14th of last month, the Federal General stated
that the rebel' army was totally demoralised' and
utterly 'routed.' Subsequently a New York telegram
informs us that:—

• ••.••••. •
'The battle was rerewed on the 17th by the Con-
federates with great vigour, lasting till four o'clock in
the afternoon, when the Confederates retired leaving the
Confederate General Longstreet and part of his division
prisoners.!
This telegram itself is an illustration of the saying,
particularly applicable to American news, that we should
never believe more than half of what we hear. Part
of it is true ; but that is only the first part. The battle was
renewed with great vigour by the army which M'Clellan
had described as demoralised and routed—an extra-
ordinary army! General Longstreet and his division
were captured by General Hooker—who commanded a
division on the Federal side—with a hook.

pARTS Permanent Universal Exhi-
TO BE OPENED IN 1863.
For many years National Exhibitions have beeen held
in various cities, with universal success in stimulating
industry and developing trade between the countries
represented by the Exhibitions.
The central position of Paris, and the vast nnmber of
visitors passing through the city every year, have sug-
gested there the establishment thare of a Permanent
Exhibition: where specimens of the manufactures and
products of every country will be collected together in
one spacious building, in order that dealers and con-
sumers from all parts of the world may see them, and
base their orders upon the quality and cost of the arti-
cles exhi ited.
The project has met with the entire approval of the
Emperor Napoleon 111. and a special license has been
granted by the Ministers of Finance and Commerce for
admission to the Permanent Universal Exhibition,
during the entire period that it is open, of all Foreign
Products, Free of Duty, with liberty to re-export them
without payment of duties or to sell them on the spot,
on paying the duties imposed by the new International
Tariff.
The whole of the capital, amounting to £600,000, has
been subscribed in France, and the Palace (now in
course of construction) will be opened early in the sum-
mer of 1863.
The amount of space allotted to France and several
other continental countries has already been taken up.
A dmission will be gratuitous on at least five days of
the week.
The British Exhibitors will be reyresented by a Com-
mittee of twenty members, who, with those appointed by
other countries will form a General Committee, to
organise the distribution of space, and frame a code of
rules for general observance; and agencies will be esta-
blished in Paris to receive orders.
All products and manufactures will be classified, so
that those of the same nature from different countries,
being placed in juxta-position, may be easily compared.
Two rates of rental (payable annually in advance)
will be charged, the space being taken for six years.
The first rate (£2 per square metre per annum) will
apply to all products and manufactures.
Tile second rate (£1 per square metre per annum)
will apply to wall surface for advertisements.
N.B.—Five square metres are equal to six square
yards.
Drawings of the Building can be seen at the principal
Railway Stations and Exchanges in London and the
Country; in the Refreshment-rooms of the present
London Exhibition, and at the Offices of Messrs. J.
STUDDY LEIGH &CG., 27. Ltadenhall-street, London.
Agents for Great Britain, l reland, and the Colonies, from
whom forms of agreement and full information may be
obtained.

Baarimit ii onsING MEN: It is with a feeling of reluc-
tance that we, the London 0, erative Ropemakers, ven-
ture to draw your attention to our present position,
knowing as we do the great depression of trade in almost
every department of manufacture, and yet we f.-el
encouraged to lay our case before you, soliciting your
sympathy and aid, by the conviction that we are well
known by the London trades, and to many trades in the
country, for our willingness to assist thers in times of
difficulty. We will therefore simply state our case to
you, hoping that you will deem it worthy of your kind
consideration.
On the 11th of last June one of our employers offered
a reduction of sevenpence per day, or three and six-
pence per week, from our wages, and we, having a well
organised trace society, could not submit to any reduc-
tion of wages,' recognising as fair workmen should do
that a lair days work is entitled to a fair day's pay, and
having enjoyed the present rate of wages tor the last
seven years, and there being no reasonable plea given
why such reduction should take place.
Having sent depu, ations to the employers to reason
the matter with them, and used every effort to pre-
vent a strike, but finding that the emptoyers were
determined if possible to effect a general reduction of
wages throughout the trade, there was no other course
ieft us but to withdraw the whole of the journeymen
from the firm, viz.—Messrs. J. and li. Baker, Bermond-
sey, this is the eighth week of the strike, and our
'nen are film and in good spirits, being convinced of the
Yastness of their claims and ultimate success, for al-
though the firm has resorted to all kinds of misrepre-
qentation to obtain men their shop is still empty. for as
last as the men come up from the country through their
sgents and advertisements in the country local papers,
they (the men) after having the question of dispute
f xplained to them, leave their work, and by our assis-
tance leave London again, which creates a large expense
over the actual cost of keeping our own members on
strike. We have expended over £l5O, a large sum for
only one firm, but then we are fighting for the whole
trade, for some of the other employers have already
given notice to their men, that as soon as Messr. Baker
and Brothers get supplied with men at thd reductien
that they will give no more for their work than the
Messrs Baker's, and if we are compelled to submit to
this reduction we shall lose £1,500 per year in wages
(then leaving a la, ge surplus of men out of work), a sum
yon will admit worth-struggling for.
Having thus briefly stared our present position we
earnestly appeal to the sympathy of our fellow workmen
in other trades. soliciting their assistance to enable us to
defend successfully our right of wages and t ade against
these grasping employers. In appealing to our fellow
working men, we may say that we have had always a
willing heart and ready hand to assist other trades
placed in similar cirtinmscances ; indeed, since 1853 there
has not been a question affecting the interest of the
-working classes, or a dispute in any other trade, but
what we have supported and sustained to our utmost
ability. We therefore make this appeal with some
~egree of confidene, that you will rdadily respond to us
ia our present diffieulties, and show to the employing
:lasses that there is a spirit of union aud brotherhood
amongst the working men of England, that will enable
them to rally round their fellow but oppressed brother
Workmen.
We beg to remain yours very respectfully, on behalf of
the trade. Thomas Hay, Charles Howe, William Matthews,
Charles Terdre, R.,bert Still, committee; Richard Bur-
ridge, treasurer; Daniel smith, seer, tary.
